Sports.title: Anthony Joshua vs Kristian Prenga RECAP: AJ WINS in second round after dramatic opener saw him DROPPED to the canvas
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua up the script. And for a moment on Saturday night in Jeddah, it looked as though another shock was unfolding as the British heavyweight was dropped twice and wrestled to the canvas in a chaotic opening round.

But Joshua dug deep, weathered the storm and, after finding another gear in the second, produced a devastating combination that flattened Albanian heavyweight Kristian Prenga, leaving the 35-year-old sprawled on his back and bringing a dramatic end to a fight that had threatened to derail his comeback before it had even begun.

They're the words of Charlotte Daly, our reporter who was out in Saudi Arabia to watch this palpitating event. Catch the rest of her words below.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's bouts are fights in name only - their opponents are merely useful punchbags who'd be unlikely to get work as their sparring partners: JEFF POWELL MBE
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's bouts are fights in name only - their opponents are merely useful punchbags who'd be unlikely to get work as their sparring partners: JEFF POWELL MBE

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

It will be possible to be at ringside to watch Tyson Fury box in Thailand this Friday evening and then attend Anthony Joshua’s fight in Saudi Arabia on Saturday night.

The Gypsy King will prove that by flying from Bangkok to Jeddah soon after his encounter with the veteran Mariusz Wach in time to see AJ take on somebody called Kristian Prenga.

It is safe to presume that precious few, if any, of their respective thousands of fans will join Fury on that journey or pitch up at either occasion. And not only because many of them will have sacrificed a year or two’s wages, perhaps their mortgages, maybe their marriages on England’s ill-fated World Cup expedition.

Even the rich boys on tour are likely to jib at forking out another small fortune to attend distant events which are fights in name only. Joshua’s flight booking gives the game away, as does the choice of venues. No capital cities this time. Fury goes through the motions in the notorious Thai beach resort of Pattaya. Joshua at Saudi Arabia’s Jeddah-on-sea.

Of course these are by way of preparation for them fighting each other in that forever awaited box-office boomer later this year. But to be honest these match-ups are not so much warm-ups as water-treaders. These opponents would be unlikely to get work as their sparring partners.

Describing Poland’s Mariusz Wach as a ring veteran is actually an understatement of his decline since he went into a world heavyweight title fight against Wladimir Klitschko as 27-0 unbeaten challenger. He not only lost that night in Germany 14 years ago but failed a drugs test which interrupted for two years his descent into today’s 39 wins, 13 defeats record.

Anthony Joshua is back in action on Saturday when he faces Kristian Prenga in Saudi Arabia

Tyson Fury is fighting Mariusz Wach in Bangkok on Friday as he prepares to secure a long-awaited bout with Joshua

The longer he drags on, as he approaches his 46th birthday, the more he becomes a useful punch-bag, given his masochistic capacity to absorb punches for several rounds. A painful service he has provided to a number of British heavyweights, Dillian Whyte, Frazer Clarke and Hughie Fury among them. This is so patently a mismatch that it is not being televised anywhere in the world, but being saved by Netflix to help promote Fury v Joshua when that finally comes around,

Two years ago Wach was flattened in as many rounds by our world heavyweight champion-in-waiting Moses Itauma. That mercifully swift ending made for more comfortable viewing than some of the pointless beatings he has taken down the years. Make it quick, Tyson.

Kristian Prenga is a virtually unknown entity outside his native Albania. He has passed almost equally unnoticed on undercards mostly around New York, New Jersey, Philadelphia and across the Canadian border since he emigrated to the US.

At least he is ten years younger than Wach and has 20 knock-out wins on his record against one points defeat. Not that you are likely to recognise any of the names on that dance card. Try Joey Dawejko, Aldo Callendar, Tim Chemelli, Willie Jake Jr, or the only man to beat him Giovanni Auriemma. Me neither. Most of them appear to have other jobs, such as barmen, bouncers or cab drivers.

Prenga, a pleasant enough feller, made the right noises at his London press conference: ‘A J and his team have made a mistake. They’ve overlooked my knock-out record. They’ve forgotten that he can no longer take a big punch like mine. Get ready for the world-wide shock which will change my life forever.’

He seems not to have noted that AJ is a former Olympic gold medallist and two-time world heavyweight champion. Nor that he is stepping into an altogether higher realm. Nor that Joshua is highly motivated emotionally by this being his first fight since his two close friends and team members were killed in a car crash in Africa which he was lucky to survive. ‘This is for them,’ he says. Get it done early, AJ. before he has a chance to land.

Fury is set to fly from Bangkok to Saudi Arabia to watch Joshua a day after his own fight

Then you can invite Fury to join you in the ring – ‘but don’t forget Tyson I’m the landlord for this one’ – so they can start the big sell.

November is the likely month for Fury v Joshua 1. Wembley the stadium of choice but only if Brent Council agree to lift their usual 11 pm curfew and permit it to be transmitted live to the American TV audience at somewhere between 2 am and 4 am London Sunday time.

So enormous will be the difference from this weekend that Fury is about to entertain no more than a thousand or so locals in a small, screened-off hall. He is donating the revenue from those tickets to good causes in Thailand, of which he has become fond as a training camp. It will be charity all-round. What with Wach and Prenga picking up probably the biggest purses of their lives for their roles as fall guys. But what if the inconceivable did happen?

Not only would the gigantic pay-days of Fury’s and Joshua’s last hurrah go down the drain but at least one or maybe both their careers would be terminated.

Don’t dare mention it.

*Fury v Wach this Friday night will be for private screening only.

*Joshua v Prenga will be televised live on DAZN pay-per-view this Saturday night

*Fury v Joshua is expected to be televised live to Netflix subscribers in the early hours one Sunday morning in November

Sports.title: Spence Jr vs Tszyu card rocked for a second time as another major fight collapses - after US star was denied visa by Albanese government
Sports.content:
Tim Tszyu and Errol Spence Jr will fittingly slug it out at exactly the same weight in an intriguing blockbuster where no one can predict the outcome.

Tszyu (27-3, 18KOs) and Spence (28-1, 22KOs) both hit the scales at 159 pounds (72.1kg) at Saturday's weigh-in, as Australia's home hope places his career on the line in Sydney.

'A lifetime of work and I thank you, Australia, each and every one of you guys. Let's do it,' Tszyu said ahead of the boom-or-bust showdown at Afterpay Arena on Sunday.

'Let's do it for this country, man.'

After three shattering world-title defeats in the USA and defending his family's incredible 55-0 unbeaten record in Australia, the former WBO world super-welterweight champion knows his career could be over if he loses again.

But the 31-year-old isn't entertaining any such prospect.

'Look, why would I go into a fight if I think I'm going to lose? It doesn't work like that,' Tszyu said.

'We're all warriors. We've got something in here (our head) that makes us tick.'

Errol Spence Jr (left) and Tim Tszyu (right) will slug it out at exactly the same weight

The pair will face off at Afterpay Arena, Sydney, on Sunday

Tszyu (pictured) knows his career could be over if he loses again during Sunday's bout

With the American superstar's only ever loss coming against undefeated pound-for-pound legend Terence Crawford, Spence is also risking tarnishing one of boxing's great legacies.

'Pressure is something you create in your mind. It's a mentality. I don't have any pressure on me,' Spence said.

'Pressure is people not having food to eat. That's pressure. This ain't no pressure. This ain't going to make me as a guy, fighting another man.

'I thank everybody for coming out, and there's nothing more to say. It's fight time. I'm ready to go.'

While Tszyu and Spence are ready to punch on in one of the biggest bouts in Australian boxing history, the luckless Liam Wilson has been dealt another cruel blow, with his scheduled world title eliminator against Stephen Fulton cancelled after the American failed to make weight.

In farcical scenes, Fulton hit the scales at 139.5 pounds on Saturday, almost 10 pounds more than the two-division world champ was originally supposed to fight Wilson at in Sydney.

Fulton and Wilson were supposed to square off at the super-featherweight of 130 pounds before officials on Friday raised the weight to 133 pounds for the feature bout on the Tszyu-Spence card.

Wilson had happily agreed to the late allowance, saying he was desperate to earn another world title shot with a victory over the former unified super-bantamweight world champion and ex-WBC featherweight belt holder.

US boxer Stephen Fulton badly missed weight by 6.5lbs or nearly 3kg before his scheduled fight with Aussie boxer Liam Wilson was cancelled on Saturday morning

Spence (pictured) is also risking tarnishing one of boxing's great legacies after his only ever loss coming against undefeated pound-for-pound legend Terence Crawford

But Team Fulton is now being accused by Wilson's camp of never intending to fight on Sunday.

'This feels like a stitch up,' Wilson's manager and Tszyu's long-time ex-agent Glenn Jennings said.

'If you are serious and you sign a contract at 133, there is an expectation that you will deliver.

'It is not only unacceptable, it is a blight on the sport. This is professional, there is nowhere to go for this bloke now.'

Wilson was devastated at missing his potentially life-changing opportunity.

'I put my heart and soul into this sport. I train very hard,' the 30-year-old Queenslander said.

'It's uncontrollable for me. I did everything correct on my end.'

Undefeated Olympian Paulo Aokuso will move to the main card, taking on Luis Tejeda from the Dominican Republic in a light-heavyweight bout.

Wilson's fight is the second co-main event to be cancelled this week after Fulton's fellow American Jermall Charlo was denied a visa to face rising Australian Koen Mazoudier.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua gives up 10lbs to Kristian Prenga as he bids to avoid shock defeat in return to the ring after devastating loss of his two friends in car crash
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua gives up 10lbs to Kristian Prenga as he bids to avoid shock defeat in return to the ring after devastating loss of his two friends in car crash

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Anthony Joshua will head into his comeback bout carrying more weight than he did for his last outing after tipping the scales at 251lb ahead of Saturday night's clash with Kristian Prenga in Jeddah.

The two-time heavyweight world champion has added 7.6lb since stopping Jake Paul in December, when he weighed in at 243.4lb.

Prenga, meanwhile, came in even heavier at 261.4lb, giving the unbeaten Albanian a weight advantage of 10.4lb over Joshua.

Despite the increase, Joshua is still short of the biggest weight of his professional career. That came in April 2023, when he weighed 255.4lb before outpointing Jermaine Franklin.

Joshua's return comes less than a year after his career was thrown into uncertainty following the devastating car crash that claimed the lives of two of his closest friends and members of his inner circle.

AJ has since vowed to honour their memory by continuing the work they had planned together, supporting their loved ones financially and using his career to build the future they had all spoken about.

Anthony Joshua has weighted in at 251lbs ahead of Saturday night's clash with Kristian Prenga

Now, in Jeddah, Joshua finally steps back between the ropes.

Standing opposite him is Albanian heavyweight Kristian Prenga, a dangerous puncher whose record suggests he should not be overlooked.

Twenty of Prenga's victories have come inside the distance, with just one defeat on his professional record, but those numbers come with an important caveat.

The 35-year-old has never faced an opponent remotely comparable to Joshua. While Prenga possesses genuine knockout power, Saturday represents a monumental leap in class against a man who has shared the ring with the likes of Oleksandr Usyk, Daniel Dubois, Joseph Parker, Andy Ruiz Jr, Wladimir Klitschko and Alexander Povetkin.

Joshua has refused to entertain talk of what comes next, insisting throughout fight week that his full attention remains on Prenga. Yet there is little escaping the significance of what victory would mean.

The contest has widely been viewed as the perfect opportunity for Joshua to build momentum before finally landing the long-awaited showdown with Tyson Fury, a fight British boxing fans have spent the best part of a decade demanding.

Fury did his part on Friday evening by returning to action with victory over Mariusz Wach in Pattaya, Thailand.

The expectation had been that Fury would fly directly from Thailand to Saudi Arabia and enter the ring after Joshua's fight for the first official face-off between the pair, setting the stage for one of the richest fights in boxing history.

Joshua is seeking to avoid upset in his first fight since losing his two friends in a car crash

However, those plans now appear to have hit a stumbling block. Fury suggested prior to his victory that he may instead return home to spend time with his family, casting doubt over whether the highly anticipated confrontation in Jeddah will now take place.

For Joshua, though, those discussions remain irrelevant unless he gets through Saturday night safely.

He made that point emphatically during Thursday's press conference, insisting there is no point talking about conquering the heavyweight division – or finally facing Fury – if he cannot first overcome the man standing across the ring from him.

Everything beyond Prenga can wait. 'The comeback' starts here.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury stops Mariusz Wach inside seven rounds in Thailand... as Saudi organisers try to rush him to Jeddah for Anthony Joshua's return ahead of proposed British megafight
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury took care of business with the minimum of fuss as he dispatched Mariusz Wach in a low-key contest in Thailand on Friday night - before attention quickly shifted to what is next.

Daily Mail Sport understands the former heavyweight world champion is expected to board a flight to Jeddah after the victory, with Saudi organisers Sela arranging travel in the hope Fury will be in attendance for Anthony Joshua's return against Kristian Prenga on Saturday night.

Fury stopped Wach inside seven rounds of a schedule 10 to emerge victorious on Friday evening, with the Polish fighter retiring on his stool.

The fight - not carried by any major broadcaster - is understood to have been one-sided, with Fury connecting with five uppercuts in a row in the fifth round.

Fury was always expected to come through unscathed against Wach, ranked outside the world's top 200, in what was widely viewed as a stay-busy fight ahead of the biggest assignment of his comeback.

Tyson Fury emerges for the untelevised bout in Pattaya, Thailand

Fury dispatched Wach inside seven rounds in a dominant display

The contest itself attracted little attention compared to a usual Fury fight week but it served its purpose by allowing Fury to continue building momentum before his proposed showdown with Joshua later this year.

The event also raised funds for the Father Ray Foundation, with all the gate receipts from a 1,500 crowd donated to the Pattaya-based charity, which has spent more than 40 years supporting orphans, children with disabilities and underprivileged young people across Thailand.

The focus now turns to whether the Gypsy King will make the trip to Saudi Arabia.

Daily Mail Sport understands Sela have made arrangements for Fury to fly directly from Thailand to Jeddah, where Joshua returns to action on Saturday in his first fight since the devastating car crash that claimed the lives of two friends and members of his close team.

Joshua has described the tragedy as the toughest period of his life and has vowed to continue the work and ambitions of those he lost, while also pledging long-term financial support to their families. His return against Prenga therefore represents far more than simply another outing inside the ring.

Whether Fury and Joshua come face-to-face this weekend, however, remains uncertain.

Fury and Wach were clashing ahead of Fury's proposed megafight with Anthony Joshua

Fury takes the plaudits at the end of the bout, which

... and celebrates in the ring having extended his career record to 36 wins from 39 fights

Fury has insisted in recent interviews that he had no plans to attend the event, despite speculation gathering throughout fight week that he would make the journey after boxing in Thailand.

One possible explanation is what unfolded following Fury's victory over Arslanbek Makhmudov earlier this year.

Joshua, who had been ringside, opted against climbing into the ring afterwards as the contract hadn’t been officially signed, meaning the much-anticipated first face-off between Britain's two biggest heavyweight stars never materialised.

Fury may now be taking a similar approach, choosing not to hand Joshua the moment after his own comeback, despite the paperwork being done.

Even so, there remains hope behind the scenes that the pair will finally share a stage should Joshua come through safely against Prenga.

Sports.title: What McLaren thought of Piastri's explosive F1 Hungarian GP radio outburst
Sports.content:
McLaren team principal Andrea Stella has explained the Formula 1 squad's thinking behind its second pitstop sequence in the Hungarian Grand Prix amid frustration from Oscar Piastri over his run-in with backmarker Carlos Sainz.

In their quest to deliver a first grand prix win of the season, both Piastri and team-mate Lando Norris showed frustration in the heat of the moment, belying the sense of urgency for the reigning world champions to gain a foothold in the 2026 campaign.

Early season dominator Mercedes had been challenged by a resurgent Ferrari and its innovative, heavily upgraded car. But last year's dominant team had started 2026 on the back foot, so when a significant floor upgrade finally appeared to put McLaren in the mix, neither Norris nor Piastri needed any further encouragement to put it to good use.

Having done the heavy lifting by putting the MCL40 on pole, Norris couldn't afford any slip-ups on lap 1, but did exactly that by drifting offline through the dust in Turn 2. Having had a disappointing qualifying session, Piastri benefitted from penalties to take third on the grid and then swooped past Norris into the lead.

With overtaking extremely difficult without a tyre offset, that was Norris' afternoon ruined. And trying as he might to pressure Piastri into a mistake, Norris soon started hinting at how much quicker he could go in clear air. The situation continued until the second stint, when Norris was requested to be called in first.

"We can't," race engineer Will Joseph said. The usual etiquette is that the leading car gets pitstop priority and in this case Piastri had earned that right by passing Norris fair and square on lap one.

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

So when on lap 34 Hamilton, who had already pitted several laps earlier, was 25 seconds behind the leader and closing, the thinking at McLaren was that it needed to cover off the Ferrari as its main threat.

"When Hamilton pits, he is in condition to undercut the two McLarens, so we needed to respond," Stella explained. "Oscar was in the lead, and we thought that he was the right car to stop for that."

Piastri emerged ahead by four seconds, leaving Norris a gap to slot into as well. But through a combination of Piastri being baulked by Williams driver Sainz and Norris finding extra pace in clear air, Norris made a rare overcut work to take the lead, much to Piastri's chagrin.

"Get out of the f****** way you idiot, oh my god," Piastri raged at Sainz, before redirecting some of that frustration towards his own team when he saw his chance to win the race evaporate.

"Nice of you guys to factor that one in by the way, thanks," he said sarcastically.

Afterwards Piastri conceded that McLaren had no other choice but to pit him when he did, and that in the heat of the moment his racing driver brain had taken over from reason, hoping McLaren could somehow rectify the injustice.

"When Lando came out ahead, I knew I had no pace to go and attack him, so I knew my chances of winning the race were done from there," Piastri acknowledged. "I felt maybe the team could have not pitted Lando if it was a two-car race, but I know it's not a two-car race. They can't just not box Lando because of something out of his control and out of my control.

Oscar Piastri retired from the race with a late gearbox failure. Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

"From that side of things, it's fine. I was just very, very pissed off in the moment about what happened. Without getting crashed into, I would have been ahead of Lando still."

That's also how team principal Stella saw it, and he revealed that Piastri had explained his team radio comments afterwards.

"Immediately after the race, Oscar clarified that his comment was a comment in anger," Stella said when asked by Autosport for comment.

"There were a couple of unfortunate episodes. Obviously, the most important is the fact that Oscar had a collision with a backmarker. And at the same time, once Lando was released, then his pace was simply mega. I think he found half a second per lap. And this pace meant that Lando could be ahead of Oscar."

He added: "I think Oscar understood it immediately. It's absolutely understandable that when you lead the race for almost half [of it], and then you see yourself losing the lead because of an episode with a backmarker, then you may have a moment and make a comment in anger, but there's absolutely no problem."

By the same token, McLaren also couldn't do much for the intrinsically faster Norris up until that moment. Stella explained that the pitwall had at least "evaluated all the options" in case the team had come under more significant pressure from behind, like swapping positions to let Norris try and build a gap, and then revert positions again at the end of the race if McLaren was still controlling a 1-2.

But Stella felt like Piastri had also "deserved an opportunity to try and win the race" by passing Norris at the start and then keeping him at bay.

Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

"You constantly evaluate all the options," Stella added. "You can look at what's the way to score as many points for the team, but there's also a way to be consistent with the way we go racing.

"I think up until the time Oscar pitted, Oscar had gained the lead in a fair manner with the action in corner one and two, so he deserved an opportunity to try and win the race. On other tracks, probably Lando might have overtaken Oscar, but in this case it's difficult."

With McLaren the pick of the field on Sunday, swapping the order didn't prove necessary, but the team did try to calm a flying Norris down as it was managing various reliability concerns, both when he was chasing Piastri and when he was leading. Piastri's eventual retirement through a gearbox failure suggested that was not an unwise decision.

"The main thing with Lando is that we were managing a couple of things from a reliability point of view, so there was absolutely no need to use kerbs that we then instructed a couple of times quite explicitly," said Stella. "But Lando wasn't [trying to] prove anything. He was in the lead, in clean air, and he just had a lot of pace in hand."

In any case, McLaren's first race-winning outing of the season brought back memories of its many team order quandaries over last year's title winning campaign. With Piastri frustrated over his belated access to this weekend's floor upgrade, having been made to wait until FP3 on Saturday, Sunday's race only further put the spotlight on McLaren's fairness mantra.

Sports.title: New Honda F1 engine to debut in Aston Martin filming day ahead of Dutch GP
Sports.content:
Honda has announced it will debut its new Formula 1 power unit at an Aston Martin filming day this Wednesday at the Hungaroring.

Fresh from a confidence-boosting Hungarian Grand Prix where Aston Martin released its B-spec AMR26 F1 car with a clear pace improvement in both qualifying and race trim, Honda will debut its updated engine at a team filming day on Wednesday at the same venue.

Honda had previously lined up the first race after the F1 summer break, the Dutch GP, as the event it would deliver its power unit updates, its first permitted under ADUO.

But it has now announced its official debut will be at the Hungaroring before its first F1 session at Zandvoort on 21-23 August.

“In Hungary, we have been supporting the team with the power unit integration. We’ve also been able to collect vital data, which will help us come to the next race,” Shintaro Orihara, Honda trackside general manager and chief engineer, said.

“We will now take the important step of introducing our new-spec power unit in the Netherlands.

“Before then, during Wednesday’s filming day, we will run the new engine in the AMR26 for the first time, before the summer shutdown commences.”

Shintaro Orihara, Trackside General Manager and Chief Engineer of Honda Racing Corporation Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

Stroll led Aston Martin to 13th in Budapest, directly ahead of team-mate Fernando Alonso, who broke into Q2 for the first time this year. The performances saw Aston Martin outperform Cadillac, Williams and Haas.

“I think it was a good step forward, both in quali and the race, so yes, a new baseline to work with for the second part of the year,” said Alonso.

“The correlation is good and the performance gains are there, what we expect. It's obviously early days with this new car. It's a completely new car, new concept, so more to come maybe on setup, optimisation and things like that.

“So, next race is also with the engine upgrade, will be an interesting check in Zandvoort, where we are and what we can fight for.”

Sports.title: Piastri slams "unacceptable" Sainz blue-flag incident, accepts McLaren strategy in Hungarian GP
Sports.content:
McLaren driver Oscar Piastri was hugely frustrated by being hit by a lapped Carlos Sainz in Formula 1's Hungarian Grand Prix, but saw no bones in McLaren's strategy.

Piastri pitted from the lead for his second stop and was put into lapped traffic, behind Williams driver Sainz and Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso scrapping over a position out of the points.

As Sainz cut back to the racing line in Turn 2, he veered into Piastri's McLaren, unaware of the Australian's position on track. Piastri avoided damage but still lost a significant chunk of time, which ended up costing him the lead to team-mate Lando Norris.

While there had been intermittent GPS issues that interfered with the blue flags signals being displayed on the steering wheel, Sainz and Alonso were still shown blue flags by the marshal-operated light panels.

Piastri tore into Sainz after the race, deeming it "unacceptable" for the Spaniard not to be observing the blue flag regardless of the system glitch.

"Yeah, I knew there were blue flag [issues], but there were blue flags on all the marshal signals," Piastri said.

"I was right behind him. I couldn't believe what happened. Getting crashed into by a lapped car is never one of the things you expect that can go wrong in your race. I don't really care if he didn't see me. The fact that he didn't and no one told him or there was a lack of complete awareness is unacceptable.

Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

"He was fighting Fernando for last place like it was the world championship. It cost me the lead of the race. He's quite critical of others. Others have given him some stick before for being frustrating on track. When you go and do something like that, I think maybe you should look in the mirror a bit."

On top of not getting blue flags on his dash, Sainz explained Piastri was in his blind spot, so he wasn't expecting the McLaren to be where it was.

"We didn't have blue lights on the steering which normally when we are in fights like that one where we are fighting for position, it helps us to understand whether we're getting lapped or not," he explained.

"At this stage, I had no idea I was about to get lapped and on top of that I was in a big fight with Fernando trying to undercut him into the corner and I wouldn't have expected Oscar to be there.

"Even I had expected [him], he was in my dead angle, so it was impossible, honestly, from my side to avoid it. Probably a bit better communication would have helped but at the same time a racing thing that sometimes happens."

Piastri also redirected his frustration at his own team at the time, sarcastically thanking them for putting him in that position in the first place.

But having cooled down somewhat, Piastri acknowledged having to cover off Lewis Hamilton's pitstop was the right decision, and given Piastri was handed pitstop priority over Norris, he would have easily kept his lead if it hadn't been for a rare interference from lapped traffic.

Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

"I think the timing of my stop was fine," he acknowledged. "We wanted to cover off Hamilton, which was perfectly normal. Without getting crashed into, I would have been ahead of Lando still.

"Obviously, when Lando came out ahead, I knew I had no pace to go and attack him, so I knew my chances of winning the race were done from there. So, in the moment, I was pissed off that I'd lost the lead of the race. But that wasn't the fault of the team. It was Carlos' fault."

At the time, Piastri felt McLaren could have delayed Norris' stop too, but afterwards he admitted that wouldn't have been a logical thing to do.

"I felt maybe the team could have not pitted Lando if it was a two-car race, but I know it's not a two-car race," Piastri added. "I know that Lando's got his own race to try and win and there's other people.

"They can't just not box Lando because of something out of his control and out of my control. From that side of things, it's fine. I was just very, very pissed off in the moment about what happened."

While Norris went on to win the grand prix, McLaren's first of 2026, Piastri ended up retiring due to a gearbox failure, costing him a chance at second.

Sports.title: How blue-flag malfunction caused chaos in F1 Hungarian GP
Sports.content:
A sudden, unexpected wave of Formula 1 drivers ignoring blue flags in the Hungarian Grand Prix was caused by a system failure.

Flag signalling has evolved along with technology with F1. Previously, it was just physical flags being waved trackside, but more visible light panels were subsequently added, and drivers now see blue flags pertaining to them on their steering wheel display.

However, in Sunday’s race at the Hungaroring, blue flags were reported to be shown randomly and without driver numbers on the dash, which caused a number of close calls and, at times, incidents.

“We didn't have any feedback on the dash, on the cars,” Esteban Ocon explained. “So, we only had the blue flag panels, but not with our numbers.

“For example, I was racing Isack [Hadjar] exit of pitlane, but I was a lap down, I didn't know. So, I might have blocked him for three corners. But by the time the engineers told me, ‘Well, you're not racing him’, you don't know because the blue flag is always flashing the whole lap. So, yeah, it's not really clear.”

Autosport understands the FIA was aware of the ongoing issue and therefore relied on physical flags and light panels.

Carlos Sainz, Williams Photo by: Liam Fabre

This did not prevent confusion out on track, with the highest-profile example being Carlos Sainz’ collision with Oscar Piastri coming out of Turn 2, which contributed to the McLaren driver losing the lead of the race to team-mate and eventual winner Lando Norris as he attempted to lap the Williams.

“At this stage, I had no idea I was about to get lapped, and on top of that I was in a big fight with Fernando [Alonso], trying to undercut him into the corner,” Sainz explained.

“I wouldn't have expected Oscar to be there. Even if he was there, or I would have expected, he was on my dead spot on the angle, so it was impossible, honestly, from my side to avoid it.

“Probably a bit better communication would have helped, but at the same time, [it is] a racing thing that sometimes happens.”

Sainz still copped a five-second penalty, with stewards viewing the McLaren’s position in the Spaniard’s blind spot – but not the blue-flag situation – as a mitigating factor, hence why it wasn’t a 10-second penalty.

A similar sanction went Oliver Bearman’s way as the Haas driver failed to respect blue flags when lapped by Isack Hadjar. The contrite Briton felt it was difficult to do better in those tricky circumstances.

Oliver Bearman, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

“I feel bad about the blue-flag penalty with Hadjar, because honestly it was a bit of a nightmare out there,” he lamented.

“You go through basically the infield, you don't have time to check in the mirrors, and basically every lap I did I had blue-flag screens coming up. This race, they weren't working properly, so it was tough to know if it was you or the car behind or the car ahead or whatever getting the blue flag.

“Obviously, it wasn't malicious, I'm a lap down, I'm not trying to do anything bad, but obviously I feel bad for anyone's race that I may have compromised.”

Bearman further explained: “At the start of the race, I was getting blue flags after six laps, and I thought, ‘Wow, that's strange. We're not that slow to be lapped in six laps’.

“So from lap six basically until lap 70, there were some blue flags every single lap, so it was really tough to know what was real, what was fake, what was for me, what wasn't, because normally you have your number, this time it was just the blue. So, like I said, nothing malicious, I had to really rely on the team to help me through those blue flags.”

Additional reporting by Ronald Vording and Stuart Codling

Sports.title: Why Sainz only got a five-second penalty for Hungarian GP clash with Piastri
Sports.content:
The Formula 1 Hungarian Grand Prix stewards have explained why they were more lenient with Carlos Sainz, issuing only a five-second penalty for his collision with Oscar Piastri.

Piastri, who was leading the race in Budapest during the opening phase, was nearly taken out by Sainz on lap 38 while the Spaniard was being lapped by the McLaren driver. Despite the incident, the Williams driver received only a five-second penalty, with the stewards stating there was a mitigating factor.

On top of the problems with the blue flag system, which meant drivers did not receive clear signals during the race, the stewards stated that Piastri "was not visible" to Sainz in the mirrors immediately before the contact, as the Australian attempted to pass the Williams into Turn 3.

Taking that mitigating factor into account, the stewards decided not to impose the standard 10-second penalty for causing a collision, instead handing Sainz a five-second penalty.

Piastri was able to continue without damage despite the contact, but the incident ultimately contributed to him losing the lead to Lando Norris.

"On Lap 38, at the approach to Turn 3, Car 55 [Sainz] was engaged in a battle with Car 14 [Fernando Alonso]," the statement said. "The driver of Car 55 had been informed by the team that blue flags were being shown due to the approach of Car 81 [Piastri]. As Car 81 attempted to overtake, contact occurred between Cars 55 and 81.

Oscar Piastri, McLaren Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

"The Stewards determined that the driver of Car 55 was wholly responsible for the collision with Car 81. While the standard penalty for causing a collision is a 10-second time penalty, the Stewards identified a mitigating factor.

"At the point of the incident, the positioning of Car 55 relative to the circuit and the other cars meant that Car 81 was not visible to the driver of Car 55 prior to the attempted overtake. Although the driver had been informed that Car 81 was approaching, the Stewards accepted that the limited visibility reduced the degree of culpability.

"Taking this mitigating circumstance into account, the Stewards determined that a five-second time penalty, rather than the standard 10-second penalty, was appropriate."

Piastri retired from the Hungarian GP later due to a mechanical failure. Sainz finished 18th, two laps behind race winner Norris.

Sports.title: F1 Hungarian GP: Norris wins from Verstappen and Antonelli, Piastri retires with gearbox failure
Sports.content:
Lando Norris has won his first grand prix of 2026 at Formula 1's Hungarian Grand Prix as early leader Oscar Piastri lost the lead due to lapped traffic, and then retired with a gearbox failure.

Piastri passed polesitter Norris at the start with a cutback at Turn 2 controlled the first half of the race, with Norris appearing quicker but unable to find a way past on the twisty Hungaroring.

Max Verstappen moved to third ahead of Ferrari duo Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, as the latter was sandwiched by his two rivals. Meanwhile, George Russell suffered a terrible start as anti-stall kicked in on his Mercedes, dropping him as low as 19th.

Both Ferraris started on softs, as opposed to mediums for the other frontrunners, but as they were stuck behind Verstappen, Hamilton and Leclerc were unable to put their faster tyres to good use.

On lap 14 Hamilton rolled the dice with an early stop for hards. Verstappen responded on the following tour, but while he was unable to avoid the undercut from Hamilton, Verstappen lunged down the inside of Turn 1 to regain his position.

The end result of the first pit sequence was that the top five held station, with the exception of Kimi Antonelli going long to try and pull off a one-stop strategy. However, the Italian was losing too much lap time to pull it off, having to come in on lap 23 for hards; too early to make it to the end of the 70-lap contest. Russell had meanwhile clawed his way back to seventh.

Oscar Piastri, McLaren Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

McLaren drama as Piastri loses lead

After the first round of pitstops Norris was still sticking to Piastri, though the world champion did lose adhesion through Turn 4 on lap 29, an innocent off which handed the Australian a temporary reprieve.

Norris' off-track excursion prompted a cautionary message from his race engineer to settle down as the team suspected the Briton was trying to show off how much quicker he was than his leading team-mate. But with little pressure from Verstappen behind and Piastri having taken the lead fair and square at the start, McLaren didn't seem particularly motivated to instigate any kind of team orders.

An impatient Norris urged his team to pit him first and gain an undercut, which the team naturally refused, but it did bring in Piastri for a second stop on lap 34. That put Piastri into lapped traffic as he was caught up in a battle between Carlos Sainz and Fernando Alonso in the first sector, with Sainz staying on the racing line and veering into Piastri.

"Get out of the f***ing way you idiot, oh my god", a furious Piastri raged over team radio as he escaped damage, but lost enough time to be overcut by Norris after the Briton came in for his own pitstop. Seeing Norris emerge from the pitlane ahead, Piastri also redirected his frustration at his own team, sarcastically thanking them for putting him in that position in the first place. Sainz received a lenient five-second time penalty for ignoring the blue flags.

Norris then passed championship leader Antonelli, who was unsuccessfully trying to nurse home an ambitious one-stop strategy. Piastri was unable to follow Norris for a 1-2, though, as he dramatically retired from the race with a gearbox failure on lap 56 to cap a frustrating Hungary weekend.

The subsequent virtual safety car delivered a twist in the battle for the remaining podium places behind Norris, who had plenty of buffer to pit for used softs.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Steven Tee / LAT Images via Getty Images

With Antonelli having already bailed on his one-stopper, Hamilton had moved to second but also came in for fresh tyres, while Verstappen stayed out to gain track position. Hamilton also lost third to Antonelli on pit exit, with Leclerc fifth after his own third pitstop.

At the front Norris comfortably controlled his lead to take both his and McLaren's first grand prix win of the 2026 campaign, though one that will prompt a lengthy debrief at the Woking squad.

Verstappen salvaged an unexpected second place after struggling all weekend with the behaviour of his RB22. The entertaining battle for third between Antonelli and a chasing Hamilton was defused by a five-second penalty for the Ferrari driver for speeding in the pitlane, which dropped him to fifth behind Leclerc in the final result.

Isack Hadjar was a distant sixth for Red Bull, with Russell salvaging seventh from his horror start, albeit unable to avoid losing further ground in the championship.

Liam Lawson and Racing Bulls won the midfield battle in eighth, followed by Audi's Nico Hulkenberg and Arvid Lindblad, the end result of an enthralling four-car battle between the two teams, with Gabriel Bortoleto in 11th.

Lance Stroll and Alonso took an encouraging 13th and 14th place for Aston Martin in its vastly upgraded car, while both Cadillacs of Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas joined Piastri in retirement as their brakes caught fire.

F1 now heads into its summer break, with Antonelli going into it with a 50-point lead on Hamilton and a 59-point advantage over Russell. The action resumes on 23 August with the final edition of the Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort.

Sports.title: Malaysia will officially host F1's 2026 Bahrain GP
Sports.content:
Sepang will host the Bahrain Grand Prix from 2-4 October, as Formula 1 returns to Malaysia for the first time since 2017.

Initially featuring four rounds in the Middle East, the 2026 F1 calendar was compromised by the US-Israeli war on Iran, which has destabilised the whole region. The Bahrain and Saudi Arabian grands prix were initially cancelled, creating a five-week break in April.

F1 has therefore been seeking alternatives, and the Singapore round provided a perfect opportunity to run a race in Malaysia, with Sepang just 300km away.

Bahrain was still keen to have its own race on the calendar and has found an agreement with the FIA, F1 and Malaysia for Sepang to host it.

There will therefore be a triple-header from Baku to Singapore from late September to mid-October. The Azerbaijan Grand Prix is taking place on a Saturday, which makes the logistics much easier.

“We are delighted to confirm that Malaysia will host the Bahrain Grand Prix in 2026,” F1 president and CEO Stefano Domenicali said. “Once again, the sport has demonstrated its ability to adapt, find solutions, and deliver, creating an exciting moment for everyone who follows Formula 1.

F1 at Sepang in 1999 Photo by: LAT Images via Getty Images

“This is fantastic news for our fans. They will continue to enjoy a full and exciting Formula 1 calendar, while also seeing the sport return to a great venue. Malaysia is an incredible country, and Sepang holds a special place in Formula 1 history. It will provide a spectacular setting for racing and an unforgettable experience for fans at the circuit and watching around the world.”

Malaysia previously hosted F1 every year from 1999 to 2017. Declining ticket sales and TV ratings, allied to feeling “ripped off” by its deal with Bernie Ecclestone’s Formula One Management, led Sepang to terminate its contract early, giving up on its 2018 race.

No fewer than 10 current F1 drivers have raced at Sepang in the past. The final Malaysian Grand Prix coincidentally was Pierre Gasly’s F1 debut.

Sebastian Vettel is the most successful driver at the track near Kuala Lumpur with four wins to his name, while Fernando Alonso has the most of the current crop – three. Lewis Hamilton took a record five pole positions there but converted just one into victory, with his 2016 engine failure famously contributing to his world title defeat to team-mate Nico Rosberg.

It is worth noting that F1 is sticking to a theoretical 23-race calendar with the Qatar and Abu Dhabi season-ending rounds unchanged, though their fate obviously depends on the Iran war and alternative options are known to be considered.

Sports.title: Antonelli hit with grid drop for yellow flag infringement in F1 Hungarian GP qualifying
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli has been given a three-place grid drop for Formula 1's Hungarian Grand Prix after being penalised for not heeding yellow flags.

Antonelli took fourth on the grid at the Hungaroring as Mercedes was beaten by both McLaren's polesitter Lando Norris and the two Ferraris. On his final qualifying run, however, Antonelli caught yellow flags in the final corner - where Red Bull's Max Verstappen was stationary in the runoff area after a spin.

Antonelli still improved his final sector time to take fourth, with the stewards investigating if the Italian had lifted enough to respect the local yellows.

The championship leader has been handed a three-place grid drop, which will demote him to seventh on the grid, because the stewards felt he had only lifted by the tiniest amount and was still faster through the corner than on his previous push lap.

Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton also received a three-place grid penalty for impeding Oscar Piastri in Turn 1, with Piastri now moving up to third and Verstappen joining him on the second row.

Read Also: Formula 1 Hamilton slapped with grid drop for impeding Piastri in F1 Hungarian GP qualifying

"The driver of Car 12 stated that on seeing the yellow flag and light panel, he lifted off the throttle earlier than his previous push lap," the stewards wrote in their verdict. "This was verified by the telemetry. However the reduction in speed occurred for a very short period, and in fact the car’s speed when passing the scene of the incident involving Car 3, was slightly higher than that on the previous push lap.





Watch: Lando Norris Takes a Shock Pole | F1 Hungarian GP Qualifying

"The mini sector time was only 0.03 second slower than his best time for that mini sector, and whilst, because he had lifted 16 metres earlier, he was 14 km/h slower entering the yellow flag sector, but was 3 km/h faster when passing the incident site due to less application of the brakes entering the corner. The FIA representatives noted that the speed reduction in the mini sector was less than 1%.

"The Stewards considered this incident to be different to other incidents that have resulted in no further action, because unlike those cases, there was no significant speed delta through the mini sector compared to the driver’s previous fastest time under similar circumstances."

Antonelli could have faced a five-placed grid drop for the offence, but the stewards felt that the Italian at least scrubbing off some speed warranted a more lenient penalty. The 19-year-old also gets a penalty point on his licence.

"The recommended penalty according to the penalty guidelines, for this offence, is a drop of 5 grid positions," the FIA stewards added. "However in mitigation of penalty, we considered that the driver did make a reduction in speed, albeit, in our determination, an insufficient and unsustained one. Further, the driver had limited time and distance to react. Hence a lower penalty is applied."

Antonelli also received a warning for driving too slowly and exceeding the minimum delta times on his in-lap following his final qualifying attempt.

Sports.title: “Disgraceful”: Wolff criticises “Teletubbies” at rival teams over blue flags delay | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff criticised engineers at rival teams for failing to react to blue flags during the Hungarian Grand Prix.

A system fault during the race meant the light panels stopped working and drivers were only shown blue flags manually. This caused problems for Andrea Kimi Antonelli when he was trying to catch Max Verstappen over the final laps while under pressure from Lewis Hamilton behind.

“The marshalling system was not functioning and cars in the back were defending on a Lewis and Kimi fight,” Wolff told Sky. “It’s just disgraceful from some of the Teletubbies engineers that sit on the pit walls of these teams not telling the drivers what’s happening behind.”

However some of the same drivers who delayed Antonelli had already held Verstappen up.

“It’s unacceptable how long that takes here with this car,” Verstappen told his race engineer Gianpiero Lambiase at one point. “Mate, what are they doing?”

After being held up by another car Versstappen exclaimed: “They should get a penalty. This is fucking ridiculous, these morons, my god.”

Wolff admitted he was “not happy about the whole situation” after the team left Hungary with third place for Antonelli and seventh for George Russell, who fell to the back of the field at the start after a problem with his engine.

“We did a mistake on screwing George’s start,” said Wolff. “It’s just not acceptable and not good enough for us.”

Russell said there was “nothing I could do, unfortunately.”

“I was on the throttle, waiting, and then all of a sudden the engine was going all over the place. It was revving really high, really low.

“Right now we don’t know but it’s added to the list of things that has happened this first half of the year and pray things calm down in the second half.”

Sports.title: Sainz collision was “one of the dumbest things I’ve ever seen” – Piastri | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The stewards ruled Carlos Sainz Jnr was entirely to blame for the collision which cost Oscar Piastri the lead of the Hungarian Grand Prix.

Piastri was vying for the lead of the race with team mate Lando Norris when he tangled with Sainz while trying to lap the Williams. Sainz was preoccupied with his fight for position with Fernando Alonso

Although Piastri avoided spinning after the pair made contact at turn three, he lost time which allowed Norris to make his second pit stop and emerge ahead of his team mate.

The stewards handed Sainz a five-second time penalty for the collision. Although they considered some factors in mitigation they ruled Piastri was not to blame for the contact.

Sainz indicated he was unaware how close Piastri due to a problem with the flag marshalling system which occured during the race.

“The incident with Piastri could have been avoided with a bit better communication and a bit of bad luck with a [blind] angle in my mirror,” he said. “I just didn’t know he was there so I had no clue. He was lapping us and he was in my [blind] spot in the mirror.”

However Piastri said “that’s no excuse at all.”

Sports.title: Norris pounces on Piastri’s clash with Sainz to grab first win of 2026 | 2026 Hungarian Grand Prix report
Sports.content:
Lando Norris claimed his first victory since winning the world championship in the Hungarian Grand Prix.

The McLaren driver capitalised on a clash between his team mate Oscar Piastri and a backmarker to regain the lead he lost at the start of the race.

Norris held his lead from pole position but immediately ran wide at turn two. That opened the door for Piastri, who started third, to dive by into the lead.

Piastri maintained the effective lead of the race after the drivers made their first pit stops. But Norris closed on his team mate during their second stint on hard tyres.

Norris urged McLaren to give him the opportunity to pit first but the team resisted, sticking to their policy of giving the leading car the first tyre change. They duly brought Piastri in for the second time on lap 34.

Piastri’s race went awry soon afterwards, however, when he caught Fernando Alonso and Carlos Sainz Jnr. The Williams driver was so preoccupied with trying to pass his rival he failed to notice Piastri poking his nose alongside into turn three. The pair made contact and only Piastri’s quick reactions kept him from spinning.

Norris’s pit crew pounced, swapping his tyres immediately and jumping one McLaren ahead of the other. That left only Andrea Kimi Antonelli between him and his first victory of 2026, and Norris easily breezed past.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

A final blow struck Piastri with 15 laps to go, when his gearbox failed. Norris took advantage of the subsequent Virtual Safety Car period to take a set of soft tyres for his final sprint to the flag.

When the race resumed Max Verstappen held second place on a worn set of soft tyres, pursued by Antonelli and Lewis Hamilton. The Ferrari driver overtook the Mercedes as he rejoined the track following a pit stop under the VSC, but after his team took a close look at the replay they told him to let Antonelli by to avoid a penalty.

Antonelli and Hamilton set off in pursuit of Verstappen but found progress difficult as they lapped a success of slower cars. Hamilton was further compromised when the stewards issued him a five-second time penalty for speeding in the pits.

The pair ran out of time to catch Verstappen, so Norris ran out the winner by 15 seconds. Verstappen prevailed in a spirited battle with Hamilton early in the race, re-passing his former championship rival after their first pit stops.

Antonelli took the final podium place, increasing his championship lead. Hamilton’s penalty dropped him to fifth behind. Charles Leclerc.

George Russell’s championship hopes suffered another blow as his car went into anti-stall at the start, dropping him to 20th place. He recovered to finish seventh after running out of time to catch Isack Hadjar.

Liam Lawson prevailed in a scrap with his team mate to take eighth place. Nico Hulkenberg also passed Arvid Lindblad as he finally claimed his first points finish of the season,

The only drivers to join Piastri in retirement were Valtteri Bottas and Sergio Perez, who both suffered technical failures on their Cadillacs.

Sports.title: Spencer Brown Dismisses Anthony Joshua Victory: Tyson Fury Wins That Fight Comfortably
Sports.content:
“I was in shock. I was in a lot of shock,” Brown told Seconds Out. “Wait till he gets in with big Tyson Fury. That’s a different beast. He’s a different beast. That performance was an easy performance yesterday.”

Brown admitted he believed Joshua’s comeback bid had already ended after the opening round.

“Thought we’d lost the fight. It was all over. The dream was over. Thank God he got up and he did what he did,” said Spencer.

Brown’s view matched criticism from several figures in boxing who questioned Joshua’s display despite the knockout victory. Getting dropped twice by a late replacement left many wondering how Joshua would fare against elite opposition after returning from his lengthy layoff.

He believes Joshua’s struggles confirmed his view that Fury wins if the long-discussed British heavyweight fight finally happens. Instead of treating Joshua’s knockout as proof he has returned to top form, Brown saw a performance that Fury would handle comfortably.

Brown also rejected criticism that Fury looked sluggish during his own return, suggesting much of it came from Joshua supporters.

“The people criticizing him are Anthony Joshua fans, aren’t they? Simple. Social media. They criticize me, they’ll criticize you, they criticize everybody. That’s what it is,” said Brown.

Brown believes Joshua’s struggles confirmed his view that Fury wins if the long-discussed British heavyweight fight finally happens. Instead of treating Joshua’s knockout as proof he has returned to top form, Brown saw a performance that Fury would handle comfortably.

While Brown was quick to dismiss concerns over Tyson Fury’s own recent outing, the contrast on the canvas is hard to ignore. In his return against 46-year-old Mariusz Wach, Fury offered little of the fleet-footed brilliance that defined his victories over Wladimir Klitschko or Deontay Wilder. Looking slow, heavy, and visibly faded, Fury relied on raw size to wear down Wach over seven grueling rounds before forcing a clubbing stoppage.

The last eight years have exacted a heavy toll on the former champion. Brown may dismiss the sluggish display as simple social media blather, but Fury’s labor against an aging journeyman suggests time has caught up to both heavyweights, making any potential meeting far less predictable than his manager claims.

Sports.title: Tim Tszyu Should Face Yoenli Hernandez Next
Sports.content:
Yoenli is one of the best young middleweights in the sport. The unbeaten Cuban has combined his outstanding amateur pedigree with power, stopping nine of his first 10 opponents. He has looked like a future world champion from the start of his professional career, making him the ideal measuring stick for anyone with title ambitions at 160 pounds.

At 31, Tszyu doesn’t have the luxury of taking three or four tune-up fights before stepping into meaningful competition. If his goal is another world title, he’ll eventually have to beat fighters on Hernandez’s level or deal with champions like Carlos Adames. Defeating lower-ranked contenders first would do little to answer the questions surrounding his future in the division.

A victory over Hernandez would immediately establish Tszyu as a legitimate middleweight contender. It would erase much of the doubt created by his recent defeats and place him within striking distance of another title opportunity. Losing would provide an equally valuable answer by showing that the division’s bigger, stronger fighters present a hurdle he may not overcome.

Tszyu rebuilt momentum with his victory over Spence, but that win came against an opponent making his first appearance in nearly two years. Middleweight presents an entirely different challenge. Hernandez offers the type of test that reveals exactly where Tszyu belongs.

Instead of spending months collecting routine victories, Tszyu should take the direct route. If he wants to reinvent himself at middleweight, there may not be a better first opponent than Yoenli Hernandez.

Sports.title: Keyshawn Davis Sees Haney Win Changing Boxing
Sports.content:
When I stop Devin Haney it will be a new face of boxing.⭐️ — Keyshawn Davis (@KeyshawnDavis8) July 26, 2026

Bill Haney quickly fired back, placing the burden of making the fight back on Davis’s side.

“Stop ducking meetings with your manager and promoter; let’s get this deal done. ⭐️” Bill replied on X.

The public back-and-forth comes just ahead of Monday’s WBO purse bid if Haney’s side fails to reach an agreement with Keyshawn beforehand. Davis has repeatedly pushed for the fight, viewing it as the ultimate opportunity to claim a world title.

Stopping Haney would give Keyshawn, 27, the type of signature victory that every contender chases. It would also answer questions about how he compares against one of the sport’s best-known names.

Becoming boxing’s new face is another matter. Winning over fight fans across the U.K. alongside the American market requires real star power. Defeating Haney in a tactical chess match won’t instantly transform Davis into a global superstar. Haney is a defensive specialist lacking explosive power, whose recent performances against Brian Norman Jr. or Jose Ramirez failed to excite audiences.

Inside the ring, Keyshawn’s composure under fire remains a major issue. When opponents land solid shots, he sometimes loses his cool and resorts to wrestling tactics. Fans saw it against Miguel Madueno when the bout turned ugly, and again in his May rematch with Nahir Albright, where sheer frustration over holding led Keyshawn to execute an illegal body slam that cost him two points. That habit of losing his head and turning fights into dirty grappling matches turns off fight fans who expect disciplined brilliance from a star.

To earn true crossover stardom, Keyshawn needs more than a single win over a defensive champion. He would likely need to clear out the entire welterweight division, sweeping through marquee names like Ryan Garcia, Conor Benn, Rolly Romero, Teofimo Lopez, Richardson Hitchins, plus potential moving contenders like Andy Hiraoka and Ernesto Mercado.

If the fight gets finalized, Keyshawn will get his opportunity to back up his claim inside the ring, but proving he belongs at the top spot will require a far longer journey.

Bill Haney reacted to Keyshawn’s post from above, telling him to stop ducking his manager so they can make the fight.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua Admits He Never Expected First-Round Scare Against Prenga
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua admitted he never expected to find himself fighting through a first-round crisis after being dropped by Kristian Prenga on Saturday night in Jeddah. Instead of panicking, Joshua said he accepted the situation, tightened his defense, and trusted he would eventually wear his opponent down before scoring a second-round knockout.

“It’s not what you expect, honestly,” Joshua said to iFL TV. “One thing I’ve learned is these guys are starting fast. They’re not coming to box 12 rounds and see if they can outbox me. They’re coming to try and take my head off. “In the second round I said to myself, ‘I can do the same. What am I waiting 12 rounds to break them down for?’ I’ve got some power in my hands, so I might as well land some leather as well. I learned a lot in that moment.”

Joshua said he expected to build behind his jab before breaking Prenga down, but the first-round knockdown changed everything.

Sports.title: Gene Tunney Stops Tom Heeney, Retires Four Days Later
Sports.content:
The bout carried the NYSAC, NBA, and The Ring world heavyweight titles. Promoter Tex Rickard presented it as what many believed would be Tunney’s final appearance. Tunney weighed 192 pounds. Heeney came in at 203½ pounds. Jack Dempsey, whom Tunney had defeated twice, worked in Heeney’s corner in an effort to help the challenger dethrone his former rival.

A paid crowd of 43,191 attended, with thousands more admitted on complimentary tickets. The gate reached approximately $691,014.50, producing a net of about $521,422 after expenses. Tunney received a remarkable $525,000 purse, while Heeney earned $100,000. Motion picture rights generated another $20,000. Radio rights produced $15,000.

Referee Eddie Forbes officiated. Charles F. Mathison and Tom Flynn served as judges.

Heeney fought exactly as expected, charging forward in an effort to force exchanges at close range. Tunney relied on disciplined footwork. His steady left jab repeatedly disrupted the challenger before sharp counters landed cleanly. Much of the early action featured clinches as Heeney struggled to trap the champion along the ropes.

By the eighth round, Tunney had opened a damaging cut over Heeney’s left eye. The punishment increased in the 10th when a double jab followed by a chopping right hand dropped the challenger near the ropes. Heeney rose immediately. He kept pressing forward despite absorbing heavy punishment.

The finish came at 2:52 of the 11th round. Tunney unloaded another sustained attack, but Heeney refused to fall. Seeing the exhausted challenger taking unanswered punches, Forbes stepped between them and awarded Tunney a technical knockout victory.

The victory became the final chapter of one of boxing’s finest championship careers. Tunney retired as heavyweight champion. Later that year, The Ring magazine selected him as its inaugural Fighter of the Year for 1928. Heeney earned lasting respect for his determination, although the defeat effectively ended his pursuit of the world heavyweight title.

Sports.title: Tim Tszyu Outworks Errol Spence Jr. Over 12 Rounds
Sports.content:
The opening rounds were competitive. Tszyu stunned Spence with a right hand in the closing seconds of the first round, but Spence answered in the second with effective body work and a hard left that briefly shifted the momentum. The third round also favored Spence, although Tszyu finished strongly with another right hand.

Tszyu regained momentum in the fourth before another close fifth round. He began taking control in the sixth and seventh, landing the cleaner punches while increasing his work rate. Both fighters developed swelling under their left eyes.

Referee Will Soulos warned Spence several times for low blows in the eighth round as blood began flowing from Spence’s nose. Tszyu continued pressing the action over the final four rounds, repeatedly landing right hands while Spence’s output slowed.

Tszyu finished strongly in the twelfth, rocking Spence with another right hand during the closing minute to seal the victory.

Following the decision, Spence applauded Tszyu before announcing his retirement from boxing.

Reda Defeats Fleming

In the co-feature, Ahmad “Bloodshot” Reda earned a unanimous decision over former Olympian Paul “Showtime” Fleming after 10 entertaining rounds.

Reda controlled most of the early action with his speed and activity, although Fleming enjoyed his best success in the fifth after inviting Reda to exchange while standing against the ropes.

A clash of heads opened a cut over Fleming’s left eyebrow in the seventh. Reda continued to outwork the veteran over the closing rounds despite suffering a cut late in the fight.

The judges scored the bout 99-91, 97-93 and 96-94.

Peters Stops Actis

Australian Olympian Callum “50 Cal” Peters remained unbeaten by stopping Ivan “Gringo” Actis in the seventh round.

The opening rounds featured heavy exchanges before Peters gradually took control with sharper punching. A right hand opened a cut over Actis’ left eye in the fourth, and Peters continued to wear him down until referee Will Soulos halted the bout at 55 seconds of Round 7.

Aokuso Knocks Out Tejeda

Former Olympian Paulo “Sweet P” Aokuso captured the vacant IBF Intercontinental light heavyweight title with a dramatic 10th-round knockout of Luis Antonio Tejeda.

Aokuso rocked Tejeda early, but the Dominican battled back and had the Australian badly hurt against the ropes during the seventh round.

The fight ended suddenly in the final round when Aokuso landed a crushing counter left hand that flattened Tejeda for the count.

Rahimi Wins Pro Debut

Former Olympian Tina Rahimi opened her professional career with a unanimous decision over Sacha Ryan Dryden.

Rahimi boxed well throughout the four-round contest, using her speed and combinations to edge most of the rounds before finishing strongly.

The judges scored it 40-36, 40-36 and 39-37.

Grach Defeats Pluto

Heavyweight Brandon “The Bull” Grach earned a unanimous decision over Ike “From Pluto” Pluto in a five-round battle.

Grach hurt Pluto with a right hand in the third round and scored a knockdown in the fourth. Pluto rallied late and landed several solid punches in the fifth, but Grach had already done enough to secure the victory.

The judges scored the fight 49-45, 49-45 and 48-46.

Jimmy Lennon Jr. served as the ring announcer for the main event.

Sports.title: Errol Spence Jr. Retires After Tim Tszyu Loss
Sports.content:
“It was a great fight. Congratulations to Tim and Jeff Fenech. It was a good showing by Tim. I answered a lot of questions about myself, and now it’s time to go home with my family and start a new life,” Spence said before confirming his decision. “Yeah, for sure. I’ve got my faculties intact. My money is good and working for itself, so everything’s good, man. I’ve got a beautiful family and I thank God that I’m able to leave this sport with my faculties intact and my family by my side. Everything’s going to go well.”

The judges scored the fight 117-111, 117-111 and 118-110 for Tszyu, who gradually took control after a competitive opening. Spence was returning from a layoff of nearly three years and showed flashes of his former ability, but Tszyu’s pressure and higher punch output proved decisive over the second half of the contest.

At 36, Spence chose to leave the sport on his own terms rather than continue chasing another title opportunity. His remarks made it clear that preserving his health outweighed any desire to fight again.

Spence retires as one of the standout welterweights of his era after holding multiple world titles and defeating many of the division’s leading names. His final appearance ended in defeat, but he walked away satisfied that boxing had provided both financial security and the opportunity to leave with his long-term health intact.

Ghana News.title: IOC says Infantino complaint outside its scope
Ghana News.content:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino gave US president Donald Trump the inaugural Fifa Peace Prize in December

The International Olympic Committee says it will not investigate Gianni Infantino as a complaint about the FIFA president is outside its scope.

Human rights campaign group FairSquare complained to the IOC that Infantino had breached its charter by failing to adhere to rules on political neutrality "through statements or other clear expressions of support for the US president".

US President Donald Trump admitted during the World Cup that he had called Infantino to ask him to review a red card given to US striker Folarin Balogun.

The forward was expected to miss his side's last-16 tie against Belgium after being sent off during their 2-0 win over Bosnia-Herzegovina.

But after the intervention from Trump, the one-match ban was suspended for 12 months. No reason was given, beyond citing a rule that allows punishments to be suspended.

Balogun started the match, which Belgium won 4-1.

Infantino has been a member of the IOC since 2020.

Section two of the Olympic Charter states: "Members of the IOC will not accept from governments, organisations, or other parties, any mandate or instructions liable to interfere with the freedom of their action and vote."

The IOC said the complaint against Infantino fell outside the jurisdiction of its ethics commission.

"The current complaint, with regard to the FIFA president, refers only to the international federation's decisions on its governance and its management, including its relations with government, and to the international federation's implementation of the rules of its sport, which are both outside the scope of application of the IOC code of ethics," it said.

The IOC statement came a day after it emerged the Norwegian Football Federation was considering filing a formal complaint to Fifa's ethics committee about the decision to suspend Balogun's automatic one-match ban.

In a statement provided to the BBC, NFF president Lise Klaveness said the federation had reacted with "strong concern" and that a decision on whether to file a complaint would be made at its next board meeting.

The federation has already filed a complaint about Fifa's first Peace Prize being awarded to Trump.

FIFA has been contacted for comment.

Ghana News.title: Kane set for talks with Bayern Munich over new deal
Ghana News.content:
Harry Kane is set to open formal talks with Bayern Munich over a new contract with the German champions.

England captain Kane's current deal expires at the end of the coming season, but Bayern are keen to extend the striker's stay.

It is understood the 32-year-old is aware of the Bundesliga club's intention to offer him a new contract, with discussions expected to progress in the coming weeks.

Kane joined Bayern from Tottenham in 2023 in a deal worth a reported £86m.

The striker has enjoyed great success in Munich, helping the club win two Bundesliga titles and the German Cup.

Kane, who scored six goals for England at the recent World Cup, has scored 146 goals in 134 appearances for Bayern since his arrival.

Despite Bayern's desire to tie him down to a new deal, Kane continues to attract interest from clubs across Europe and beyond.

Barcelona have a long-standing interest in the England captain, while clubs in Saudi Arabia have also been linked with the centre-forward.

Ghana News.title: Howe unsure over Guimaraes amid Arsenal interest
Ghana News.content:
Newcastle United head coach Eddie Howe says he has had positive discussions with Bruno Guimaraes but is unable to offer any guarantees on his captain's future.

BBC Sport reported this week that Arsenal are set to make a £70m offer for the Brazil midfielder, but Newcastle do not want to lose their talisman.

"I've had some really good conversations with him before the World Cup, during the World Cup and after the World Cup," Howe said after Newcastle's 1-1 draw against Gateshead in a pre-season friendly on Saturday.

"What we speak about has to remain private, but he's just a great player, a great person.

"I don't know what's going to happen with Bruno's future. That's for other people to speculate about. They are conversations that I'm not part of."

Guimaraes has been on holiday with his family following Brazil's last-16 exit from the World Cup at the hands of Norway this month.

He is due to return to Newcastle on Friday and fly out with the squad for a pre-season training camp in Spain.

Comparisons have been made with Liverpool's pursuit of Alexander Isak last summer - the striker ultimately pushed to leave Newcastle - but Howe said there is "nothing to say Bruno won't be back training with us".

"You've got to look at it in its own right," he said.

"Bruno is the captain of our football club. He's been an unbelievable player and person all through the time we have worked together.

"I speak on behalf of everyone at the football club. We absolutely love him and, of course, everyone will want him to stay."

Steur catches the eye as midfield rebuilt

Newcastle's midfield has been weakened by the departure of Sandro Tonali, who joined Tottenham this month in a deal worth up to £100m.

Young midfielders Sean Steur and Aladji Bamba have since arrived from Ajax and Monaco respectively.

Although Saturday's game came too soon for Bamba, whose move was announced on Friday, Steur played 90 minutes.

"He played really well today," Howe said. "He can be really pleased with his performance and first showing in Newcastle colours."

It is rare for an academy graduate to leave Ajax at 18, and for a fee worth up to £23m.

However, Newcastle have to take calculated risks before potential signings like Steur potentially explode in value and are out of reach.

Dutchman Steur clearly has promise.

Willem Weijs, who managed Steur at Jong Ajax - the club's reserve side - has described him as "one of the highest-rated" players in their academy.

There were glimpses of Steur's technical ability, composure and vision against National League side Gateshead.

But he will need time to adapt to the physicality and intensity of the Premier League.

"He's outstanding in his first touches and creating options when playing a possession game," Weijs said.

"He's good at scanning; really comfortable on the ball; really good in tight spaces.

"He's a typical Dutch-type midfield player, but he should focus on his points to develop as well, which is for sure the defensive part.

"He should compete better in the duels, spending much more time in the gym. I know he's working on that, but he can improve and he has to improve."

Newcastle have shifted strategy this summer, targeting players aged 20 and under and based on the continent.

Steur, Bamba and fellow newcomers Ewen Jaouen and Bazoumana Toure will need patience.

It is one of the many reasons why Howe will desperately want to keep hold of Guimaraes, having lost Isak, Tonali and Anthony Gordon in the past year.

"We all need to be very supportive to the players that have come in," Howe said.

"I don't think we can put too much pressure on them. It's part of my job to try and take the pressure off them and allow them to develop and to enjoy their time here."

Ghana News.title: Japan legend Miura, 59, scores first goal since 2022
Ghana News.content:
Kazuyoshi Miura, the world's oldest professional footballer, scored his first goal in nearly four years at the age of 59 for Japanese third-tier side Fukushima United.

Miura found the net in the 52nd minute to make it 5-0 to Fukushima in an eventual 7-0 win over Iwaki Furukawa in the Emperor's Cup on Saturday.

It is his first competitive goal since netting for Suzuka PG, now Atletico Suzuka, against FC Osaka in November 2022.

Dubbed 'King Kazu' in Japan, he is one of the country's most loved sportsmen and was the face of the J League when it launched in 1993.

He started his career with Brazilian side Santos in 1986 and has also played club football in Italy, Croatia and Australia.

The forward's long career will enter a 42nd season after extending his loan at Fukushima from J2 League side Yokohama FC until June 2027.

Miura signed for Yokohama in 2005 but has not played a minute for them since 2020.

He scored 55 goals in 89 games for Japan and has previously talked about playing into his 60s.

Ghana News.title: Richarlison scores as Spurs beat Auckland at Eden Park
Ghana News.content:
Tottenham manager Roberto de Zerbi said he did not want to take any risks as he fielded a young side in a pre-season win against A-League champions Auckland FC in New Zealand.

Dane Scarlett and Richarlison scored the goals for Spurs as Mateus Fernandes, an £85m signing from West Ham, was the only one of the club's major summer arrivals to feature.

Sandro Tonali, who joined Tottenham in a £100m deal from Newcastle United, missed out with "one small problem", while defenders Jan Paul van Hecke, Andy Robertson and Marcos Senesi also didn't figure.

"It's a chance for the young players," De Zerbi told TVNZ before kick-off.

"After a very long trip, we can't take a risk with the players who are not ready to play yet."

Scarlett put Spurs into an early lead before some of Tottenham's more experienced players in Ben Davies, Mathys Tel, Conor Gallagher and Richarlison came on, along with Fernandes, just after the hour mark.

Richarlison added his side's second in a game watched by a record crowd for a men's football game in New Zealand.

There were 40,112 at Eden Park, a ground where the usual occupants, the All Blacks, are unbeaten in 32 years, as the figure surpassed the previous best of 37,034 who turned up when the New Zealand men's team played a World Cup qualifier against Peru in 2017.

Tottenham's next game is against Sydney FC on 29 July (10:45 BST).
