A Historic Venue at the Centre of Cartagena’s January Revival

The Teatro Adolfo Mejía, known widely by its initials TAM, sits inside Cartagena’s walled city and is described by the Mayor’s Office as “one of the most important cultural settings in the country.” Its 2026 programme launches during the city’s peak cultural month, when international visitors fill hotels and restaurants across the historic centre.

The Instituto de Patrimonio y Cultura de Cartagena (IPCC) manages the theatre’s year-round cultural programming and agenda from January through April, a window that now anchors the city’s high season for cultural tourism. For property owners and hospitality investors, the January festival surge provides a reliable spike in footfall and premium room rates inside the walled city.

The Cartagena Festival de Música: Twenty Years of Programming Power

The 2026 edition marks two decades for the Cartagena International Music Festival, which runs from 4 to 12 January. Twenty-seven concerts are scheduled, with Teatro Adolfo Mejía serving as the principal night-time venue for the symphonic and chamber music programme.

The festival’s 2026 theme translates as “The Soul and the Body: Musical Universalism and National Schools.” It examines how composers across centuries have balanced a shared musical language with distinct national voices, a framing that resonates in a city where European heritage architecture meets Afro-Caribbean rhythms daily.

The Franz Liszt Chamber Orchestra returns as the resident ensemble, anchoring a programme that draws soloists and conductors from Europe, Latin America, and beyond. Ticket prices and exact schedules are published on the festival’s official channels closer to the opening date.

Where Gaitas Fit into Cartagena’s Broader Cultural Landscape

Traditional gaita music, played on long indigenous flutes and accompanied by drums, is deeply woven into the identity of Cartagena and the surrounding Bolívar department. The region hosts dedicated gaita festivals, including the Festival Nacional Autóctono de Gaitas in San Jacinto and the Festival de Gaitas, Cantos y Tambores in the El Socorro neighbourhood.

At previous editions of the Cartagena International Music Festival, groups such as Gaiteros de San Jacinto have appeared in workshops and crossover concerts, creating a dialogue between classical forms and traditional Caribbean sounds. While the formal 2026 season opening at TAM is a classical music event, gaitas remain a living presence in Cartagena’s streets, plazas, and community festivals throughout the year.

For expats and long-stay visitors, this dual musical identity is part of the city’s appeal: a morning of symphonic rehearsal inside a restored 19th-century theatre can be followed by an evening of gaita and bullerengue in a neighbourhood square.

What Follows: Hay Festival, FICCI, and a Packed First Quarter

The IPCC’s published calendar shows that Teatro Adolfo Mejía’s season does not pause after January. The Hay Festival Cartagena, a major literary and ideas gathering that draws international speakers and audiences, occupies the theatre in late January or early February.

The Cartagena International Film Festival (FICCI), the oldest film festival in Latin America, follows in March, using TAM for premieres and gala screenings. Jazz nights, choral performances, and theatre productions fill the gaps, making the theatre a year-round engine for the city’s creative economy.

The Read-Through for Investors and Expats

A well-programmed cultural season at Teatro Adolfo Mejía 2026 signals more than entertainment. It indicates that Cartagena’s public and private sectors continue to invest in heritage infrastructure and international programming, which supports property values inside the walled city and in adjacent neighbourhoods like Getsemaní.

For expats considering Cartagena as a base, the density of high-quality cultural events from January through April reduces the sense of seasonal isolation that can affect smaller Caribbean cities. The presence of a resident orchestra and a reliable festival calendar also creates demand for short-term rentals, hospitality services, and bilingual professional staff.

Colombia’s broader push to grow cultural tourism as a share of GDP, supported by ProColombia and local mayoral offices, means venues like TAM are likely to see continued public funding and international partnership. The 2026 season opening is a concrete data point in that longer trend.

Frequently Asked Questions

When does the Teatro Adolfo Mejía 2026 cultural season begin?

The season opens on 4 January 2026 with the inaugural concert of the 20th Cartagena International Music Festival. The festival runs through 12 January, with Teatro Adolfo Mejía hosting the main nightly symphonic and chamber music performances.

Does the 2026 season opening feature traditional Colombian gaita music?

The formal season opening is a classical music programme led by the Franz Liszt Chamber Orchestra. Gaita music is central to Cartagena’s cultural identity and appears in dedicated festivals such as the Festival Nacional Autóctono de Gaitas in San Jacinto, as well as in community events and occasional crossover workshops at the music festival.

What other events does Teatro Adolfo Mejía host in early 2026?

After the January music festival, the theatre hosts the Hay Festival Cartagena, a major literary and ideas event, followed by the Cartagena International Film Festival (FICCI) in March. Jazz, theatre, and choral performances continue through April and beyond under the management of the IPCC.

World.title: Latin American Players to Watch at the 2026 Cincinnati Open
World.content:
Latin America will send one of its deepest groups of men’s players in recent years to the 2026 Cincinnati Open, led by established Argentine contender Francisco Cerúndolo, Brazilian star João Fonseca and Peru’s rapidly rising Ignacio Buse. The combined ATP and WTA 1000 tournament will hold qualifying rounds on August 11 and 12 at the Lindner Family Tennis Center in Mason, Ohio. The expanded 96-player main draws begin August 13, with the singles finals scheduled for August 23.

The tournament field includes players from Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Peru and Paraguay. Several will arrive with realistic hopes of advancing beyond the opening rounds rather than simply adding regional representation to a field headed by the world’s leading players.

Fonseca is likely to attract the most attention. The 19-year-old Brazilian is listed at No. 28 in the Cincinnati field and has already developed one of the loudest and most visible fan bases on the men’s tour. Tournament organizers specifically identified him as a player whose supporters bring flags, noise and energy wherever he competes.

His 2026 season has included interruptions caused by back and shoulder problems, but he reached two clay-court quarterfinals and advanced to the third round at Wimbledon. Cincinnati will offer another test of how quickly he can adjust to the faster North American hard courts ahead of the US Open.

Francisco Cerúndolo enters as Latin America’s highest-ranked man in the announced field at No. 22. The 27-year-old has produced one of the strongest seasons of his career, winning titles in Buenos Aires and at Queen’s Club in London.

His Queen’s Club victory was especially significant. Cerúndolo became the first Argentine to win the tournament and earned the first ATP 500 title of his career, showing that his success is no longer limited to clay. That versatility could make him the region’s most credible candidate for a deep Cincinnati run.

Cerúndolo also leads an unusually large Argentine contingent. Tomás Martín Etcheverry, Mariano Navone, Juan Manuel Cerúndolo, Sebastián Báez, Román Andrés Burruchaga, Thiago Agustín Tirante and Camilo Ugo Carabelli are all listed in the main draw.

Etcheverry is ranked No. 31 in the field after reaching the semifinals in Kitzbühel, while Navone, Báez and the younger Cerúndolo brother give Argentina additional depth. The size of the delegation reflects the country’s continuing ability to produce tour-level players even without a current superstar competing near the very top of the rankings.

One of the more intriguing names is Ignacio Buse. The 21-year-old Peruvian is listed at No. 35 and has climbed rapidly enough to enter the discussion around possible seeding at major tournaments.

Buse reached the Rio Open semifinals earlier this year after defeating former Wimbledon finalist Matteo Berrettini. His rise is particularly notable because Peru does not have the player-development depth or tournament infrastructure associated with Argentina or Brazil. Cincinnati will provide another opportunity to measure his progress against a field containing nearly every leading player in the world.

Chile’s Alejandro Tabilo is another dangerous opponent. The left-hander is ranked No. 30 in the Cincinnati field and reached the semifinals in Bastad in July before losing a close three-set match to Andrey Rublev. Tabilo’s serve and left-handed patterns can make him an uncomfortable early-round matchup, particularly if he can transfer his recent clay-court form to the hard courts. He has already defeated Fonseca this season, winning their three-set meeting in Buenos Aires.

Paraguay will be represented by Adolfo Daniel Vallejo, who is listed at No. 63. His presence adds another country to a men’s field that is considerably more geographically diverse than Latin American representation on the women’s side.

Colombia’s Camila Osorio is currently the region’s only confirmed direct entrant in the women’s main draw. Her speed, defensive ability and willingness to extend points have helped her compete effectively across surfaces, but she will face a difficult field containing the full women’s top 10 and numerous Grand Slam champions.

Other Latin American women will have to earn their places through qualifying. Colombia’s Emiliana Arango, Argentina’s Solana Sierra and Nadia Podoroska, and Mexico’s Renata Zarazúa are included in the 48-player qualifying field. Twelve women will advance to the main draw after two rounds.

The final draw will determine whether Latin America’s leading players receive manageable openings or immediate assignments against the tournament favorites. Even before those matchups are known, Cincinnati offers a revealing test. Cerúndolo has already demonstrated that he can win a major title away from clay.

Fonseca is trying to convert exceptional promise into consistent results. Buse is carrying Peruvian tennis into unfamiliar territory, while Tabilo and Argentina’s deep group remain capable of disrupting almost any section of the draw.For Latin American tennis, the question in Cincinnati will not be whether the region is represented. It will be how many of its players remain standing when the tournament reaches its decisive second week.

World.title: Watching the 2026 World Cup Final in a Costa Rica Dive Bar
World.content:
Since moving to Costa Rica in 1990, I have not missed a World Cup final. I’ve watched them from a bar, from a friend’s house, and from the comfort of my own home. For 2026, I planned on something different. I took the trip over the mountain to San José, ready to attend the huge public party at La Sabana Park.

It seemed the perfect way to watch the match, surrounded by thousands of enthusiastic fans in an atmosphere of pure fiesta de fútbol. When I got to San José and informed my friend Roberto of my plans, he immediately set out to change my mind. The park would be packed with rowdy drunks and screaming kids, he said, and an older dude like myself would feel alone and out of place amid the throngs.

So I didn’t go to the big party. Instead, I joined my friend at one of his favorite San José dive bars. It was a casual, unpretentious, open-air place on a narrow street in a downtown barrio, with a 12-seat bar and several tables and chairs in an area next to the bar. The crowd was an assortment of older gringos and younger Ticos, with a couple of aging hookers completing the mix.

The bar had a representative liquor selection and Stella Artois beer in addition to the domestic brands. There were two TVs above the bar, but they were not in sync. One was a few seconds ahead of the other.

The largest-screen TV was in the separate part of the restaurant. This TV, which no one watched, was about 25 to 30 seconds ahead of the ones over the bar. I sat at the bar, turned at an angle to keep an eye on play. Any time there was an exciting run, I would look to the bar TV for a quick replay.

By the time Spain scored the winning goal, many of the clients had figured out that the TV with no sound was the one that was actually live. Spain completely dominated the game, and virtually everybody in the bar was happy with the result. In my small sampling, I was surprised by how few Ticos I spoke with were for Argentina.

Only two that I knew of supported them. One was a friend of mine who was actually born in Argentina, and the other was a huge fan of Lionel Messi. I thought more people would be rooting for the Argies, as they’re part of the Americas just like Costa Rica. Instead, I heard people complain of referee favoritism in their favor, calling them names like VARgentina and ArgenFIFA.

My younger daughter, who’s half Tica, half gringo and very proudly Latina, told me that people here are against Argentina because Argentinians reject being called Latinos. They consider themselves transplanted Euros and far superior to all the mestizos and mulattos to their north.

Another person told me that in 2014, the year of Costa Rica’s great run to the final eight, Diego Maradona appeared on ESPN before the Cup. When he looked at the group that Costa Rica was in, the so-called group of death that included three former world champions, Uruguay, England and Italy, he said Costa Rica should just take a gun, put it to their head and pull the trigger.

Alas, Maradona is dead, Messi is near retirement and Argentina has been dethroned as world champions. And until 2030, it’s Vive España!

Read more of Don Mateo’s writing from his newly published ebook.

World.title: Crown seeks video-link testimony from witness in Robert Arnold murder trial
World.content:
Crown seeks video-link testimony from witness in Robert Arnold murder trial

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Crown intends to apply for its main witness to testify by video link in the upcoming murder trial of Belize City resident Robert Arnold, citing concerns for the woman’s safety and immigration status.

Arnold, 21, is charged with the June 3, 2024 murder of Cruz Magana, who was shot and killed during an armed robbery at his family’s home and shop in the Fresh Pond Community of Burrell Boom.

During Arnold’s appearance before Justice Candace Nanton on Wednesday, Crown Counsel Joseph Perez told the High Court that the witness has left Belize and is seeking asylum in the United States.

According to the Crown, the woman remains fearful for her life and does not intend to return to Belize. Prosecutors also argued that travelling back to testify could affect her asylum application.

Justice Nanton instructed the Crown to formally file its application and set September 18, 2026, to deliver her decision on whether the witness will be permitted to testify remotely.

Arnold, who is represented by attorney Dale Cayetano, is scheduled to stand trial between October 18 and 23, 2026.

Police allege that two armed men entered the Magana family’s home and business, stole cash and a cellphone, and fatally shot the 32-year-old victim. Witnesses reportedly told investigators that they were able to identify the gunman.

Arnold previously faced a separate murder charge in connection with the death of Rudolph “Bobo Youth” Lewis. However, the case against Arnold and co-accused Travis Jamaal Herbert ended in June 2026 after the Crown entered a nolle prosequi.

World.title: Pre-trial hearing set for Kentroy McKoy in Mark Francisco murder case
World.content:
Pre-trial hearing set for Kentroy McKoy in Mark Francisco murder case

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A pre-trial hearing has been scheduled for October 1, 2026, for Kentroy McKoy, the sole remaining accused in the August 2024 murder of Belize City fisherman Mark Francisco.

McKoy appeared before Justice Candace Nanton in the High Court on Wednesday, accompanied by his attorney, Oscar Selgado. He remains on remand while awaiting trial.

McKoy was initially charged alongside Degron Shakeel Joseph, but the murder charge against Joseph was withdrawn earlier this year on the direction of the Director of Public Prosecutions. Joseph was reportedly granted immunity in exchange for his testimony in the case.

Francisco, 53, was fatally shot on the morning of August 4, 2024, while preparing for a fishing trip near Cemetery Lane and Yarborough Road.

Police said a gunman exited a silver Toyota 4Runner and opened fire before fleeing. Investigators reportedly tracked the vehicle through surveillance footage from Ladyville into Belize City and later to Santa Barbara Street.

The investigation allegedly linked Joseph and McKoy to the vehicle shortly before the shooting. Both men were arraigned for murder on August 13, 2024.

World.title: Trial of Three San Pedro men accused of shooting at fishermen and burning their boat deferred to 2027
World.content:
Trial of Three San Pedro men accused of shooting at fishermen and burning their boat deferred to 2027

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The trial of three San Pedro residents accused of pursuing and firing at two fishermen before allegedly setting their boat ablaze has been pushed into the High Court’s 2027 criminal calendar.

John Hernandez, 26, Shelby Jonathan Hernandez, 22, and Hector Pop, 29, appeared before Justice Nigel Pilgrim on Wednesday, July 22. The judge informed the accused men that the court’s remaining 2026 trial calendar was full and their case could not proceed until sometime in 2027.

The matter was adjourned until September 16, 2026, for mention, when the court is expected to consider a tentative trial date.

The three men are jointly charged with one count of arson and two counts of aggravated assault stemming from an incident on July 31, 2024, in the Tranquility Bay area of northern Ambergris Caye.

According to reports published shortly after the incident, then-23-year-old fisherman Eliezer Aldana and another man were fishing at around 4:30 a.m. when they were intercepted by a boat carrying four men. The men allegedly threatened the fishermen and ordered them to leave the area.

When Aldana attempted to leave, the other vessel allegedly pursued them while its occupants fired several shots in their direction. The fishermen were not injured and managed to reach a nearby resort, where they sought refuge.

The prosecution alleges that the fishermen’s 18-foot white boat, named La Gringa, was subsequently taken farther out to sea and deliberately set on fire. The burning vessel reportedly drifted onto the beach and sank before it was later recovered and taken to a mechanic shop.

The boat was valued at $21,000.

Public reports indicate that John Hernandez and Pop were the first two men taken before the court in August 2024 in connection with the incident. They were represented at the time by attorney Orson “OJ” Elrington, who indicated that he would apply for bail on their behalf.

John Hernandez and Pop are presently out on bail. Shelby Hernandez remains on remand in connection with a separate case in which he is charged with the March 2026 murders of Karim Nazim Espat, Oscar Modesto Mas and Yerlin Marisol Bueso Alvarez in San Pedro. No plea has been taken in that matter.

World.title: Burrell Boom man fined $2,000 for breaking into Fresh Pond house while 13-year-old girl was at home; He didn’t steal anything – Girl locked herself in room
World.content:
Burrell Boom man fined $2,000 for breaking into Fresh Pond house while 13-year-old girl was at home; He didn’t steal anything – Girl locked herself in room

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Burrell Boom resident has avoided imprisonment after pleading guilty to burglarizing a woman’s home while her 13-year-old daughter was inside.

Christopher Smith Jr. was fined $2,000, along with $5 in court costs, when he appeared for sentencing in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday, July 20. He must pay the fine by November 15, 2026, or serve six months in prison.

Smith had pleaded guilty to burglary on July 17 and was remanded until sentencing.

The court heard that on May 5, the homeowner left her daughter doing homework inside their Fresh Pond Community residence while she briefly visited her mother. During that time, Smith allegedly damaged a lock and entered through the rear of the house.

The frightened child later called her mother and reported seeing a man standing outside her bedroom door. He reportedly said “hello” before leaving. The girl locked herself inside the room and was found crying when her mother returned.

Nothing was stolen, and no one was physically harmed.

In determining the sentence, the Senior Magistrate considered the minimal property damage, Smith’s early guilty plea and the apparent lack of planning. A starting fine of $3,300 was reduced because he had no previous burglary conviction and received a further one-third discount for pleading guilty.

Smith previously faced two murder charges in connection with a double killing in Hattieville, but the charges against him were withdrawn in November 2025. Two other accused men remain before the court.

World.title: Tatiana Alvarado dies in fiery collision near Bella Vista village
World.content:
Tatiana Alvarado dies in fiery collision near Bella Vista village

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating a fatal road traffic accident that claimed the life of a 39-year-old woman near Bella Vista Village on Saturday afternoon.

The accident occurred at approximately 4:35 p.m. on July 25, 2026, along the Thomas Vincent Ramos Highway between Miles 44 and 45.

Initial investigations indicate that 26-year-old Daunte Oliver Eden Noralez, of a Belmopan address, was driving a Ford Escape toward Punta Gorda when he allegedly attempted to overtake a Lifan 150 motorcycle travelling in the same direction.

During the attempted overtaking maneuver, the vehicles collided, causing the motorcyclist, Tatiana Alvarado of Bella Vista Village, to sustain fatal injuries. Police arrived at the scene and found the motorcycle engulfed in flames.

Alvarado was transported to the Southern Regional Hospital, where she was pronounced dead on arrival.

Noralez has been detained pending further investigation.

World.title: 19-year-old injured in early-morning Cemetery Road shooting
World.content:
19-year-old injured in early-morning Cemetery Road shooting

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 19-year-old construction worker was injured in an early-morning shooting in Belize City on Sunday following the Jouvert in July event.

Police say the incident occurred at approximately 4:55 a.m. on July 26 as Arnize Young was walking along Cemetery Road.

Two men travelling on a motorcycle reportedly approached and fired several shots in Young’s direction, causing him to sustain gunshot injuries.

Young’s injuries have been classified as non-life-threatening. Police have not announced a motive or any arrests as their investigation continues.

World.title: BREAKING: Denvoy Bartley identified as tonight’s murder victim in Unitedville triple shooting
World.content:
BREAKING: Denvoy Bartley identified as tonight’s murder victim in Unitedville triple shooting

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Breaking Belize News has confirmed that Denvoy Feliciano Bartley of Banak Street, Belize City, is the man who was murdered in a triple shooting in Unitedville Village on Saturday night.

Bartley was reportedly travelling with his twin brother and another man when the group was targeted near a bus stop while carrying out an errand in the village. All three men were rushed to the Western Regional Hospital, where Bartley later succumbed to his injuries. The two other victims remain hospitalized.

Bartley had previously survived a shooting in Belize City in April 2021. He was later charged in 2023 with the murder of Lionel Budna; however, the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions discontinued the case in November 2024 by entering a nolle prosequi, and Bartley was released after spending more than a year on remand.

Police investigations into Saturday night’s murder are continuing.

World.title: BREAKING: Belize City man murdered in triple shooting in Unitedville, Cayo
World.content:
BREAKING: Belize City man murdered in triple shooting in Unitedville, Cayo

By Jose Luis Cruz: A Belize City man was murdered in a triple shooting that occurred on Saturday night in Unitedville Village in the Cayo District. The incident occurred near a bus stop in the village in the same vicinity that a policeman in uniform was also shot and killed.

A group of young men had gone to do an errand in the village when they were targeted by the gunman(men). Three (3) of the men received shooting injuries and were rushed to the Western Regional Hospital in Belmopan for treatment.

One of the shooting victims has succumbed to his injuries while the other two (2) are receiving treatment. The victim who died is a resident of Banak Street in Belize City.

This murder is the latest in a recent spike of shootings and murder that has occurred in Unitedville in the last two (2) years.

World.title: PEP transfer trap
World.content:
Head of the Jamaica Association of Principals of Secondary Schools (JAPSS), Anniona Jones, is urging parents to carefully consider requests to transfer their children to other high schools following the Primary Exit Profile (PEP) placement process, warning that such decisions should be based on what is best for the child’s development rather than the perceived prestige of an institution.

Jones also cautioned school administrators against accepting an influx of transfer students primarily for financial gain, arguing that overcrowding can undermine the quality of education and place unnecessary strain on teachers and school resources.

She said she is aware that some schools have received 60 or more transfer requests and, while she understands that every parent wants the best for their child, not every school is equipped to provide the type of academic intervention some students need.

“We have to be very careful about how we think of some schools as intervention schools or schools for children with low academic aptitudes, because as the children start to do better, people are still not going to want to place their children necessarily in those schools. You have schools that have low levels of enrolment, and then you have other schools that are bursting at the seams.

“It becomes an issue, though, for school governance to be able to say to a principal and have that conversation at the board level that, ‘Listen, this school was built for X amount.’ I still don’t know why we have schools on [the] shift [system] when we have so many schools that are underpopulated.

“It’s really…a policy issue, but a board can make a decision that we are going to limit our school sizes to no more than 22 to 30 children per class,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

Jones argued that limiting class sizes is particularly important for schools offering science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) subjects, which she said are best taught in smaller classes. She added that smaller class sizes would also ease the burden on teachers by reducing the volume of books to be marked and allowing more targeted feedback and individual attention for students.

She noted that, in many cases, schools are reluctant to reduce enrolment because funding is largely allocated on a per-student basis, making lower student numbers financially disadvantageous. However, she welcomed the Government’s move toward a more equitable funding model, describing it as a positive step in the right direction.

Jones also expressed concern about the growing costs parents incur while seeking transfers, noting that some schools charge application fees between $1,000 and $5,000.

“If you look at the cost for transfer requests, you could have a school, in theory, getting a request of 100 children wanting to come in. If you charge each child $1,000, that’s $100,000 even if your school can only take in 20, so you could do a lot with an additional $100,000. Some parents are going around paying five schools $1,000 a pop or more,” said Jones.

She added: “Some schools, I hear, transfers are as much as $5,000 just to request a transfer, and they are not guaranteed to get in. Parents have to also look at that as well and understand that placing your child in a school where your child may be in the bottom quarter, or smack in the middle, may not be as good for your child as placing them in a school where your child may come first, second, or third and get a confidence boost, or placing a child in a school that can cater to their needs,” she reasoned.

Jones, who is the principal at Haile Selassie High School, added that, while traditional high schools often have a wider range of programmes and extracurricular activities, they can also place a greater financial burden on families.

In contrast, she said some non-traditional

schools may offer programmes that are better suited to a child’s interests and abilities while remaining more affordable.

“Sometimes we have to be very discerning that we don’t spend all the money to buy the car but turn around and can’t buy gas and can’t change the tyre, or can’t deal with the servicing and upkeep after the free servicing is finished.

“Schools need support to grow, so allow your child to be placed in an institution that can give you the financial wiggle room as well, to do some other things for your child. Otherwise, your child may go into these spaces, can’t function, and you can’t participate fully to keep the school offering what you say you want,” said Jones.

She further urged parents to do their part in ensuring that the children they send off to these institutions can have a positive impact, especially for non-traditional high schools that have a stigma of being violent environments.

“Send us the best version of your children, then we wouldn’t have to worry about the children, and every space can be a safe, developing, nurturing space for every child to be able to do all the things that they want to do, if parents are willing to help build it, fund it, create it,” she said.

She added: “We have the buildings, we have these teachers, we have the class sizes; it makes better sense to me to place your child in a smaller school to treat with the PEP score,” said Jones.

World.title: 140% spike in deportees to Jamaica last year
World.content:
In this Jamaica Observer file photo, Deportees from the US are on the move after arriving in Jamaica and being processed by local security officials.

SIXTY of the 1,317 people deported to Jamaica in 2025 were convicted of murder, manslaughter or attempted murder in the deporting country, with 52 of them being sent from the United States.

One was deported from Canada, five from England, and two from ‘other’ countries.

The information is outlined in the 2025 edition of the Economic and Social Survey Jamaica, a publication of the Planning Institute of Jamaica (PIOJ).

It listed 171 of the deportees having possession of drugs convictions, with a significant majority – 142 – coming from the USA. Two were deported from Canada, three from England, while 24 were sent back from other countries.

The 2025 list of deportees also included 134 people convicted for the serious offences of wounding, assault and battery.

The US again topped the list of these deportees with 115.

The sexual offences category listed 63 deportees last year, with the US sending back 50, Canada four, England five, while four came from other countries.

However for the vast majority of deportees, 610 were sent back to Jamaica for immigration violations including illegal entry, overstay of visa, and illegal re-entry.

There were 95 deportees convicted of firearm offences, with 88 running afoul of the law in the US. Other offences on the list included larceny, fraud/false document, kidnapping, and money laundering.

Of the total 1,317 deportees in 2025, 967 came from the US, which has a set policy of deporting Jamaicans to their homeland on the last Thursday of each month.

Last year saw Jamaica also receiving 70 deportees from Canada, 25 from England, and 255 from other countries.

The total represents a 140 per cent increase when compared to the 547 who were returned to Jamaica in 2024.

In May, Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Senator Kamina Johnson Smith said approximately 2,500 Jamaicans have been confirmed for deportation from the US this year.

Johnson Smith provided the update while speaking at a press conference at the Office of the Prime Minister as she moved to dismiss reports that some 4,000 Jamaicans are set to be deported from the US as part of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.

“Allow me to be clear that 4,000 Jamaicans are not being returned now. For some time it has been in the public domain that the US authorities had close to 4,000 persons in their records with final orders for deportation against their names. It is now our understanding that approximately 2,500 have been confirmed for removal over a period of time, to be determined by logistics, their own legal processes, and other factors,” said Johnson Smith.

She pointed out that the deportation of Jamaicans is not a new phenomenon, and said the Government remains committed to honouring its international obligations to receive its citizens while safeguarding national security and public safety.

“It is not a new phenomenon. For decades, Jamaica has facilitated the repatriation of its citizens under established international arrangements. We receive our citizens when they are returned to us. Just as we expect, and we do, repatriate foreign nationals who commit serious crimes or breaches of our immigration laws,” added Johnson Smith.

The foreign affairs minister further pointed out that the Government has expanded the National Reintegration and Rehabilitation Strategy to coordinate reintegration services for the deportees.

“On May 5th, Cabinet approved the establishment of a National Technical Working Group on Voluntary and Involuntary Migrants, recognising that not only is the grouping not homogeneous in and of itself, but we now have a sub-grouping of those who are returning of their own motion — determining the circumstances in the US to not be where they wish to remain — and those who are being returned, those who have the decision made for them. This technical group is chaired by the Planning Institute of Jamaica. Oversight is provided by the ministries of national security and foreign affairs and foreign trade; and the technical group comprises several ministries, departments, and agencies, as well as civil society partners.

“Its mandate is to coordinate reintegration services and to ensure that returnees are supported in a structured, sustainable manner — and this includes their reception, verification, health checks, security, vetting, and access to social and legal support where necessary,” Johnson Smith said as she sought to allay fears about the possible security threats the deportees might bring.

“Monitoring and detention measures are in place [and] they will be applied. Again, stakeholders play key roles in helping us as partners in this reintegration and return process,” declared Johnson Smith.

Meanwhile, the PIOJ also reported that the total number of voluntary returned migrants stood at 852 in 2025, an increase of 52.1 per cent when compared with the 560 who returned home in 2024.

Voluntary returned migrants are people who choose to return to their homeland.

World.title: Sunday Jones transforms ‘pain 2 power’
World.content:
Sunday Jones addresses the media launch for her five-day Jamaica Tour, Ink Breath and Bars: Pain 2 Power, on July 20, 2026 at Sador’s Ethiopian Restaurant in Negril, Westmoreland. (Photo: Rosalee Wood Condell)

NEGRIL, Westmoreland — Poet and author Sunday Jones officially launched her five-day Jamaica tour, Ink Breath and Bars: Pain 2 Power, on Monday, July 20, bringing a message of healing, reflection, and creative empowerment to audiences across Jamaica.

Rooted in the mission of transforming personal pain into purpose through spoken word, the July tour blends live poetry performances, youth engagement, and community building.

A native of Atlanta, Georgia, Sunday Jones is a poet, author, and community leader known for founding Sunday Jones Productions and the Prison Brat Foundation. She functions as an ordained minister, certified life coach, event curator, and radio personality dedicated to giving a voice to the unheard and unseen. Her work focuses on healing from childhood trauma, faith, and personal evolution.

“Ink Breath and Bars is the ink of our soul, of our journeys, our writings, our poetry, our life.” Jones explained to the

Jamaica Observer. “The breath is the breath that we take, through word sound, through healing, through all of the things. It’s the breath that we need to take sometimes. All the time we breathe, but we sometimes need to take breaths. And the bars are the lyrical word sound that come from the ink and the breath. The tour is about community, culture, love, and liberation. It is to bring people together, to pull light from people who don’t understand that they have the light, or to elevate those that do have the light and want to go further. That is Ink Breath & Bars, to sum it up shortly.”

The tour features a line-up of community showcases, school visits, and curated intimate gatherings designed to inspire, connect, and celebrate. The journey began on July 21 at Kingston Night Market, followed by a visit to Haile Selassie High School on July 23. On July 25 the tour headed to Sador’s Ethiopian Restaurant in Negril for a special community gathering. It concludes on July 30 with an exclusive healing experience and Jones’ Solar Return Celebration.

The Ink Breath and Bars tour has gained significant backing from internationally renowned Jamaican dub poet and performance artist Yasus Afari. He highlighted the vital role poetry plays in community upliftment and personal transformation, endorsing Jones’ vision to use creative expression as a vehicle for emotional wellness and youth empowerment.

“Let us use the language and the arts to heal and to redeem our people from what I described earlier as neurolinguistic sorcery, and so bring neurolinguistic healing, so that we can heal in a wholesome and full-some way. So that even our tongue can be an instrument of life. We don’t have to have so much dissing and cussing and quarrelling as a small country who have been through such great tribulation,” he stated.

The poet seized the opportunity to issue a charge: “So we are calling on our fellow so-called entertainers, which I prefer to call edutainers, let us rise to that occasion. We are a great country, unprecedented in human recorded history. We are a talented and great set of people. Let us use this gift of art, music, poetry, film, dance, comedy, literature, photography, videography to empower our people, to uplift our people, to heal our people, and to help fulfil Jamaica’s sacred, national pledge to advance the entire welfare of the entire human race. Honour, love, and prosperity. Rastafari blessings.”

In addition to live performances, the tour serves as a promotional platform for Jones’ latest book, The Art of Rising: A Love Letter to My Becoming, allowing readers and lovers of dub and spoken word poetry to connect deeply with her published works.

With stops spanning from the vibrant creative spaces of Kingston to the west coast in Negril, Ink Breath and Bars: Pain 2 Power promises an uplifting cultural journey celebrating resilience, truth, and the transformative power of the Jamaican voice.

World.title: Breaking the cycle of underperformance
World.content:
Edwin Allen High School implemented a programme of extended learning that included Saturday mathematics classes, mathematics camps during school breaks, and mathematics marathons to provide intensive revision and examination preparation.

TARGETED intervention in 56 non-traditional high schools which were previously rated unsatisfactory or in need of immediate support by the National Education Inspectorate (NEI) has started to reap success.

The schools are beneficiaries of the National School Learning and Intervention Programme (NSLIP) introduced by the Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth and Information.

The programme was established in 2022 in response to the learning gaps/loss experienced by students from the disruption in the education system due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

The tactical approach was developed to expedite school improvement by targeting the critical factors that influence student outcomes.

It included increased instructional time, strengthened leadership practices, data-driven decision-making, enhanced teacher support, improved student welfare, and stronger monitoring and accountability systems.

Its primary objective was to provide a structured and cohesive framework capable of achieving measurable gains within a relatively short time frame while promoting sustainable practices to support long-term school improvement.

The evidence emerging from NSLIP schools has provided one of the strongest arguments for sustained intervention.

In the 2025 Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate (CSEC) examinations, all 56 schools participating in NSLIP recorded improvement in English A, while 41 recorded improvement in mathematics, with several schools demonstrating dramatic gains.

Among the schools reporting improvement was Edwin Allen High School in Clarendon, which was placed under NSLIP after its CSEC mathematics performance declined to 25.4 per cent passes in 2024.

Following the targeted intervention, the school’s CSEC mathematics performance increased to 74.1 per cent passes in 2025.

Jermain Harris, principal of Edwin Allen, said he worked closely with the vice-principal of programmes, the head of the Mathematics Department, and the Ministry of Education’s mathematics specialists to ensure that the curriculum delivery was aligned with the CSEC mathematics syllabus and that curriculum pacing was closely monitored.

“Teachers used assessment data to identify priority content areas and adjusted instruction to meet students’ learning needs.

“To increase students’ exposure to quality instruction, the school implemented an extensive programme of extended learning, which included morning intervention classes before the start of the regular school day, afternoon classes conducted after the scheduled timetable, Saturday mathematics classes, mathematics camps during school breaks, and mathematics marathons to provide intensive revision and examination preparation,” Harris said.

“These interventions enabled teachers to revisit difficult concepts, address learning gaps, provide individualised support, and reinforce key mathematical skills. To promote a culture of excellence and continuous improvement, the school also introduced an incentive programme for both teachers and students,” added Harris.

He said students were recognised and rewarded for attendance, improvement, and academic achievement, while teachers were acknowledged for exceptional commitment, innovative instructional practices, and improvements in student performance.

“These incentives contributed to increased motivation, accountability, and ownership of the intervention programme,” declared Harris.

At St Thomas Technical, which posted a pass rate of 33.2 per cent in English A in 2024, the score was doubled to 67.4 per cent in 2025.

In addition, the school, which struggled with 6.9 per cent passes in mathematics in 2024, improved to 22.8 per cent in 2025.

“It was important for us, first, to critically address the whole issue of discipline,” said Principal Rochelle Taylor Brown.

“So we instituted a School Wide Positive Behaviour Intervention and Support Framework to promote positive behaviour, improve student discipline, and create a safe and orderly learning environment.

“Specific students received lunch and ‘shout out’ during general assembly, and the best class received a free field trip,” added Taylor Brown.

She said Alternative Pathways to Secondary Education (APSE) coaches — specialist educators supporting students requiring additional academic, behavioural or learning interventions — were engaged to bolster curriculum delivery for English A.

“The APSE coaches, who are one branch of the English language officer support team, provide support to teachers to better equip them to deliver high-quality instruction and increased student engagement. These officers conducted training sessions and collaborative lesson planning with the teachers, assisting them in interpreting assessment data for better placement of students.

“They also created intervention programmes for students who were deemed as ‘critical’ — those who were either performing or reading below their grade level,” said Taylor Brown.

She said the school’s improvement in mathematics, “though we must get better, was as a result of increasing the five periods [two hours and 55 minutes of teaching and learning time] for students to nine periods [five hours and 15 minutes)”.

Meanwhile, Charlie Smith High School moved dramatically from a 13.1 pass rate in English A in 2024 to 75 per cent in 2025, with its maths score shifting from 8.8 per cent to 18.2 per cent over the period.

“To break the cycle of underperformance we prioritised high-yield, research-backed interventions. The High-Dosage Tutoring method was applied, where students identified as critically underperforming received 45 minutes of small-group tutoring [3:1 ratio] three times a week. Research shows this is the single most effective tool for learning recovery,” said Principal Christopher Wright.

“The Tiered Response to Intervention Framework was, therefore, adopted: Tier 1 – high-quality, differentiated core instruction; Tier 2 – small-group targeted remediation; and Tier 3 – intensive, one-on-one specialist intervention. Importantly, we integrated local culture, music, and social justice topics into the academic content to dramatically increase engagement and relevance for our inner-city youth,” added Wright.

He argued that accountability in a rising inner-city school such as Charlie Smith High must be transparent, data-driven, and supportive.

“As a result, we have established a tripartite monitoring matrix. There is the Live Data Wall & Dashboard, where we use a digital student achievement dashboard that tracks real-time data from formative and summative assessments. Student progress is colour-coded, allowing us to spot regressions instantly.

“Teacher Performance Portfolio and Reflections is another highlighted area, where teachers maintain digital portfolios that map lesson plans against student mastery data. Finally, there is the Data-Driven Dialogue Meeting, where every three weeks I meet with grade-level teams for data dialogues. In these meetings, teachers must present their class data, identify students who are lagging, and detail the specific reteaching strategies they will employ,” said Wright.

Among the other secondary schools at which the NSLIP was implemented, which recorded improved performances in English A, were Bustamante High School, which moved from 12.1 per cent passes in 2024 to 51.9 per cent in 2025; Fair Prospect High School, which jumped from 9.5 per cent to 73.7 per cent; and Greater Portmore High School, which improved from 21.3 per cent to 78 per cent.

World.title: BRIGHT START
World.content:
Jamaica’s Sunshine Girls celebrate during netball competition at the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham, England, at which they won the silver medal.

Jamaica’s Sunshine Girls opened their Commonwealth Games netball campaign with an emphatic 81-22 win over Trinidad and Tobago at the Hydro Arena in Glasgow, Scotland, on Saturday.

The Sunshine Girls will be aiming for back-to-back wins today when they take on New Zealand in Pool B, after the Silver Ferns beat Scotland 74-44 in their opening game.

Led by 33 goals from 41 attempts from UK-based Azara Wilmot on her senior team debut, the Jamaicans dominated a young Trinidad and Tobago team.

Meanwhile, Sabrina Lyn qualified for today’s final of the women’s 100m breaststroke, while Jamaica’s 3×3 men’s basketball team won one of their three games.

Also today, Martez Cope will make his first appearance of the Games when he takes on Lesotho’s Pooana Khoahli in their men’s 65kg round-of-16 boxing contest.

At the Hydro Arena yesterday, Jamaica’s netball Captain Shamera Sterling-Humphrey was pleased with the team’s execution after they restricted Trinidad and Tobago to a Commonwealth Games low in scoring.

Sterling-Humphrey said they had planned to stifle the Trinidadians’ offence and restrict their scoring chances.

“I’m really, really proud. I feel like each quarter we had a target,” she said after the match. “We started off at five, and then we lowered it. Unfortunately, they got, I think, seven in the second, but yeah, it’s good to keep them at two [in the final quarter] and know that we’re on target.”

Sterling-Humphrey said they were well aware of the advantage they had over their opponents and wanted to use the game as preparation for tougher matches.

“The emphasis lies on keeping possession of the ball. We cannot have that much turnovers when we come up against teams like Trinidad, because when it comes to the harder games, it will be much more difficult for us.”

The number-three-ranked Jamaicans led 24-5 after the first quarter, 43-12 at half-time and 60-20 after the third quarter before emptying the bench in the fourth, which they took 17-8.

The Jamaican defence also had 35 interceptions and 22 deflections, compared to four and seven, respectively, by their opponents.

Wilmot, who came off the bench in the second quarter, led the scoring with 33 goals from 41 attempts on her senior team debut.

Veteran Romelda Aiken-George scored 25 goals from 27 attempts, while Shanice Beckford converted all 16 of her attempts and Rhea Dixon scored seven from 11 attempts.

Afeisha Noel scored 17 of Trinidad and Tobago’s goals from 19 attempts, with Joelisa Cooper scoring the other five from seven attempts.

Lyn became the first Jamaican swimmer to reach a final after finishing fifth in her semi-final in 1:08.43 minutes at the Tollcross swimming centre. She had placed fourth in her first-round race in 1:09.11.

Lyn was also part of the Jamaican mixed 4x100m relay team that placed third in its first-round heat in 3:43.07, teaming with Collin McKenzie, Kito Campbell and Jessica Calderbank.

Today, Lyn and Calderbank will contest the women’s 100m butterfly, while McKenzie and Campbell are set to swim in the men’s 50m breaststroke.

The Jamaican men’s 3×3 basketball team beat Singapore 22-20 but lost 22-16 to England and 21-13 to Fiji in their opening games.

Also on Saturday, Jamaica’s Robert Simpson lost his third straight match in lawn bowls, going down 2-0 to Wales’ Ross Owen in the men’s singles.

Simpson is set to face England’s Sam Tolchard today and will complete his schedule on Monday against Pakistan’s Mohammed Ayub Qureshi.

World.title: A Love Story Woven in Couture
World.content:
(Photo: Lena Isely Photography)

When Trinbagonian style aribiter and designer Peter Elias’s daughter, Alexandra Nicole Elias, married Michael Andrew Gabriel on June 27, 2026, it was always destined to be a celebration at which the fashion would be every bit as memorable as the love story. Dressed in a custom Naeem Khan creation inspired by the timeless elegance of American actress and princess of Monaco Grace Kelly, Alexandra delivered a bridal moment that balanced couture craftsmanship with modern romance.

The romance, however, began long before the dress.

Although their families had been close friends in Trinidad for decades, Alexandra and Michael’s own love story blossomed from a quiet friendship during the COVID-19 lockdowns before flourishing while they were both studying in New York City.

Their shared appreciation for history made Stollmeyer’s Castle (Killarney) in Port of Spain the perfect setting for Michael’s proposal on July 30, 2025. There, the chief investment officer and managing partner of Samaan Capital Management Ltd surrounded Alexandra with hundreds of roses before asking her to spend forever with him — a grand gesture that beautifully foreshadowed the regal celebration to come.

Couture Before the Ceremony

The engagement celebrations unfolded six months later with an intimate soirée at Alexandra’s grandparents’ residence in St Clair. Held beneath the stars on January 3, 2026, the gathering embraced understated elegance, where candlelit tables, lush gardens, and thoughtful details created an atmosphere of effortless sophistication.

For the occasion, Alexandra turned to Naeem Khan, wearing a custom design inspired by one of the couturier’s early bridal creations. Eschewing traditional ivory in favour of a romantic sage-green palette, the look was perfectly attuned to its garden setting. Equal parts couture and contemporary, the gown foreshadowed the refined, fashion-led aesthetic that would become the signature of the couple’s wedding celebrations.

The Making of a Modern Grace Kelly

When June 27, 2026 arrived, Alexandra Nicole Elias and Michael Andrew Gabriel’s wedding unfolded as a masterclass in timeless elegance — where romance, heritage, and couture craftsmanship met in perfect harmony.

At the Church of the Assumption, Alexandra walked up the aisle for a nuptial Mass celebrated by Father Ronald Mendes, Father Emmanuel Pierre, and Father Leslie Tang Kai, beneath a breathtaking floral installation by Sandra Debs of Sandee’s. Inspired by Alexandra’s love of the outdoors and her affinity for colour, the floral design transformed the sacred space into an enchanting garden tableau, with delicate yet abundant blooms creating a setting that felt both organic and exquisitely refined.

For Alexandra, the wedding was an extension of her personal style language — a celebration of artistry, fashion, and the details that make a moment unforgettable. With a lifelong appreciation for design, influenced in part by her father’s own sartorial sensibility, the bride approached every element of the celebration with a couture mindset.

The centrepiece was her custom Naeem Khan bridal gown — a collaboration with the Indian-American designer that paid homage to one of fashion’s most enduring icons: Grace Kelly. The vision was a modern interpretation of classic bridal glamour — regal, yet effortless; dramatic yet impossibly light.

Crafted from layers of silk tulle and organza, the gown achieved an ethereal volume without weight, allowing Alexandra to move with grace. Rather than traditional beadwork, every embellishment was hand embroidered, creating a sense of texture and artistry reminiscent of haute couture. The accompanying veil mirrored the gown’s intricate detailing, extending the romantic silhouette with an air of timeless grandeur.

The bride’s accessories carried an equally personal significance. Alexandra designed her own tiara, a bespoke creation intended to transcend the wedding day and become a treasured family heirloom — a future symbol of love and legacy for generations to come.

Michael’s wedding-day look embraced understated sophistication. His custom black tailored tuxedo featured refined, subtle details that complemented Alexandra’s couture aesthetic while reflecting his own classic sense of style.

Together, the couple embodied a modern vision of wedding elegance — where fashion was not simply worn, but thoughtfully curated; where every stitch, bloom and detail told the story of a love built on tradition, artistry, and forever.

Flower girls in Meiling…

No detail was overlooked, including those for the youngest members of the bridal party. Alexandra enlisted Trinidad and Tobago’s pre-eminent designer Meiling Esau to create bespoke looks for her flower girls, each one conceived with the same couture sensibility as the bride’s own ensemble. Crafted from luminous silk taffeta and weightless silk tulle, the dresses showcased Esau’s signature heirloom fagoting stitch at the empire line — a painstaking hand-sewn technique synonymous with the house. Delicate hand-made, hand-dyed florals were artfully scattered across each silhouette and echoed on tiara-like bandeaus, lending the collection the romance of an English garden in bloom. The result was unmistakably Meiling — timeless, impeccably crafted and imbued with a sense of heirloom beauty that transcends the occasion itself.

Following the ceremony, guests made their way to the Hyatt Regency Trinidad Ballroom for the reception.

World.title: Woman among three fatally shot by police in Mandeville shootout
World.content:
MANCHESTER, Jamaica — Police have confirmed that a woman is among three people who were fatally shot during an alleged shootout on Caledonia Road in Mandeville Saturday afternoon.

Preliminary reports are that about 4:00 pm, police were alerted to a robbery spree and subsequently intercepted a getaway vehicle near Horseshoe Curve.

A highly placed police source said the occupants of the intercepted vehicle opened fire on the cops who then returned fire. A shootout ensued resulting in a prolonged standoff and running gun battle.

Police said a woman and two men were taken from the intercepted vehicle and taken to hospital where they were pronounced dead on arrival.

The incident happened in the vicinity of last Saturday’s double murder where nursing student Deenekia Pounall and Sadefa Henry were gunned down in a taxi by a gunman who posed as a passenger.

— Kasey Williams

World.title: MegaMart Catherine Hall property goes on sale for US$15 million
World.content:
The former MegaMart Catherine Hall location is on sale for US$15 million.

The property that once housed MegaMart’s Montego Bay operations has gone on sale for US$15.09 million, or $2.41 billion, nearly eight months following the impact of Hurricane Melissa on western Jamaica.

Cost Club Limited, trading as Megamart Wholesale Club, occupied the 89,674 square feet property since December 2007 when it first opened to customers in western Jamaica. However, the location was closed following the devastation caused by the Category 5 storm which flooded the location and left substantial damage.

The former Catherine Hall location is being offered on an ‘as-is’ basis, with realtor REMAX Elite Realty indicating that the property could be used for a range of commercial uses.

The property and building is being sold by Wilco Ltd which acquired the property in April 2015 for US$1.05 million ($119.63 million). The location was developed at a cost of US$20 million ($1.3 billion).

The MegaMart Catherine Hall and Portmore properties were sold to a group of pension funds in 2013 as part of a sale and leaseback transaction that was arranged by Scotia Investments Jamaica Limited (SIJL). That deal, which was reportedly valued at $2.3 billion, resulted in MegaMart maintaining operations at both locations and receiving cash from the transaction, but paying a monthly lease cost under a 15 year lease arrangement.

The Portmore location closed on June 30, 26 years after it opened in September 1999. The loss-making location was effectively subsidised by the operations of the Catherine Hall location. The closure of both locations resulted in the loss of more than 300 jobs as Cost Club undergoes a strategic consolidation for its remaining two locations.

The Portmore property was transferred in January 2013 for $1.05 billion. The owner is listed as Scotia Investments Jamaica on the property title, but transfer documents lists the National Insurance Fund (NIF), SIJL NCB Insurance Company Limited, Montego Bay I.T. Centre Limited, Grace, Kennedy & Co. Limited Pension Scheme, Jamaica Money Market Brokers Limited (JMMB) and Appliance Traders Group Pension Scheme as paying a transfer tax. The future of this property is unknown at this time.

Scojampen Limited, The Bank of Nova Scotia Pension Fund, owns the MegaMart Mandeville location while Lord Nelson Investment Limited owns the Waterloo Road location in St Andrew.

World.title: Extension du marché carbone : le jour où Macron et Bayrou ont dit non à quatre ministres
World.content:
Leur courrier faisait suite au conseil de planification écologique de mars 2025 qui, regrettaient-ils, “n’a pas permis d’échanger sur cette perspective”. Aucun des quatre intéressés, tous contactés par POLITICO, n'a souhaité faire de commentaire.

Tous les ingrédients du “backlash”

Le quatuor recommandait à l’Elysée et Matignon d’oser instaurer l’ETS2, l’extension du marché carbone européen, aux transports routiers et aux bâtiments. Malgré une échéance fixée en juin 2024, la France est l’un des seuls pays de l’Union européenne à ne pas avoir transposé cette directive. Comme 18 autres Etats, elle n’a pas non plus soumis son plan pour l’utilisation du Fonds social pour le climat, censé aider les plus modestes.

Le retard est pour l’instant sans conséquence puisque le marché carbone, censé s’appliquer au 1er janvier 2027, a finalement été reporté d’un an.

Il faut dire que la réforme est très sensible. Elle va alourdir le coût d’un plein à la pompe ou d’un chauffage au gaz ou au fioul, l’idée étant d’inciter les ménages à passer à l’électrique. Appliquée telle quelle, elle augmenterait les prix de l'essence en France de 12 à 15 centimes d’euros par litre, d’après les calculs des ministres.

Et ce n'est pas tout : décidé à Bruxelles, rappelant la taxe carbone, qui avait poussé les Gilets jaunes sur les ronds-points, l’ETS2 réunit tous les ingrédients d’un dossier politiquement inflammable. Le Rassemblement national ne s'y est d'ailleurs pas trompé et demande sa suppression.

1,2 milliard d’euros dès 2026

Mais dans ce courrier, les quatre ministres s'attachaient à présenter l’ETS2 comme une opportunité.

World.title: Police kill suspect in deadly Berlin Pride assault
World.content:
Ballout had rammed a van into a crowd on a path at the Tiergarten near the main venue of a weekend Pride event and then attacked people with a bladed weapon “believed to be a machete,” injuring many seriously, Dobrindt told journalists, confirming that one woman was killed and 29 people were hurt.

He added that Ballout “had previously come to the attention of authorities because of numerous criminal offenses, his radicalization, and his association with the Islamist scene.” Dobrindt said the suspect’s radicalization had previously resulted in a conviction.

According to a report by WELT (like POLITICO, part of the Axel Springer group), the suspect had been classified as a security threat and sentenced under the German Criminal Code for preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state. WELT also reported that a court had ordered Ballout to attend counseling as part of a de-radicalization program that aimed to prevent extremism.

Dobrindt said it could not be ruled out that “such horrific terrorist attacks could inspire copycats,” although he said the risk was low. He advised Germany’s federal states to strengthen security measures to avoid similar events.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz condemned the attack, and several European heads of state expressed their condolences.

Merz and several members of his Cabinet attended a memorial on Sunday. Ahead of the service Merz told journalists: “These attacks have only one purpose. They seek to divide our society. They seek to take away what is most precious to us: our openness and our freedom.”

He added: “We will not allow this poison of terrorism, this poison directed against our freedom, to spread farther through our society.”

This story has been updated.

World.title: Massive forest fires reignite political tensions in Spain
World.content:
The measure is notable because it has only been enacted once before, when the entire Iberian Peninsula suffered a massive blackout in April 2025. It is also a source of political tension, because the emergency declaration was made at the request of one of Sánchez’s most aggressive critics, Madrid’s center-right regional president, Isabel Díaz Ayuso.

Spain’s regional authorities normally have legal jurisdiction over disaster management, and are only meant to petition the government to declare a national emergency and take charge of response operations when they cannot handle them on their own.

Ayuso’s decision to request the declaration prompted center-left figures like Transport Minister Óscar Puente to slam the center-right leader and her People’s Party, and to argue her policies had undermined the Madrid region’s firefighting capabilities.

“We all know that the Military Emergency Unit [the branch of the Spanish Armed Forces responsible for providing disaster relief ] has become the new firefighting service for the autonomous communities governed by the People’s Party,” Puente wrote in a post on X. “They cut taxes for the rich, slash public services, and then ask the central government to solve their problems.”

Manuela Bergerot, spokesperson for the left-wing Más Madrid party, similarly criticized Ayuso, highlighting that firefighters have spent years demanding the regional government invest more in staff and equipment.

Madrid Forest Fire Prevention and Extinction Service is meant to have a staff of 124 firefighters, but 64 of the positions are currently vacant. Staff members complain of having lower salaries than those offered in the rest of Spain, and of being obliged to work with expired respiratory equipment and suits that haven’t been proven to be fireproof.

World.title: Russia wants 30,000 more troops from North Korea, Zelenskyy says
World.content:
Kim Jong Un sits with Vladimir Putin during a meeting in Beijing on Sept. 3, 2025. | Pool photo by AFPTV via AFP/Getty Images

Moscow and Pyongyang in 2024 signed a pact of “mutual assistance in case of aggression.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Moscow wants to bring in 30,000 additional troops from North Korea to fight alongside Russian forces in the Kremlin’s war against Ukraine.

"We also see Russia’s cooperation with North Korea. Russia wants to receive another 30,000 troops from North Korea," Zelenskyy said in his nightly address Saturday evening. "Since June, preparations have been under way in Russia’s Voronezh region to receive them."

According to estimates, Pyongyang already has transferred about 12,000 troops to Russia's Kursk border region, under a mutual defense pact signed with Moscow in 2024.

World.title: Romania blames Russia as military shoots down third drone
World.content:
Dassault Rafale fighter jets set off from Fetești air base in Romania in October 2023. | Daniel Mihailescu/AFP via Getty Images

Sunday’s incident marks the third drone shot down over Romania in as many days, in a further escalation for the NATO member.

A Romanian fighter jet on Sunday shot down a third drone that had entered its national air space in as many days, prompting President Nicușor Dan to blame Moscow for the "inadmissible and intolerable" incursions.

Sunday's incident marked the latest escalation for the NATO member. The series of incursions comes as Russian attacks on Ukraine's Danube region have increasingly spilled over the border.

"It is inadmissible and intolerable for the Russian Federation to continue violating Romania's airspace, which is, at the same time, NATO airspace and European Union airspace," Dan said on Sunday.

World.title: Berlin police hunt suspect in attack on pride parade that left 1 dead
World.content:
Police are seen at the scene of an attack during Berlin’s Christopher Street Day parade on July 25, 2026. | Nadja Wohlleben/Getty Images

Manhunt is under way for the suspected attacker, who is considered “to be part of Berlin’s Islamist scene,” according to police.

A man drove a van into a crowd at Berlin’s Christopher Street Day parade late Saturday, killing at least one person and injuring others.

Berlin police told POLITICO Sunday morning that one person was killed and 25 others were injured in the attack, some of them severely.

Police also said the suspect, identified as 21-year-old Abdul B., was “known to the police” before and is considered “to be part of Berlin’s Islamist scene.”

World.title: Romanian airspace violated by drones twice in 2 days
World.content:
Romanian fighter jets shot down drones in separate incidents on Friday and Saturday.

Romanian fighter jets on Friday and Saturday morning shot down two drones that were violating the country's airspace.

On Saturday morning, Romanian radar "detected another unauthorized penetration of the national airspace by a drone operating in the vicinity of the Ukrainian border" and two Romanian F-16 jets shot it down in an unpopulated area close to the border, the Romanian defense ministry said in a statement. Romania already shot down another drone on Friday.

Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Toiu said that the drone shot down on Friday "was a Shahed-type drone, the same kind Russia launches, night after night, against Ukraine."

"Two incursions in 48 hours are not an accident, they are a pattern, and our answer to that pattern is consistency: detection, interception, protection of our citizens, full transparency with our allies," Toiu said.

In a social media post, European Council President António Costa "commend[ed] the Romanian authorities for their swift and effective response."

World.title: Israel's move to recognise Armenian genocide stalls under regional pressure
World.content:
The Israeli parliament's decision to postpone a vote on recognising the Armenian genocide by Ottoman Turkey is being seen as a triumph for regional diplomacy, as Azerbaijan in particular seeks to avert a further escalation in tensions between its close allies.

Advertising

The Israeli government gave no official reason for postponing the vote to formally recognise the Armenian genocide by Ottoman Turkey during World War I, which would have ratified a motion approved by the cabinet last month.

Ankara strongly denies the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Armenians constitute genocide.

While the motion's architect, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar, called recognition a “moral duty”, critics say the move took aim at Turkey amidst rising tensions.

Based in Tbilisi, Israeli defence and security expert Eugene Kogan claims Israel badly miscalculated. “Foreign Minister Sa'ar could have waited and not just dropped a bomb that led to different repercussions coming from different sides,” he said.

Armenia, which is seeking to normalise ties with Turkey, reacted coolly, with Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan saying he saw no need to comment. Meanwhile, Israel’s close ally Azerbaijan reportedly lobbied Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to drop the motion.

“At the end of the day, it might be either dropped or dismissed, and it will not come again to the new parliament agenda,” predicted Kogan.

The Knesset dissolved on 17 July and won't reconvene until after elections scheduled for 27 October.

Israel's recognition of the Armenian genocide unsettles Turkey and Azerbaijan

Azerbaijan's influence

The Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that pressure from Azerbaijan tipped the scales, though officials deny it.

Azerbaijan supplies nearly 40 percent of Israel’s oil and is a major customer for Israeli arms. The two countries’ partnership involves frequent Israeli ministerial visits and strong military cooperation, especially crucial for Israel given Azerbaijan’s border with Iran.

Baku also maintains a deep alliance with Ankara, summed up in the phrase “one nation, two states”. As Israeli-Turkish tensions flare over the Gaza conflict and Ankara’s support for Hamas, Azerbaijan is walking a diplomatic tightrope.

Zaur Gasimov, a Caucasus expert at Istanbul’s Turkish-German University, believes Baku viewed the Israeli genocide motion as a direct threat to its difficult balancing act.

“I can imagine that there were negotiations and talks on various levels between political elites of both countries,” he said. “For Israel, Azerbaijan is still of paramount importance. I would even say it's much more significant than it used to be with regard to the situation in and around Iran. So Baku was and is maybe the key intermediary between Israel and the Republic of Turkey.”

In what may be a calculated move to turn up the heat on Israel, Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev welcomed Palestinian Prime Minister Mohammad Mustafa this month. It was the first visit by a Palestinian leader since 2011.

“They [Israel] perceive it with a great sense of caution,” claimed analyst Kogan. “They don't know exactly what came out of this particular meeting between Aliyev and the Palestinian prime minister. And so there is a lot of guessing games right now taking place in both Tel Aviv and Jerusalem about the outcome.”

Such ambiguity over Baku’s intentions could strengthen its diplomatic hand, he suggested: “If Aliyev is involved in this Palestinian issue directly and no longer indirectly, it makes the situation very different for the Israelis.”

Turkey warns it could be Israel's 'next enemy' as tensions escalate

Syrian precedent

Baku is already leveraging its strong relationships with both Israel and Turkey to cool tempers.

“We have organised meetings between Turkey and Israel in Baku, specifically at the very beginning of the change of the Assad regime in Syria, where both parties had their own legitimate concerns,” said Hikmet Hajiyev, chief foreign policy adviser to the Azerbaijani president.

Syria is viewed as a potential flashpoint, with Israel and Turkey having a military presence. One tangible outcome of Azeri-brokered talks was the establishment last year of a military hotline in Syria, providing a rare glimmer of hope as tensions continue to mount.

“It's not unavoidable that Israel and Turkey will reach confrontation. I think we can stop this process,” argued Gallia Lindenstrauss, a specialist in Turkish foreign policy at Tel Aviv University's Institute for National Security Studies.

“They have a hotline between the Israeli Air Force and the Turkish Air Force, making sure that we will not have a collision in the skies of Syria, because we know both air forces are operating there. And the hotline has managed to keep the situation quiet. If I'm trying to find some anchor of reassurance that Turkish-Israeli relations can be controlled, it's Syria.”

As Israel approaches elections, a temporary lull in Turkish-Israeli tensions is anticipated. Still, since the main opposition shares the government’s concerns over Turkey, relations are set to remain fraught.
