Los conocidos como tecos han copado muchísimos puestos dentro del Ministerio de Economía y del Banco de España. Pero también muchos de ellos han dado salto a la empresa privada. José Manuel Campa, que fue secretario de Estado de Economía y director de la Autoridad Bancaria Europea, trabajó durante cuatro años como director global de asuntos regulatorios del Banco Santander y ahora es profesor del IESE.

Probablemente el sector financiero es el que más clanes concentra entre sus directivos. Al ser un sector muy regulado, los bancos tienden a contratar a esos altos cargos administrativos. Y casi todos sus ejecutivos han pasado por alguna escuela de negocios. Otra de las figuras que en su día marcaron el devenir de la Bolsa española y que aún hoy siguen teniendo presencia es la de los antiguos agentes de cambio y Bolsa, una figura regulada, con similitudes a los notarios.

Algunos de ellos montaron sus propias empresas. Fue el caso de Francisco González, quien fundó FG Valores Brusátiles y acabó siendo presidente del BBVA. Otra firma creada por antiguos agentes de cambio y Bolsa fue AB Asesores. Tras vender la firma al banco estadounidense Morgan Stanley, este clan se dispersó y acabó recalando en muchas grandes compañías financieras, desde Bankinter a Mutua Madrileña. ¿Quién fue su socio más famoso? Un desconocido teco, llamado Luis de Guindos, que acabó presidiendo Lehman Brothers en España, siendo ministro de Economía y luego vicepresidente del Banco Central Europeo. Otro caso de libro de redes de poder, círculos superpuestos y agendas privilegiadas que definen el poder económico en España.

World.title: La democracia de las cucarachas: desarmadas y peligrosas
World.content:
Empezó con un insulto: un juez del Tribunal Supremo indio llamó “cucarachas” a unos jóvenes en paro. Siguió con un caso de corrupción: la filtración de los exámenes de acceso a las facultades de Medicina. Estos han sido los detonantes de un movimiento de protesta de miles de estudiantes enfrentados al Gobierno de Narendra Modi, cada vez menos democrático. El sábado el ministro de Educación dimitió y respondió así a la principal demanda de los manifestantes

Por primera vez en años, siento que es maravilloso ser india. Justo cuando parecía no quedar ninguna esperanza, han aparecido: las jóvenes cucarachas que llegaron con la lluvia. Los descendientes de la unión profana entre un juez y un chiste.

Todos conocemos la historia, pero la voy a repetir aquí, para que conste. En respuesta a un comentario arrogante y despectivo del presidente del Tribunal Supremo de la India, Surya Kant, que llamó “cucarachas” a unos jóvenes indios en paro, Abhijeet Dipke, un estudiante residente en Boston, publicó un comentario en Instagram: “¿Y si todas las cucarachas se unieran?”. Respondieron millones de personas. Y así nació el Partido Popular de las Cucarachas (Cockroach Janta Party, CJP). Dipke se convirtió en su flautista de Hamelín. Su primera exigencia fue la dimisión de Dharmendra Pradhan, el ministro de Educación [ayer dimitió, provocando la desconvocatoria de las protestas estudiantiles], que preside con aire de suficiencia un ministerio corrupto y podrido, en el que es habitual que se filtren los exámenes públicos: aproximadamente 152 desde 2014, según los partidos de la oposición. Estas filtraciones han destrozado la vida de millones de jóvenes que llevan años preparándose para ellos y cuyos padres, en algunos casos, han tenido que vender sus tierras o su casa para financiar los estudios de sus hijos y pagar las tasas de examen. Una nueva forma de extorsión legal. Tras la reciente filtración del examen de la Prueba Nacional de Elegibilidad y Acceso —a las facultades de Medicina— (NEET por sus siglas en inglés), 12 estudiantes desesperados se suicidaron.

Más información Quiénes son y qué quieren las “cucarachas” que están detrás de las manifestaciones masivas en la India

Mientras la indignación por el uso de la palabra “cucaracha” crecía hasta convertirse en un tsunami en internet, Dipke regresó de Boston el 6 de junio y fue directamente desde el aeropuerto a Jantar Mantar, el famoso lugar en el que se organizan las protestas en Delhi. El conocido activista y reformador educativo de Ladakh Sonam Wangchuk compareció con él y anunció que iniciaba una huelga de hambre indefinida. Seis estudiantes universitarios —Neha Bora, Manish Kumar, Aameen Amitosh, Danish Ali, Hrishikesh y Deepak, miembros de la Asociación de Estudiantes de la India (AISA), la rama estudiantil del Partido Comunista de la India (Liberación)— proclamaron que se sumaban al ayuno y se sentaron en un escenario vecino. Empezaron a surgir protestas en otras ciudades. A medida que el estado de salud de los huelguistas de hambre se agravaba, empezaron a llegar en persona a Jantar Mantar las masas de jóvenes cucarachas que se habían apoderado de internet. El CJP anunció que planeaban ir en manifestación hasta el Parlamento el 20 de julio, el día en el que se inauguraba el periodo de sesiones del monzón. Dos días antes de la marcha prevista, la policía sacó por la fuerza del escenario a Sonam Wangchuk y lo retuvo, primero en un hospital público y, más tarde, ante la insistencia de su esposa, en un hospital privado. Él continúa en huelga de hambre [al cierre de esta edición, Wangchuk había dado por concluido su ayuno]. Los estudiantes de AISA pusieron fin a la suya en la mañana del 20 de julio, día de la manifestación.

Las cucarachas se adueñaron de la capital. Llegaron en tren, autobús, avión y metro, más numerosos con cada hora que pasaba. Horas antes de que los primeros rayos de sol iluminaran los cielos monzónicos de Delhi, empezaron a congregarse decenas de miles en Jantar Mantar. Al amanecer, era evidente que una generación de jóvenes desesperados y furiosos que habían visto con sus propios ojos desvanecerse su futuro iba a reivindicar algo a lo que las generaciones de sus padres y sus abuelos habían renunciado: nuestra dignidad como pueblo y como país. Nuestros derechos como ciudadanos de una democracia. Los manifestantes, con su valentía y su integridad —y con su sentido del humor—, han expurgado el miedo corrosivo que se ha vuelto connatural en todos nosotros. Cuando acababa el día ya estaba claro que el motivo de la protesta era algo mucho más importante que la pura reivindicación de los manifestantes o sus líderes. Dharmendra Pradhan es una minucia. Nos jugamos mucho más: la podredumbre de todo el sistema de gobierno, de arriba abajo, ha quedado al descubierto y ha empezado a apestar como un cadáver en descomposición. Hasta las cucarachas más pequeñas, niños de apenas siete u ocho años, supieron expresarlo con claridad.

A pesar del nombramiento rápido y casi clandestino de un nuevo jefe de policía días antes de la manifestación y de los inquietantes rumores sobre la aterradora eficacia de nuestro aterrador ministro del Interior, tanto la policía como el ministerio erraron por completo sus cálculos sobre la magnitud del tsunami que se abatió sobre Delhi el 20 de julio. Lo intentaron todo. Bloquearon autobuses, carreteras y estaciones de metro. Fue en vano. Intentaron impedir el acceso a internet. Pero las jóvenes cucarachas —la generación de internet— desbarataron su campaña con un aluvión de memes y vídeos que hacían reír y llorar a la vez. En Delhi, nada menos que en Delhi, las chicas que formaban parte de la protesta dijeron que se sentían seguras entre la multitud, aunque algunas se quejaron de que las había manoseado la policía. Vimos a musulmanes, hindúes, cristianos, sijs, budistas, personas de todas las castas y clases sociales unirse, ayudarse y protegerse unas a otras mientras se enfrentaban a la policía. En lugar de sermonearnos o pronunciar grandes discursos, nos mostraron, nos demostraron, la India posible, la hermosa India de nuestros sueños.

Ante semejante peligro, la policía plantó barricadas metálicas de color amarillo soldadas entre sí y su atrezo habitual: camiones llenos de piedras y vehículos ya dañados, para que pareciera que los jóvenes se habían vuelto violentos y la policía había tenido que defenderse. Llevaron un ejército de matones vestidos de civil, armados con porras y palos. Antes de entrar en acción, los miembros de la Fuerza de Acción Rápida (RAF, por sus siglas en inglés) se quitaron la placa identificativa del uniforme. Las grandes cadenas de televisión se prepararon para difundir fielmente las mentiras. (Algunas se adelantaron y empezaron a contar cosas que todavía no habían pasado. En la India, los informativos suelen hablar del futuro, no el presente). Todo inútil. La policía y la RAF blandieron sus lathis (bastones) de forma salvaje, partieron la cabeza a niños y les fracturaron brazos y piernas. Lanzaron gas lacrimógeno. Pero los jóvenes siguieron manifestándose. Derechos al Parlamento. Derechos a donde habían dicho que irían. A medida que se acercaban, las fuerzas de seguridad tomaron posiciones y apuntaron sus AK-47 contra los estudiantes desarmados. Pero las cucarachas siguieron adelante. Y con su marcha, arrebataron al régimen cualquier resto del guante de terciopelo que cubría el puño de hierro del Gobierno y lo dejaron tal como es, tal como siempre ha sido. Un puño de hierro fascista. Una confederación de brutos sin capacidad de comprender la historia ni la diversidad del país que gobiernan. Gente que solo sabe odiar, pero que no tiene ni idea de lo que es amar. Ni pensar.

Cuando estaba ya cerca la manifestación, a nuestro valiente y fanfarrón primer ministro lo trasladaron a toda velocidad a un lugar seguro. A los miembros del Parlamento les impidieron salir del reluciente y nuevo edificio cuyo único propósito parece ser socavar la Constitución día tras día.

A última hora de la tarde, la policía de­sa­lojó el escenario principal del lugar de la protesta. Al caer la noche, la gente lo había recuperado. Cuando los policías se retiraron hasta el día siguiente, las cucarachas los ovacionaron en pie. Por golpear niños. ¡Wah Modi ji! ¡Wah! [¡Bravo, señor Modi! ¡Bravo!, en referencia al primer ministro Narendra Modi].

Es ingenuo pensar que esto va a derivar en un cambio político importante. Pero sería una estupidez no considerarlo más que un mero momento de euforia. No es extraño que las agencias de noticias y las cadenas de televisión, con sus retransmisiones en directo, estén plagadas de rumores, insinuaciones y teorías conspirativas que hablan de financiación extranjera y complots de la CIA. Yo, que soy una orgullosa andolanjeevi (“agitadora profesional”, el nombre despectivo que emplea Modi para referirse a gente como yo), confieso que, cuando todo empezó, yo también era suspicaz. Me preocupaba que nos dirigiéramos hacia otro momento como el de Anna Hazare: el supuesto movimiento popular de 2011 contra la corrupción que, fueran cuales fueran sus intenciones originales, acabó regalándonos tres mandatos de gobierno de un partido político que ha destruido todas las instituciones de este país, no hace ninguna distinción entre el partido y el Gobierno de la India, no respeta el país ni a sus ciudadanos y, en el plano internacional, nos ha avergonzado y ha puesto a la India de rodillas.

Pero mis sospechas sobre el Partido Popular de las Cucarachas se desvanecieron cuando vi la hostilidad con la que los trataban los grandes medios de comunicación. Esa fue para mí la primera señal y la más tranquilizadora. Me emocionó que Abhijeet Dipke perteneciera a una comunidad dalit (intocable) y me emocionó todavía más que nadie le diera importancia. Todo cambió para mí cuando le oí decir: “Si me llamara Khalid, o si fuera musulmán, a estas alturas ya estaría en la cárcel”. Tuvo el valor de denunciar la vulgaridad con que funcionan las cosas en la India: el hecho de que en nuestro país no hay nada (ni siquiera, y sobre todo, la ley) que sea igual para todo el mundo. Todo depende por completo de la religión, la casta, la clase social, el origen étnico y el sexo de cada uno. Fue una observación profunda, expresada con sencillez. El hecho de que dijera algo así en público, cuando incluso los políticos de la oposición se limitan a hablar de “comunidad minoritaria” en vez de “musulmana”, por miedo a una “reacción violenta de los hindúes”, me animó a ir inmediatamente a Jantar Mantar. También sabía que, cuando Dipke eligió el nombre de “Khalid”, podía muy bien estar refiriéndose a Umar Khalid, el profesor de la Universidad Jawaharlal Nehru que, como Sharjeel Imam y otros muchos, lleva ya casi seis años en prisión sin que lo hayan juzgado. ¿De qué delito se le acusa? De exhortar a los manifestantes a no caer en la violencia durante las protestas de 2020 contra la Ley de Enmienda de la Ciudadanía, a pesar de que en esos momentos Delhi sufría una oleada de incendios provocados, asesinatos e incendios de mezquitas instigados por matones de patrullas ciudadanas hindúes bajo la mirada de una policía complaciente y, en ocasiones, incluso partícipe. Todas las peticiones de libertad condicional han sido denegadas por unos jueces que, por lo visto, han dejado de tener la valentía de hacer, o incluso comprender, lo que es justo.

Mientras avanzaban las cucarachas, cada vez más numerosas, me vino a la cabeza una reflexión: “Menos mal que no son mayoritariamente musulmanes, ni sijs, ni cristianos, ni adivasi [los habitantes originales de la India]. Los habrían aplastado, matado, disparado o encarcelado. Gracias a Dios que no son cachemires. Quizá los habrían dejado ciegos (aunque algunos sí sufrieron heridas causadas por perdigones). Menos mal que son en su mayoría hindúes”. Así de triste es este momento en la India. Ahora bien, las cosas podrían variar en cualquier instante. Estamos en lo que llaman una “situación cambiante”. Hay noticias de que se está trasladando en avión desde otros Estados a miles de efectivos paramilitares. No sabemos qué va a pasar en los próximos días.

¿Cómo nos deja todo esto? A diferencia del movimiento de Anna Hazare, del que se informó de manera frenética e ininterrumpida día y noche durante semanas, en cientos de canales de televisión histéricos de los grandes grupos mediáticos, las cucarachas del PCJ solo cuentan consigo mismas y con internet. A diferencia del movimiento de Anna, en el que se infiltró y atrincheró la Asociación Patriótica Nacional (Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, RSS), mientras el BJP de Modi se congregaba a las puertas, perfectamente dispuesto a aprovechar electoralmente el frenesí generado por la televisión, las cucarachas no tienen a ningún partido de la oposición esperando entre bastidores, preparado para tomar el relevo. La ira espontánea que estamos presenciando se disipará si no se lleva a cabo un verdadero trabajo político; si los adultos y los partidos de la oposición no aparcan sus maniobras y sus disputas mezquinas y muestran algo de solidaridad. El Gobierno sabe que hay pocas probabilidades de eso. Se mantiene impertérrito porque piensa que le basta con esperar. Los Estados tienen el poder de esperar. La gente, no.

Manifestantes detenidas durante una protesta frente a la residencia del primer ministro Narendra Modi, el pasado 21 de julio. Adnan Abidi (REUTERS)

En estos momentos, la revuelta de las cucarachas es una más de las numerosas protestas que están desarrollándose en toda la India. Los adivasi de Madhya Pradesh se manifiestan contra el proyecto de conexión entre los ríos Ken y Betwa. Los habitantes de las aldeas de Uttarakhand protestan contra la tala masiva de árboles. La gente protesta contra la destrucción medioambiental de las islas Nicobar Mayores. Manipur es un hervidero. Los puestos de trabajo están desapareciendo. Los precios se disparan. La furia va en aumento. Y la utilización de la religión que hacen el BJP y la RSS está quedando en evidencia como lo que siempre ha sido: un engaño. Una fiebre del oro impulsada por mafiosos. El saqueo del templo de Ram en Ayodhya [el robo de donativos desde 2020 y denunciado en junio] nos ha proporcionado la representación de un mal guion de Bollywood: acicalados líderes espirituales y políticos corruptos que construyen hoteles, acumulan propiedades inmobiliarias y circulan en todoterrenos, enriquecidos a costa de la fe de los pobres e ingenuos. Los tentáculos de la corrupción y el robo a plena luz del día llegan hasta la cima.

¿Podrá la energía de las cucarachas sacarnos de este pozo? No es fácil. Un repaso rápido a los resultados de los movimientos populares en la India no invita al optimismo. Es una historia resumida de ambiciones menguantes y sueños rotos. En los años sesenta y setenta, varios movimientos —entre los que estuvo la rebelión armada de los naxalitas— exigieron la redistribución de la riqueza y las tierras para los labradores; los aplastaron. En los años ochenta y noventa, otros movimientos sociales, entre los que destacan el Narmada Bachao Andolan y, más tarde, los maoístas de Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh y Jharkhand, lucharon contra la expulsión de los agricultores y las tribus indígenas de sus tierras. Es decir, pedían que no arrebataran a los pobres lo que les quedaba. También a ellos los aplastaron. En la primera década de 2000, ya no alcanzaban más que a mostrarse agradecidos por la Ley Nacional de Garantía de Empleo Rural (NREGA), el derecho a tres meses de empleo con el salario mínimo; una cantidad que equivale al precio de una buena comida en un restaurante caro de la ciudad. Pero el régimen también ha dejado de lado esa promesa y la ha sustituido por raciones de supervivencia —unas bolsas de provisiones con el rostro de Modi impreso— que arrojan con desdén a la gente, como las limosnas que se echan a los mendigos desde un coche en marcha, a cambio de gratitud y votos. Y, con todo, a medida que se va hundiendo la economía, también eso está en peligro.

Hoy, en 2026, nos hemos visto reducidos a luchar por nuestro derecho al voto y nuestra ciudadanía. La Ley de Enmienda de la Ciudadanía (CAA), acompañada del Registro Nacional de Ciudadanía (NRC), es la versión del nacionalismo hindú de las Leyes de Núremberg aprobadas en 1935 por la Alemania nazi, mediante las cuales el Tercer Reich concedía la ciudadanía a los alemanes en función de sus “certificados de origen” (¿cuántas personas en la India tienen esos documentos?). El movimiento contra la CAA y el NRC fue desdibujándose después de que las protestas masivas desembocaran en el asesinato de manifestantes y el encarcelamiento de activistas. Pero sirvieron para que el Gobierno aplazara la aplicación de esas nuevas leyes. Sin embargo, la CAA y el NRC, que muchos consideraban —con razón— pensados sobre todo para los musulmanes, han vuelto a aparecer ahora con el nombre de SIR (Revisión Especial Intensiva) de los censos electorales. Se nos ha comunicado como si nada que ni siquiera el pasaporte es prueba de ciudadanía. Se está borrando a millones de personas de los censos electorales. El país entero ha emprendido una búsqueda desesperada de su “certificado de origen”. No sabemos cuál es nuestra situación. ¿Somos legítimos? ¿Ilegítimos? ¿Tenemos derechos? ¿Quiénes de nosotros acabarán en esos enormes centros de detención que se están construyendo para los “ciudadanos dudosos”? ¿Pasaremos todo el día corriendo de un tribunal a otro? Los fascistas adoran el caos y la confusión.

Nuestro pánico y nuestra angustia pueden empujarnos a depositar demasiadas esperanzas en el movimiento de las cucarachas. Algunos ya lo han comparado con las revueltas juveniles que provocaron cambios de régimen en Bangladés, Nepal y Sri Lanka, pero la India es un país demasiado extenso para eso. Otros lo equiparan con el movimiento encabezado por [el político y activista] Jayaprakash Narayan que derrocó a Indira Gandhi en 1977. Sin embargo, esas comparaciones no sirven de nada. El Partido Popular de las Cucarachas no es nada de eso, tiene su propia identidad. Es un producto peculiar de su época. Son jóvenes vulnerables que se enfrentan a un Gobierno cruel y vengativo que ha demostrado ser despiadado con quienes se le oponen. No hay ninguna duda de que ya está tramando una venganza contra aquellos a los que considere los principales instigadores.

Abhijeet Dipke, líder e impulsor del Partido Popular de las Cucarachas, durante una de las protestas que llevó a la dimisión del ministro de Educación, Dharmendra Pradhan. ANUSHREE FADNAVIS (REUTERS)

¿Cómo es posible que un régimen que está volviéndose, a todas luces, enormemente impopular se atreva a no hacer ninguna concesión a quienes le votaron? Seguramente porque cree que ha conseguido manipular el proceso electoral y se ha apoderado de su maquinaria. La Comisión Electoral está llena de defectos en su propia composición y ya no podemos fiarnos de que sea neutral. Las máquinas de votación electrónica (EVM, por sus siglas en inglés) están manipuladas; en los censos electorales se ha eliminado a millones de personas reales y se ha incorporado a millones de nombres fantasma; la administración encargada de supervisar las elecciones ha dejado clara su total complicidad; podemos estar seguros de que los tribunales retrasarán peticiones o harán la vista gorda ante unas irregularidades más descaradas; la policía no tiene ni idea de qué es neutralidad; y la prensa se pone de rodillas cada vez que algún poderoso le chasquea los dedos. Las circunscripciones se van a rediseñar para garantizar que el BJP siempre salga beneficiado. ¿Qué tiene que temer el partido en el poder? ¿Por qué va a escuchar a nadie? Es el partido político más rico del planeta, respaldado por los empresarios más ricos del mundo. Puede comprar cualquier cosa. Y a cualquiera. O, por lo menos, así lo cree.

Ahora bien, ¿este tira y afloja puede durar eternamente? ¿Se puede engañar a todo el mundo todo el tiempo? ¿Se puede arrastrar sin fin a un país con una población de 1.500 millones de habitantes como si fuera un cadáver? No. Las cucarachas están por todas partes. Los agricultores han vuelto a hacer una marcha hasta ­Delhi, en esta ocasión para protestar contra el acuerdo comercial entre la India y Estados Unidos, la sentencia de muerte que el Gobierno ha aceptado firmar servilmente en su nombre. Se han cerrado los límites de la ciudad, pero no parece que eso vaya a detener a los manifestantes. Tal vez los demás podamos aprender de nuestros agricultores y de nuestras cucarachas a ser un poco más peligrosos. Los jóvenes nos han hecho un regalo. Ahora nos toca a todos nosotros, a cada uno de nosotros, conseguir que sus acciones tengan consecuencias.

Cuando un primer ministro huye físicamente, no falta mucho para que tenga que huir políticamente.

Pero este régimen no va a poner fácil su final. No va a tolerar que lo humillen en las calles de la capital. Es probable que haya sangre derramada. Los jóvenes están exaltados. ¿Cuánto tiempo va a tardar algún miembro de esa muchedumbre juvenil y exaltada en perder los estribos y dar a la policía una excusa para abrir fuego? El Gobierno va a hacer todo lo posible para avasallarnos; nosotros debemos hacer todo lo posible para impedirlo.

World.title: Blood on Her Tongue: A modern vampire tale not for the squeamish
World.content:
Johanna van Veen’s gothic horror Blood on Her Tongue offers up a classic vampire tale with some modern contemplations.

The book follows Lucy Goedhart as she is called to the ominously named Zwartwater (black water) estate, where her sister has taken ill. In 1887, there isn’t much in the way of medical treatment, but Lucy’s sister Sarah isn’t fighting off a regular illness.

Sarah has become obsessed with a body found in the bog of the vast estate and since interacting with the 300-year-old corpse she has become increasingly incoherent, struggles with taking care of herself and has developed an insatiable hunger.

As Lucy tries desperately to save her sister, she finds that her sister’s husband, her sister’s doctor and childhood friend, and several other characters who are present at the remote manor house all have their own interests and motivations – some as dangerous as whatever condition is plaguing Sarah.

The book is not for those easily bothered by gore. The title – Blood on Her Tongue – is a pretty good indication of what is to come. Van Veen does not shy away from the horror elements, including two separate scenes of eyeball gouging.

Like any good horror novel, the macabre monster is not the scariest part. The threats Lucy faces are from the men surrounding her sister. Her brother-in-law attempts to seduce Lucy while badgering her to send Sarah away to an asylum.

Sarah’s doctor expresses his own interest in Lucy, pushing his vision of the future while supposedly devoting himself to his patient. The mores of 19th-century upper-class society may be the biggest piece of villainy of all.

In the tradition of Dracula, Blood on Her Tongue tells its story through letters, journal entries and newspaper clippings. The personal correspondence adds to the claustrophobia of the work, with everyone limited to an isolated house, but the media reports remind the reader that the world outside does exist.

The work is the second book from Dutch author Johanna van Veen. It was published in 2025 in English and became a USA Today bestseller. Her first book, My Darling Dreadful Thing, was nominated for the Bram Stoker Award for best horror novel. Van Veen grew up in the Netherlands as a triplet, something that influenced her writing about the sisters Lucy and Sarah.

If horror is your thing, Blood on Her Tongue will creep you out and keep you turning the pages.

You can get your copy at the American Book Center.

World.title: Thousands cross finishing line as Nijmegen Vierdaagse ends
World.content:
The 108th edition of the Nijmegense Vierdaagse (four-day march) ended on Friday, with tens of thousands of walkers being welcomed with flowers by well-wishers.

British walker Simon Brownlee crossed the finishing line ahead of the rest of the walkers for the 27th time, local media reported. Brownlee, who completed the distance before 10am, told local broadcaster Omroep Gelderland that the walk “felt like home”. “I’m happy it is over and I can now relax,” he said.

Wheelchair participant Ronald van Dort was the very first person to finish, picking up his seventh medal for completing the event.

Over 45,000 walkers from 70 countries took part in this year’s series, which is proving increasingly popular among the young. Ten years ago, 7.5% of the walkers were aged 21 to 30, but this year their number rose to over 20%.

This year the event was marred by a fatal shooting just outside the area where the Vierdaagsefeesten, the street festivities accompanying the annual four-day marches, were taking place. One man has been arrested.

The shooting, and other crowd problems, led the organisers to cancel performances by urban scene artists such as Ronnie Flex and Lil’ Kleine because their presence was “attracting the wrong sort of people”, the AD reported.

World.title: Dozens of women forced into prostitution by Romanian gang
World.content:
Dozens of women may have been forced into working as prostitutes in Amsterdam’s red light district by a Romanian gang, Dutch police confirmed on Friday.

The statement follows a joint Dutch and Romanian campaign against human trafficking in the area earlier this month. Seven men were arrested during a string of raids on July 14 – four in the Netherlands and three in Romania. All were Romanian nationals.

Shortly after the arrests, police issued a video interview with one of the victims speaking Romanian, which has led more women to come forward and has resulted in other information reaching the police, the statement said.

Police now say they have spoken to several victims and say they believe more women have been trafficked. They too are said to be Romanian.

The women were lured to Amsterdam with the promise of high earnings but found themselves forced into working in brothels and handing over their earnings to the gang. They were also forced to pay “rent” for their rooms.

None of the men had jobs but were big spenders, buying expensive clothes and cars and gambling heavily, the statement said. The gang also treated part of the red light district as their “personal kingdom”.

Four men remain in custody in the Netherlands, one of whom was extradited from Romania. Another man may also be extradited soon, RTL said. They are all suspected of human trafficking and forming a criminal organisation.

According to the Parool, two of the suspects are half brothers aged 44 and 45 who have earlier convictions for trafficking in women in Romania.

More arrests have not been ruled out.

A year ago, Dutch and Romanian police arrested 13 people in a joint investigation into human trafficking and the forced prostitution of Romanian women, mainly in and around Amsterdam.

World.title: Singer Sophie Straat cleared of discrimination over mosh pit
World.content:
Discrimination hotlines in both the Netherlands and Belgium have concluded that Dutch singer Sophie Straat did not discriminate when she asked “all white men to step back” during two of her recent performances.

Last month at the Best Kept Secret festival in Beekse Bergen, Straat — real name Sophie Schwartz — asked for space for women, queer people and people of colour in the “mosh pit”, an area in front of the stage where fans dance chaotically.

She made the same request on Monday during a performance in Ghent, Belgium.

The Dutch discrimination hotline Discriminatie.nl said it received hundreds of complaints but maintains that Straat’s comments do not amount to discrimination against white men based on their colour or gender.

“The call only concerned one short, one-off mosh pit for these groups,” said the hotline. “Therefore, visitors were not refused entry to the concert.”

Belgian authorities reached the same conclusion after receiving some 200 complaints following her performance in Ghent.

“Although the statement may be perceived as polarizing or offensive, in this context it must be seen as a symbolic and artistic expression,” a spokesperson for the Belgian discrimination hotline Unia told the Flemish broadcaster VRT.

“According to the case law of the European Court of Human Rights, artistic and political expressions enjoy broad protection under freedom of expression, even when they provoke, shock or offend.”

Hate messages and death threats

Straat wrote on Instagram earlier this month that she has received “a wave of sexist, antisemitic hate messages and (death) threats, some more explicit and creative than others”.

She has also questioned where the left-wing media has been in all this, saying the public narrative is being controlled by the right.

The singer, who was raised in a Jewish home in Amsterdam’s de Pijp neighbourhood and is known for her protest songs, has said she never wanted to exclude anyone but rather wanted to make room for people who feel unsafe in a mosh pit.

World.title: Youngster arrested for participating in sadistic online network
World.content:
Police have arrested a young man from Noord Holland who they suspect of being part of the sadistic online Com network “764”.

The public prosecution department reported the arrest on Thursday, saying the suspect encouraged underage girls to cut themselves and write his online name on a wall with their own blood—so-called “bloodsigns”.

He also is said to have prompted them to write his name on their bodies with a marker, known as“fansigns”. Both are practices within the Com movement—short for The Community—for members to gain prestige.

The suspect himself, who was also charged with aggravated assault, exploitation of underage girls and possession of images of sexual child abuse, was a minor at the time of the alleged crimes. Because of that, no further details are being released.

The Com network consists of various chat groups where members recruit vulnerable young people and force them to commit acts including assault, sexual abuse and murder.

The members, from all corners of the globe, then share images of these acts online in private chat groups, using such platforms as Telegram and Discord.

According to NOS, at least 70 Dutch people are involved in this movement known as “nihilistic extremism” because the incitement to commit such extreme violence doesn’t have a clear ideological motive.

The phenomenon is especially attractive to young men.

World.title: Dangerous drivers face extra surveillance under points system
World.content:
The police and justice ministry officials are working on a system which would see traffic offenders being given points for dangerous driving – which will lead to persistent offenders coming under extra surveillance.

Motorists who have collected six points for using a mobile phone while driving or not wearing a seatbelt would come under the tougher regime, RTL Nieuws reported on Friday. No start date has yet been set.

The points will be awarded in addition to regular fines. The number of points will depend on the seriousness of the offences and speeding tickets recorded by camera will not be included.

The new system is being devised in an effort to tackle persistent offenders who do not change their behaviour despite being fined multiple times, RTL said. Last year, almost 30,000 people would have had at least six points if the new system had been in existence.

“Research shows that people who don’t stick to the rules are often responsible for accidents,” Achilles Damen from the public prosecution department told the broadcaster.

The privacy implications of monitoring specific individuals are still being assessed, RTL said.

World.title: Ajax beat Vojvodina in Conference League qualifier, Twente lose
World.content:
Ajax kicked off their European football campaign with a 4-1 win over Serbian club Vojvodina in the second qualification round of the Conference League competition in Novi Sad on Thursday evening.

The simple win sets the Amsterdammers up in a strong position ahead of the return match next week. If Ajax win again, they will meet either Irish side Shelbourne FC or Estonian club Nõmme Kalju in the third qualification round for the third-tier European competition.

The Amsterdam goal total included one for 16-year-old debutant Mohamed Abdalla, who became the youngest player to score for a Dutch club in Europe.

There was disappointment for FC Twente, who are hoping to qualify for the group stage of the Europa League. They lost 1-2 at home to Hungarian side Ferencváros and will have to pull out all the stops during the away leg next week to remain in the competition.

If they do lose, Twente will move down to the qualification rounds of the Conference League.

PSV Eindhoven and Feyenoord have qualified directly for the Champions League while NEC is taking part in the qualification competition. AZ, as winners of the KNVB Cup last season, will take part in the Europa League competition.

World.title: Unilever backs London for food division secondary listing
World.content:
Unilever’s food division, which is being sold to US sauce and spice producer McCormick, will have a secondary listing on the London stock exchange, despite an intensive lobbying campaign to list in Amsterdam.

Unilever itself has been based in London, and listed there, since 2020.

Unilever said in a statement that the secondary listing is separate to McCormick’s plans to establish an international headquarters in the Netherlands and maintain Unilever Food’s R&D facilities and operations in Wageningen.

This “reflects its commitment to the European market and the critical role the Netherlands will continue to play in the combined company”, the statement said.

Economic affairs minister Heleen Herbert said in a reaction to the sale when it was announced in March that the cabinet had already discussed developments with Unilever and would talk to the new owner “such as about a listing on the Amsterdam stock exchange”.

Unilever’s ice cream arm, spun off in 2024, is listed on the Amsterdam stock exchange as the Magnum Ice Cream Company and is headquartered in the Dutch capital.

The sale of the food arm means there is nothing left of the original Dutch part of Unilever, which was set up in 1930 through the merger of the Dutch Margarine Unie and British soap maker Lever Brothers. Unilever now focuses on personal care and household cleaning products.

World.title: Poland identifies remains of legendary anti-communist resistance fighter
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) has identified the remains of Mieczysław Dziemieszkiewicz (pictured above on the right), a prominent figure in the underground resistance that fought against the Soviet-installed communist authorities in the years after World War Two. Dziemieszkiewicz, who was killed by the communist security services in 1951 and dumped in an unmarked mass grave, was identified through a combination of historical detective work and genetic testing, including exhuming the remains of his deceased mother and sister to obtain DNA samples. “Once again, we can say that the communist authorities did not win. Heroes prevail,” declared Krzysztof Szwagrzyk, deputy head of the IPN. “Even in the most difficult situations, we must seek the truth, find those of whom no trace was supposed to remain, and restore their names.” While World War Two officially came to an end in 1945, tens of thousands of Poles, known as the “cursed soldiers” (żolnierze wyklęci), continued to fight against the Soviets and the communist regime they installed in Poland. While most had laid down arms by 1947, some continued fighting well beyond then, including Dziemieszkiewicz, who operated under the nom de guerre “Rój” (meaning “swarm”). Dziemieszkiewicz, who was 20 years old when the war ended, came from a family that had been part of Poland’s wartime resistance. His anti-communist views were hardened when his elder brother, Roman, was killed by Red Army soldiers in 1945. After being conscripted that year into the Soviet-backed Polish People’s Army, Dziemieszkiewicz defected and joined the underground resistance forces, where he rose to command a unit tasked with eliminating regime officials and members of the communist Polish Workers Party (PPR). Dziemieszkiewicz’s group killed around two dozen members of the communist security services and more than 20 informants, according to the IPN. In 1950, the communist authorities intensified efforts to dismantle Dziemieszkiewicz’s unit, using threats and blackmail to recruit hundreds of agents and informants in an effort to locate the resistance fighters. Eventually, one such informant gave up Dziemieszkiewicz’s location in exchange for a promise to release her parents from captivity. Dziemieszkiewicz found himself surrounded by several hundred soldiers and was killed while trying to escape. After his body had been identified by his family, Dziemieszkiewicz was buried in a section of Powązki Cemetery in Warsaw where the remains of those killed by the communist security services were placed en masse in unmarked graves. Exhumations by the IPN, which was established after the fall of communism to investigate communist and Nazi crimes in Poland, have located over 200 complete bodies at that site as well as several thousand bone fragments. During that work, one set of remains was found buried with an eagle symbol and remnants of a black cloth. IPN researchers realised that the item was similar to a beret that appeared in posthumous photographs of Dziemieszkiewicz’s body taken by the communist security services. That prompted them to carry out genetic testing on the remains and compare them to samples taken from Dziemieszkiewicz’s mother and sister, who were buried in a cemetery in the town of Maków Mazowiecki. “We have found ‘Rój’, commander of one of the longest-fighting units of the independence underground,” declared the IPN on Friday, announcing the confirmation of his identity. They described Dziemieszkiewicz as “legend in life and a symbol of the fight against communist oppression”. The identification was announced today during a press conference at @PrzystanekH. The identification is the result of many years of work carried out by the IPN. It was preceded by extensive archival and investigative research, the analysis of forensic evidence, archaeological… https://t.co/Rcf4wemJFc pic.twitter.com/XgMUAgSQc6 — Institute of National Remembrance (@ipngovpl_eng) July 24, 2026 At a conference announcing the findings, the IPN noted that Dziemieszkiewicz’s remains had been located right next to those of another prominent anti-communist resistance fighter, Zygmunt Szendzielarz, who fought under the nom de guerre “Łupaszko”. “It is an incredible situation that two great and distinguished soldiers of the Polish underground lie next to each other in this part of the Powązki Cemetery,” said Szwagrzyk. However, Szendzielarz, who was executed by the communist authorities in 1951, has a contested legacy, given evidence that his unit was involved in the massacre of dozens of Lithuanian civilians. Some other “cursed soldiers” have faced similar accusations of war crimes. While it was often IPN historians who uncovered evidence of such actions, the institution has more recently begun to honour those figures, particularly under the rule of the national-conservative Law and Justice government between 2015 and 2023. Opposition MPs walked out of parliament yesterday as the chamber commemorated an underground officer who fought against Nazi-German occupation and the imposition of communism in Poland, but has also been accused of a war crime against civilians https://t.co/MIY7krOxTw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 9, 2022 Dziemieszkiewicz himself, however, like most of the cursed soldiers, has not faced such accusations. In 2007, President Lech Kaczński posthumously awarded Dziemieszkiewicz the Commander’s Cross with Star of the Order of Polonia Restituta, one of Poland’s highest honours. In 2020, his image was featured on a commemorative silver coin issued by the National Bank of Poland. Through a combination of brutal repression and offering amnesties, the communist authorities managed to end most resistance efforts by 1947. However, the last “cursed soldier” to die in combat, Józef Franczak, was killed in 1963, 18 years after the end of the war. World.title: Three quarters of Poles support cooperation with Ukraine against Russia despite historical dispute
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A new study shows that, while most Poles were angered by President Volodymyr Zelensky’s recent decision to name a military unit after a group that massacred Poles in World War Two, they still overwhelmingly support cooperation with Ukraine and believe that Russia benefits from the dispute. The study, carried out by Polish state research agency CBOS, also finds that a large majority of Poles believe good relations with Ukraine will only be possible once historical issues are resolved. The polling was carried out this month in response to the ongoing diplomatic crisis that began in May, when Zelensky named a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”. The UPA is widely revered in Ukraine for its role in fighting against Moscow-backed Soviet rule. However, in Poland it is associated with the Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Polish civilians – mostly women and children – were slaughtered during World War Two, often with great brutality. Zelensky’s decision sparked anger in Poland, where the massacres are regarded as a genocide (though Ukraine strongly rejects that label). In June, Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped Zelensky of the Order of the White Eagle, Poland’s highest honour, which he had received in 2023. In its new survey, CBOS found that 59% of Poles support Nawrocki’s decision, while only 28% oppose it. However, they were divided over the consequences, with 41% saying it would bring Poland more losses than benefits and the exact same proportion saying the benefits would outweigh the costs. More broadly, 84% said the Polish state should react when another country glorifies historical figures responsible for crimes against Poles. However, when asked if Ukrainians have the right to honour their own historical heroes, even if those figures left a negative mark on Polish history, 44% agreed and 42% disagreed. At the same time, over three quarters of respondents (77%) said that good Polish-Ukrainian relations could not be built without addressing the past, but a similar proportion (73%) also believe that politicians on both sides “fuel conflicts between Poles and Ukrainians for their own political gain”. Poland has cautiously welcomed President @ZelenskyyUa's announcement of a five-point plan to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after a group that led massacres of Poles during WWII https://t.co/M3GXD9vtAr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2026 Yet the survey also showed that, for Poles, historical disputes have not displaced security concerns, and in particular the view that, for Poland and Ukraine, Russia is a shared enemy. Some 75% of respondents agreed with the statement that “Poland and Ukraine should, above all, cooperate in the face of the threat from Russia, rather than focus on the issues that divide them”. The most frequently cited priorities in relations with Kyiv were security cooperation (61%), building good neighbourly relations (46%), commemorating victims of the Volhynia massacres (43%), strengthening Poland’s regional leadership (41%), and ensuring Polish companies participate in Ukraine’s reconstruction (40%). Just over half of Poles (52%) agree that “Poland and Ukraine have more common aims and interests than conflicting ones”, while 32% disagreed. A huge majority (80%) agreed that “Russia benefits from the Polish-Ukrainian dispute”. W ocenie społecznej zdecydowanym priorytetem w relacjach z Ukrainą powinna być współpraca na rzecz bezpieczeństwa – wskazało ją 61% badanych.📊 ➡️Więcej w komunikacie #CBOS "Wokół polsko-ukraińskiego sporu o imponderabilia i nie tylko":https://t.co/pIvYbu8gyz#Ukraina #relacje pic.twitter.com/LOpmAKNnXn — CBOS (@CBOS_Info) July 23, 2026 Based on the answers in the survey, CBOS identified three broad groups of respondents classified by their views of the dispute. The largest, described as “moralists”, accounted for 46% and placed greater emphasis on historical grievances. Among this group, 99% supported Nawrocki’s decision and said good Polish-Ukrainian relations could not be built without addressing the past. “Pragmatists”, who made up 34% of respondents, placed greater emphasis on future cooperation. Some 96% said Poland and Ukraine should cooperate against the Russian threat rather than focus on historical disputes. The smallest group, labelled by CBOS as “withdrawn”, represented 20% of respondents who were more likely to lack a clear view on Polish-Ukrainian relations. Long-simmering tensions between Poland and Ukraine over WWII massacres have finally boiled over, prompting a diplomatic crisis.@danieltilles1 looks at how we got here and what it may mean for the two countries and Europe more broadly https://t.co/a8tiYJJHRr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 22, 2026 Recent weeks have seen moves from Ukraine towards finding a diplomatic solution to the crisis. In early July, foreign minister Andrii Sybiha visited Warsaw to propose an “anti-crisis package” of measures. Last week, Zelensky himself outlined a five-point plan to alleviate the dispute, including opening up Ukrainian historical archives and permitting more exhumations of victims of the massacres, most of whom remain buried in mass graves in Ukraine. The Polish authorities have cautiously welcomed Zelensky’s announcement, though also emphasise that they are waiting to see concrete action. Meanwhile, there is no indication that Zelensky will change his decision to name a unit after the heroes of the UPA. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Keeping dogs and cats chained up at home will be banned in Poland from next year, after President Karol Nawrocki signed into law a bill prohibiting the practice. His decision ends a long-running dispute over the issue, after Nawrocki last year vetoed a previous proposal to ban chaining because it also included what he argued were excessive and unrealistic additional measures on minimum kennel sizes for dogs. Zawetowana w listopadzie 2025 r. ustawa łańcuchowa była źle przygotowana i przeregulowana, ponieważ nakładała na obywateli obowiązki, których wielu nie byłoby w stanie spełnić. Dzisiaj otrzymujemy ustawę lepszą, z pozytywnym głosem takich podmiotów jak rolniczy samorząd.… pic.twitter.com/h7kIAI77KR — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) July 24, 2026 The new law bans owners from tethering dogs and cats at home. Animals must be kept either inside the house, in a fenced garden or, if that is not possible, in a kennel “large enough for the animal to move freely and satisfy its natural needs”. Dogs kept in kennels must be provided with daily exercise outside of it. Dogs and cats can still be put on leashes in certain situations, such as when they are being walked, but also during transport, while participating in shows, performances or training, if they are at vets or groomers, or if they represent a danger to humans or other animals. Those who are found to have violated the new law can be fined between 1,000 and 100,000 zloty (€232-23,166). If they are deemed to have acted with “extreme cruelty”, they can also face a prison sentence of up to five years, reports the Forsal news service. Now that the bill has been signed by Nawrocki, it will be published in the official Journal of Laws (Dziennik Ustaw), after which it goes into force 12 months later. The new measures represent a successful second attempt to introduce a leashing ban. A previous bill was approved by parliament last September. However, in December, Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, announced that he was vetoing it. The president argued that, “although the intention – protecting animals – is just and noble, the law itself was poorly drafted”. In particular, he said that elements introducing minimum sizes for dog kennels were unrealistic and would “harm farmers, breeders and ordinary rural households”. After an attempt by parliament to overturn the veto failed, legislators went back to the drawing board and, following discussions with the president’s chancellery and animal rights groups, drafted a compromise bill that was approved by parliament earlier this month. The bill received support from the current ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, as well as most MPs from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the main opposition party. The far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) voted against it. Thousands of people have protested in Warsaw against President @NawrockiKn's veto of a law that would have banned the chaining up of dogs Parliament will vote on Wednesday on whether to overturn Nawrocki's veto, which would require a three-fifths majority https://t.co/0GRup2sppb — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 15, 2025 “We now have a better law, with positive feedback from entities such as the agricultural chamber,” said Nawrocki today. “It demonstrates that the pressure of the presidential veto makes sense. My previous decision to refuse to sign this bill forced the government and parliament to work harder.” However, although Nawrocki said the new law would no longer entail “rigid and costly requirements” for kennels, his office noted in a separate statement that the legislation requires the agriculture minister to issue a regulation establishing “minimum kennel area, taking into account the dog’s size”. It remains unclear if and how that would differ from the requirements Nawrocki previously vetoed. The presidential chancellery also noted that the law itself already outlines that kennels must be made of “wood or wood-like material with thermal insulation”, must be insulated from the ground, and must have openings on at least two sides to allow light and air to enter. World.title: Police and park rangers step up joint patrols in Poland’s Tatras after series of tourist offences

Police officers and rangers have stepped up joint patrols in Poland’s mountainous Tatra National Park during the peak summer season, following a spate of rule-breaking including swimming in the park’s lakes and ponds, driving cars and going off marked trails. Meanwhile, national park authorities have repeated warnings that bathing, littering and breaking other rules can damage the park’s fragile ecosystem. Local police officers have joined Tatra National Park rangers on patrols on popular tourist routes. On one such patrol last week, officers focused on education and prevention, reminding visitors not to leave marked trails or litter and explaining how to behave safely and responsibly in the mountains. They also checked that organised groups were accompanied by qualified mountain guides, as required by law. Fines for such offences range from 50 zloty (€11.55) to as much as 1,000 zloty (€231) in the event of environmental damage or multiple offences. Police said that all visitors encountered during the patrol were complying with the park’s regulations. However, they added that similar patrols would continue on a regular basis. The Tatra National Park, home to Poland’s highest peaks, and the nearby mountain resort of Zakopane are among the country’s most popular holiday destinations, with crowds taking to park trails in the summer season. The park, the most visited of Poland’s 23 national parks, welcomed a record 5.3 million visitors in 2025 and offers 275 km of marked hiking trails, including high-altitude routes that connect at several points with the adjacent national park in Slovakia. 🚨 Ukraiński Influencer wjechał nielegalnie samochodem na Morskie oko 🗣️: Jesteśmy pierwszymi ludźmi w historii, którzy wjechali samochodem nad Morskie Oko. To było jedno z miejsc, do których chcieliśmy dotrzeć podczas tej podróży i wszyscy znajomi oraz przyjaciele mówili, że… pic.twitter.com/tA9shZ6Rqk — Pigułka 💊 (@informacyjnie) May 23, 2026 This season has already seen a number of high-profile cases of transgressions of the park’s strict rules. In May, a Ukrainian social media influencer sparked outrage after driving a sports car along a road closed to traffic to Morskie Oko, a picturesque lake nestled between the mountains. As a result, he was banned from entering Poland and other Schengen Area countries for five years. Tourists have also been filmed entering Morskie Oko and other protected lakes and ponds, which is not permitted in the national park. This month, a group of young Dutch tourists were filmed bathing in Przedni Staw Polski in the Valley of the Five Lakes, one of the Tatras’ best-known hiking destinations. Witnesses repeatedly warned the group that entering the lake was prohibited, but they ignored the warnings, reports Gazeta Wyborcza. Park authorities have responded to such incidents by reminding visitors of the reasons for the strict rules. “Tatra ponds are incredibly delicate ecosystems. Cosmetics, UV filters, insect repellents, and bacteria entering the water can have a long-lasting impact on its chemical composition and the organisms living in the lakes,” they warned. World.title: Polish opposition PiS party set to split, with over 30 MPs being expelled
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. More than 30 MPs from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party, have effectively resigned after refusing to sign a loyalty pledge, party leader Jarosław Kaczyński has announced. The dispute centres around a more moderate faction in the party aligned with former prime minister and deputy PiS leader Mateusz Morawiecki, who is one of those now set to be expelled from the party. They have for months been unhappy with PiS’s move in a hard-right direction. 💬 Prezes PiS Jarosław Kaczyński @OficjalnyJK. 👉 Udostępnij pic.twitter.com/bycjE0Yq0f — Prawo i Sprawiedliwość (@pisorgpl) July 24, 2026 “Around 30-something…of our group’s MPs have resigned,” revealed Kaczyński at a press conference on Friday. He added that their departures would be formalised at a meeting of the party’s political committee scheduled for Tuesday next week. Kaczyński’s announcement came after a deadline expired at midnight on Thursday for its MPs to sign a pledge of loyalty to the party that included a commitment not to be members of any external political associations. That measure was aimed in particular at an association called Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) founded by Morawiecki in April. The former prime minister had always insisted that his organisation was intended as complementary to PiS, rather than a rival to it. However, many figures in the party saw it as an attempt by Morawiecki to create a separate centre of power, and potentially to use the association as a launchpad for creating his own party ahead of the autumn 2027 parliamentary elections. The right-wing opposition PiS party has threatened disciplinary action, including exclusion from electoral lists, against dozens of its MPs who have joined a new internal group led by former PM @MorawieckiM and intended to appeal to more moderate voters https://t.co/y62Cm361U2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 17, 2026 After PiS issued a resolution on Wednesday last week requiring that its parliamentarians pledge to withdraw from any such associations, most of its 186 MPs quickly complied. However, a group of between 30 and 40 who are part of Development Plus refused to do so. “Everyone knew what they were supposed to sign, and knew the consequences of not signing,” said Kaczyński on Friday. “And so they made the decision they did.” “In this situation, we cannot view the [Development Plus] association as anything other than a component of a plan…to split our party,” he added. However, although its supporters will now leave PiS, “we want to part ways without any animosity”, said Kaczyński. After Kaczyński’s announcement, senior figures from Development Plus made clear that no one from their association had resigned from PiS. They had simply not signed the declaration of loyalty demanded by the party. Later, Morawiecki himself held a press conference in parliament surrounded by his supporters. He claimed that an unnamed “small group of schemers” within PiS had been seeking to turn Kaczyński against him and push him out of the party. “We fought for the unity of Law and Justice until the very end,” declared Morawiecki, who said that his group included 40 MPs, one senator and three MEPs. However, three of the MPs are not members of PiS, and therefore were not expected to sign the loyalty declaration. Szanowni Państwo! 🟦Do ostatniej chwili walczyłem o jedność Prawa i Sprawiedliwości. Nie o stanowiska. Nie o osobiste ambicje. Nie o wpływy. 🟦Walczyłem o jedność obozu, który przez osiem lat zmieniał Polskę – budował jej bezpieczeństwo, rozwijał gospodarkę i przywracał godność… pic.twitter.com/PP7sOkzMHp — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 24, 2026 If the expulsion of Morawiecki’s supporters is confirmed, it will mark a major shake-up of Poland’s political landscape. PiS has for the last two decades been the dominant force on the Polish right, including periods leading governments in 2005-2007 and 2015-2023. However, since losing power at elections in 2023, when the party won 35% of the vote, PiS has seen its average support in polls fall to around 23-24%, the lowest level in 14 years. Meanwhile, it has been challenged by the rise of the far right, where two parties, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), now together poll a similar combined level of support to PiS. In response, Kaczyński in March named a hardline figure, Przemyszław Czarnek, as PiS’s candidate for prime minister in next year’s elections. Czarnek was seen as someone who could appeal to far-right voters, while also potentially working with the far right if a coalition was needed after the elections. Support for PiS has fallen to its lowest in 14 years, as the party grapples with internal division, the rise of far-right challengers, living in President Nawrocki's shadow, and the unpopularity in Poland of PiS ally Donald Trump, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/QRScBpEQQG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 2, 2026 However, there has been no rise in support for PiS since Czarnek was named, prompting growing concern from more moderate figures within the party, led by Morawiecki. They argue that PiS has wrongly disowned many of the successes of its time in office before 2023, and they fear that its rightward shift damages its chances of winning over more centrist voters. Morawiecki, who was an international banker before joining PiS to become finance minister and then prime minister, wants the party to focus on more technocratic issues, such as economic development, rather than Euroscepticism and culture wars. That has led to frequent public sparring between his supporters and others in the party. In April, PiS threatened disciplinary action against members of Development Plus. Kaczyński and Morawiecki then reached an agreement that allowed the association to continue. But that uneasy truce has now fallen apart. President Karol Nawrocki has submitted a second request to parliament for a nationwide referendum on whether Poland should continue implementing the European Union’s climate policies, which he argues are too costly. Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, first proposed a referendum in May. But it was rejected by the Senate, the upper house of parliament, where the more liberal government has a majority. Senators argued that the proposed referendum question was “absurd”. The president has now submitted a revised proposal featuring a simplified question and again proposed holding the referendum on 27 September this year. Nawrocki’s originally proposed question was: “Are you in favour of implementing EU climate policy, which has led to an increase in citizens’ cost of living, energy prices and the cost of running business and agricultural activity?” However, following criticism in the Senate that the question was clearly intended to elicit a specific answer, this time he has proposed a more neutral one: “Are you in favour of Poland implementing the European Union’s climate policy?” “I’m looking for compromises, looking for solutions,” said Nawrocki on Thursday while announcing the new referendum bid. “The Senate wasn’t satisfied with the [previous] question”, so “we prepared a different one…[that] does not suggest anything”. However, the president has also proposed that the ballot paper would include information on what answering “yes” or “no” would mean in practice. Voters would be told, for example, that maintaining EU climate policy would result in, among other things, “Poland bearing costs estimated at 3.5 trillion zloty by 2040”, “burdens on agriculture”, “increasing costs for industry” and “obligations for owners of buildings”. By contrast, voting “no” would mean “negotiating exceptions and exemptions for Poland with the relevant EU bodies that will protect Polish industry and citizens from the burdens of climate policy”. Poland's right-wing opposition wants to withdraw from the EU Emissions Trading System, saying it makes Poles "a cash machine for absurd leftist climate policies"@PStrzalkowski explains what costs ETS really brings, and what prospects there are for reform https://t.co/UxpMWpG1pE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 4, 2026 Under Poland’s constitution, the president may call a referendum with the approval of a majority of senators in a vote where at least half of all members of the 100-seat chamber are present. The ruling coalition of Prime Minister Donald Tusk controls 63 seats in the Senate, making approval of proposals brought forward by Nawrocki, who often clashes with the government and regularly vetoes its bills, unlikely. While the government is generally pro-EU, it has also been critical of Brussels’ green policies, arguing that they place too great a burden on Poland. After the European Commission last Friday unveiled changes intended to soften the impact of the Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS), the EU’s flagship climate policy, they were welcomed by the Polish government as a step in the right direction. Dzisiaj robimy milowy krok w zmianie systemu ETS. Po raz pierwszy Komisja Europejska proponuje rozwiązania, które łagodzą, a nie zaostrzają wpływ systemu na gospodarkę i obywateli. To efekt konsekwentnych działań Polski i zbudowania silnej koalicji państw w UE. Dzisiejsza… pic.twitter.com/5AMd9KCBVa — Ministerstwo Klimatu i Środowiska (@MKiS_GOV_PL) July 17, 2026 However, in his written justification for the new referendum proposal, Nawrocki wrote that, while he had “given the government time” in its push for ETS reform, the final result was simply “technical adjustments” that postpone some elements but do “not change the direction” or ultimate outcome. “ETS will remain an increasingly expensive, increasingly extensive system, and increasingly burdensome for the Polish economy,” wrote the president. The national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), which is the main opposition and supported Nawrocki’s bid for the presidency last year, wants Poland to unilaterally withdraw from ETS. Government figures warn, however, that there is no way to do so without either accruing enormous fines or leaving the EU entirely. When in power, PiS launched a revolution in Poland's energy transition. But now, in opposition, it has disowned those achievements and returned to an emphasis on coal. This could be a missed opportunity to win back centrist voters, writes @OrzelBartlomiej https://t.co/8cGvubn7N2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 29, 2026 Nawrocki’s new referendum proposal was met with criticism by figures from the ruling coalition. “There is no possibility of one country suspending part of EU law,” wrote Stanisław Gawłowski, a senator from Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO) party. “This referendum is pure fraud.” Foreign minister Radosław Sikorski, also from KO, wrote that, “as the Brits have learned, the Europhobe’s dream world, in which one enjoys all the privileges of EU membership without any obligations, does not exist”. However, Nawrocki’s initiative was welcomed by Przemysław Czarnek, deputy leader of PiS, who wrote that, “on such fundamental matters as climate policy, Poles should decide, not Brussels bureaucrats”. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. The government’s majority in parliament has chosen Sylwia Gregorczyk-Abram as Poland’s new human rights commissioner. She will take office after the five-year term of the incumbent, Marcin Wiącek, expires today. Gregorczyk-Abram is a prominent lawyer and activist, who is particularly well known for opposing the overhaul of the judiciary by the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government. PiS, which is now the main opposition party, strongly opposed her election, arguing that she is politically aligned with the current, more liberal government. Gregorczyk-Abram herself, however, has pledged to “put all my beliefs and views aside” when she takes up the new role. Senat wyraził zgodę na powołanie Sylwii Gregorczyk-Abram na Rzecznika Praw Obywatelskich. pic.twitter.com/gz3rwGy3hi — Senat RP 🇵🇱 (@PolskiSenat) July 22, 2026 The commissioner for human rights (widely known by its Polish initials, RPO) is appointed by a resolution of the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, with the consent of the upper-house Senate. Candidates must meet certain requirements, including not belonging to any political party and having legal expertise and relevant experience. As well as acting as a watchdog for human rights, the RPO also has the power to submit motions to the Constitutional Tribunal to assess the constitutionality of laws and to file so-called cassation appeals to the Supreme Court and Supreme Administrative Court against rulings by lower courts. Poland’s human rights commissioner has written to the government expressing concern that a "temporary" ban on asylum claims by most migrants who irregularly cross the border from Belarus remains in place after more than a year https://t.co/9SA2TypQdK — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 28, 2026 Gregorczyk-Abram was last month nominated as a candidate to be the new RPO by the main ruling party, Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO), along with one of its coalition partners, The Left (Lewica). PiS proposed a rival candidate, Adam Borowski, a veteran of Poland’s anti-communist struggle in the 1980s. However, critics argued that Borowski, an activist and former PiS election candidate, does not appear to have the requisite legal knowledge and experience. In a Sejm vote last Friday, the ruling coalition supported Gregorczyk-Abram, who won 233 votes to Borowski’s 177. On Wednesday, her candidacy was also supported by the Senate, with 59 votes in favour and 25 against, confirming that she will become the new RPO. Gregorczyk-Abram is best known as one of the founders and leaders of the Free Courts (Wolne Sądy) initiative launched in 2017 amid a wave of protests against the then-PiS government’s efforts to take greater control over the judiciary. Free Courts was prominent in efforts to defend the rule of law. Many of its leading figures are now associated with the current ruling coalition: Maria Ejchart is a deputy justice minister, while Michał Wawrykiewicz is a member of the European Parliament representing KO. In April last year, Gregorczyk-Abram was made chairwoman of a commission established by the current government to look into cases of abuse of power against civil society under the former PiS administration. In September, her commission published its first findings, in which it said that public media outlets under PiS control had “carried out systematic repressive and defamatory actions against activists, non-governmental organisations, and civil society”. Poland's public media “carried out systematic repressive actions against activists, NGOs and civil society” during the rule of the former PiS government, a report commissioned by the new government has found https://t.co/S2MO9KGssC — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 26, 2025 PiS argues that Gregorczyk-Abram’s previous activity makes her unsuitable as a suitable candidate for RPO, which is meant to be a non-partisan role. They also point to claims that she was involved in a group of legal figures that discussed the Tusk government’s controversial takeover of public media in December 2023. “[She] is a discredited and extremely politicised person who should be brought to justice, and not receive the laurels of the commissioner for human rights,” former PiS justice minister Marcin Warchoł told the Do Rzeczy weekly last month. After a Sejm committee hearing on Gregorczyk-Abram’s candidacy earlier this month, former PiS deputy justice minister Sebastian Kaleta criticised her for ignoring questions over her alleged “role in the illegal takeover of public media”. Zadałem Sylwii Gregorczyk-Abram serię pytań o jej działania i możliwe spotkania z Ewą Wrzosek w sprawie przejęcia TVP, w tym możliwego tworzenia dokumentów prokuratorskich w prywatnej kancelarii. Kandydatka ostentacyjnie zdecydowała się ignorować te pytania. Ma bardzo dużo do… — Sebastian Kaleta (@sjkaleta) July 15, 2026 Speaking to state broadcaster TVP on Wednesday after her appointment was confirmed by the Senate, Gregorczyk-Abram declared that, “from the moment I take the oath and assume the position of commissioner, I will be independent and sovereign”. She pledged to “put all my beliefs and views – because each of us has them – aside and become an advocate for all citizens, regardless of what they believe in, how they live, or who they vote for”. Gregorczyk-Abram said that among her priorities as RPO would be the justice system, supporting the rights of disabled people and their carers, protecting older people, and fighting hate speech. With regard to the last of these issues, she noted that certain politicians present some groups as “enemies”, pointing to how this previously happened with LGBT+ people and judges, and is now being directed towards Ukrainians. Those are all groups who have at various stages been targeted by PiS and other right-wing parties. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. World.title: President to swear in new judge to Poland’s disputed constitutional court
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has agreed to swear in a new judge to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), ending weeks of doubt as to whether the opposition-aligned president would accept the judge appointed by the government’s parliamentary majority. Although Sławomir Patyra will now be accepted onto the court, four other judges appointed by parliament earlier this year continue to be excluded after Nawrocki refused to receive their oaths and the TK’s chief justice, also aligned with the opposition, blocked them from taking office. W najbliższy wtorek 28 lipca Prezydent Karol Nawrocki działając na postawie art. 4 ust. 1 ustawy o statusie sędziów Trybunału Konstytucyjnego, przyjmie ślubowanie od prof. Sławomira Patyry i tego samego dnia wręczy powołania czterem nowym sędziom Sądu Najwyższego. W przyszłym… — Zbigniew Bogucki🇵🇱 (@BoguckiZbigniew) July 22, 2026 Under Polish law, when a vacancy emerges among the 15 positions on the TK – for example when a judge’s nine-year term expires – the lower house of parliament, the Sejm, chooses who should fill it. However, to take office, the judge must swear an oath before the president. In April, after the Sejm had chosen six candidates to fill vacancies on the court, Nawrocki took the unprecedented step of inviting only two of them to be sworn in. He argued there were doubts over the legality of how all six had been chosen, but decided to accept two to ensure the TK had the necessary quorum to function. Those two have been able to take up their seats on the court, but the other four remain in limbo. Although they arranged their own private swearing-in ceremony without the presence of Nawrocki, the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, has refused to accept them. In May, the European Court of Human Rights ordered that the quartet be allowed to take up their positions. But the TK – where judges appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government retain a majority – issued its own ruling endorsing Nawrocki’s right not to swear in the new judges. On 11 June, the Sejm then chose another judge, Patyra, to fill a newly opened vacancy on the court. In his case, the legal doubts Nawrocki had expressed regarding the previous appointments, which in some instances were made more than a year after the vacancies had arisen, did not seem to apply. Yet for weeks the president refused to confirm whether he would swear him in. That prompted Patyra to write to Nawrocki in early July and then again this week, asking the president to indicate a date on which he could take his oath. Patyra himself has also made clear on which side of the dispute he stands. In an interview with news website Onet in May, he accused Nawrocki and Święczkowski of “blatantly unlawful actions” in deciding which TK judges can and cannot take office and suggested that the police should intervene. Sędzia TK prof. Patyra po raz kolejny zaapelował do Prezydenta o wyznaczenie mu terminu na złożenie przysięgi. Ignorowanie sędziego TK przez Prezydenta jest kolejnym przykładem psucia państwa. To pokazuje, jak bardzo siły anty-demokratyczne boją się odbudowy niezależnego TK.… — Dariusz Mazur (@_Dariusz_Mazur) July 21, 2026 Finally, on Wednesday this week, Nawrocki’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, announced that Nawrocki had invited Patyra to the presidential palace on Tuesday next week to take his oath. Speaking to Polsat News, Bogucki said that, in the case of Patyra, initially “there were some doubts, but the president dispelled them”, without specifying what they were. In the end, they concluded that “we had a fundamentally clean situation here” and Patyra was chosen “in accordance with all procedures”, unlike the six new judges chosen by the Sejm in March to fill longstanding vacancies. “It was not President Nawrocki or the current opposition who destroyed and are destroying the tribunal; it is the government that is doing it,” he added. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 The TK has been at the heart of the rule-of-law crisis that has developed in Poland over the last decade. In 2015, former PiS-aligned President Andrzej Duda refused to swear in three judges legally chosen by the Sejm. Shortly afterwards, PiS won parliamentary elections and nominated three replacements for those judges, who were sworn in by Duda. Those three judges and their successors have been deemed illegitimate in a succession of rulings by Polish and European courts. Due to their continued presence on the court, the current government, which replaced PiS in 2023, rejects the TK’s legitimacy and refuses to recognise its rulings. Under both Święczkowski, a former member of the PiS government, and his predecessor Julia Przyłębska, a close personal associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, the TK has been widely seen as issuing rulings aligned with the political interests of PiS.
