A second-year butcher's apprentice, Ms Drinkwater is one of a growing number of Queensland women taking up the meat cleaver in this traditionally male-dominated role.

In Queensland, 35 women started a butcher's apprenticeship last year, 10 more than in 2022.

In fact, the number of female apprentice butchers in Queensland has more than tripled since 2020, according to the National Centre for Vocational Education Research, a non-profit that analyses vocational training statistics.

It's a trend seen across other trades, including plumbers, electricians and "fridgies" — refrigeration and air-conditioning mechanics.

Conversely, numbers are dropping in traditionally female roles, with nearly 200 fewer women starting a hairdressing apprenticeship in the same time.

Ms Drinkwater said changing cultural attitudes were behind the movement of women into majority-male trades.

"I just think it's becoming more accessible for us," she said.

"There's a lot less fear of being discriminated against … I can just feel it, something is happening and the world's just becoming a little bit more inclusive."

Tamika Banks won the apprentice of the year award at the 2026 Australian Meat Excellence Awards. (Supplied)

Low completions

Sarojni Choy is a researcher in adult vocational education at Griffith University, specialising in the challenges faced by female apprentices.

Professor Choy said improved public messaging and increasing numbers of role models were drawing more women to the trades, but more support was needed to help female apprentices complete their qualifications.

Of the 25 women who started a four-year butcher's apprenticeship in 2022, only 10 completed in 2025, while some sectors had produced no female tradespeople in recent years.

"I think we are seeing a real, if modest, shift towards some of the non-traditional occupations for women," Professor Choy said.

"The challenge now is to convert that interest into sustained participation and completion."

Rae Cooper says more action is needed to attract women to a greater range of industries with national skills shortages. (ABC News: Geoff Kemp)

The challenges faced by female apprentices can extend to serious sexual discrimination and harassment.

Rae Cooper is director of the Australian Centre for Gender Equality and Inclusion at Work at the University of Sydney.

She led a research project that found 25 per cent of women working in automotive trades had directly experienced sexual harassment at work.

"Everyday sexism, or actually pretty nasty sexism, we find are an experience of lots of women apprentices," Professor Cooper said.

In 2022, the federal parliament passed laws requiring employers to take proactive steps to end workplace sex discrimination and harassment.

Protesters at 2021 March 4 Justice rallies demanded an overhaul of sex discrimination legislation. (Abubakr Mahmoud (ABC))

Professor Cooper said while these new laws had brought a positive change to many workplaces, "some aren't taking it seriously enough".

A lack of support through pregnancy and child care is also forcing women out of the trades.

"When you interview women tradies, they'll often talk about the advice they give to younger apprentices, which is, 'Try not to get pregnant during the period of your apprenticeship,'" Professor Cooper said.

Broader funding needed

Federal government programs are supporting and incentivising increased female workforce participation.

Since early 2025, the federal government's Building Women's Careers Program has awarded $54.5 million towards driving cultural change that is more welcoming to women.

Ms Drinkwater says a changing culture of more inclusive workplaces is behind growing numbers of women entering male-dominated industries. (ABC Wide Bay: James C Taylor)

However, the scope of the program is limited to construction, clean energy, advanced manufacturing, and digital and technology industries.

Professor Cooper said more needed to be done to attract women to a greater range of industries with national skills shortages.

A spokesperson for the federal Department of Employment and Workplace Relations said women accounted for most free TAFE enrolments, and that apprentices and their employers in priority industries may be eligible for additional grants and incentives.

New attitudes in the next generation

Professor Cooper said changing attitudes among younger workers were also driving cultural change.

"I think that the next generation of people who are commencing apprenticeships, particularly the young women, is less likely to put up with some of the things that women of their mothers' generation might have put up with," she said.

"And I think that's a good thing."

Following her apprenticeship Kirsten Drinkwater plans to travel to Germany and Spain to learn about the small goods trade in those countries. (ABC Wide Bay: James C Taylor)

Ms Drinkwater advised any girls seeking to follow in her footsteps to do their research when choosing an employer.

"It can be difficult to find a workplace where you're accepted," she said.

"But once you find the perfect spot, it's pretty easy to settle down and just get into it."

World.title: There's a chance your local MP doesn't live in your neighbourhood. Does that matter?
World.content:
Western Australia's upcoming Secret Harbour by-election — in which none of the key candidates live in the electorate — has raised an interesting question: should MPs live in the area they represent?

It's not a new issue. At least seven lower house members (about 1 in 8) don't live within the boundary of their seat according to analysis of parliamentary disclosures by the ABC.

All of them are Labor MPs in metropolitan Perth.

That includes Premier Roger Cook, who recently moved to West Perth, some 38 kilometres from his electorate of Kwinana.

Roger Cook recently moved to West Perth. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Others are much closer. Mandurah MP Rhys Williams lives just over the border of his electorate in nearby Wannanup, according to the records.

He told the ABC he had a deep connection to Mandurah, beginning when he was eight years old, and that living just over the boundary did not change that.

"I went to school here, and I've been helping shape our community's future since I was first elected to the City of Mandurah Council at the age of 21," he said in a statement.

Rhys Williams lives close to his Mandurah electorate, in Wannanup. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Does it matter to voters?

Cabinet ministers Meredith Hammat, Don Punch and Rita Saffioti also live outside their electorates, by varying distances.

While an MP living outside of their seat might generate headlines, research fellow at the Australian National University's School of Politics, Pandanus Petter, said it does not necessarily impact voters' decisions.

"Most voting is still based on party label and your policy preferences, or your displeasure with the incumbent government, or your desire to show your support for them," he said, noting that regional electorates may feel more strongly about having a local representative.

Dr Pandanus Petter said where MPs live is more important to regional voters. (Supplied)

There are no rules requiring politicians live in the areas they represent.

MPs just have to be over 18 years old, be an Australian citizen who has resided in the state for more than a year, be enrolled to vote and not have any legal incapacity.

Secret Harbour candidates

None of the key candidates in the race to replace retiring MP Paul Papalia in Secret Harbour live within its boundaries.

Labor's candidate Georgia Tree owns a property near the CBD but said she will be living in Port Kennedy — where she spent part of her childhood — during the campaign.

"Like many people I moved to the city for work, but that doesn't mean that I don't know the needs of this community or don't feel the needs of this community deeply," she said when that came to light.

"I believe people from this community deserve a foot in the door and deserve to stand in the room where decisions are made, and that's what's important to me."

Georgia Tree said she will be living in Port Kennedy during the Secret Harbour by-election campaign. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Ryan Robertson, the Liberals' newly-minted candidate, lives in neighbouring Rockingham and invited journalists to "run to work" with him during the campaign.

"It's 7.1 kilometres, which is roughly around 38 minutes," he said.

"As a representative for the City of Rockingham which covers a good portion of that electorate, I'm quite confident that I'm familiar with what's happening on the ground."

Ryan Robertson, who lives in Rockingham, with WA Liberal leader Basil Zempilas. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Greens candidate Rhi Davies said she has him beat though at 3.4 kilometres from the border.

"I can run here faster than the Liberal candidate," she declared at her first press conference.

Rhi Davies is the Greens candidate for Secret Harbour. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"I've spent heaps of time in Secret Harbour, my brothers live in Singleton.

"I consider myself still to be local and I think all the issues of the City of Rockingham are local and communal to all of us."

It's worth noting the seat's former representative, Paul Papalia, lived just outside Fremantle, according to parliamentary records.

How we fact-checked this story: We analysed 18 years of parliamentary disclosures, in which MPs declare any property they own or have interests in.

We then compared those addresses to electoral boundaries to identify which MPs lived inside or outside of their electorates.

We then made multiple attempts to contact MPs who live outside of their seats to confirm that information was up-to-date.

Liberals 'set tone'

Opposition leader Basil Zempilas did not give a straight answer when asked if he thought MPs should be required to live in their seats, as he does, along with the other five lower house Liberal MPs.

"So that's the tone that we've set, and you can see the tone that the premier has set," he said.

"He chose not to live in his electorate and a fair distance away from his electorate, so should we be surprised then that for Labor that's not a huge priority?"

Basil Zempilas campaigning in Secret Harbour. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Deputy Premier, Rita Saffioti, rejected the idea politicians had to live in their electorates earlier this month. Her disclosures show she lives in Victoria Park, about 12 kilometres away from her electorate of West Swan.

"My experience has been that people, your constituency, want you to deliver for them and their family," she said.

"You can't be living in everyone's household, but what you can do is represent the interests of your community and make sure you deliver for your community."

Rita Saffioti lives 12 kilometres from her electorate of West Swan. (ABC News: Kenith Png)

Dr Petter said the impact of where a senior leader like a premier or deputy premier lives is probably less, compared to a backbencher.

"They probably, even if they lived in that electorate, would be delegating a lot of that constituency work to their staff," he said.

Connecting with community

A number of politicians did not respond to questions when approached multiple times, including two who did not declare any property on their annual returns.

Of those MPs whose records indicate they live outside of their electorate, four did not respond to the ABC when asked to confirm if that information was still accurate.

Colleen Egan is one of the eight MPs who the ABC confirmed live outside of their seats, with her Bayswater home about a 23 kilometre drive from her electorate of Thornlie.

"I was raised in Roleystone and used to live in Gosnells. Having roots in and around the Thornlie electorate shaped me as a person and made me who I am," she said in a statement.

"I feel privileged to represent this wonderful community with passion and dedication."

Colleen Egan lives 23 kilometres from her electorate. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Dr Petter, whose PhD thesis researched how politicians engage with their electorates, said an MP's ability to connect with a community went beyond where they lived.

"Most MPs, when you survey and interview them will tell you that that sort of connection between the constituency they represent and themselves is very important," he said.

"A lot of them actually spend more than a full-time amount of working hours in their electorates once they're elected.

"That being said, if someone's just outside their electorate, they can still get there pretty easily and have a good idea of what the people there need."

World.title: Live: Plibersek defends PM's attendance at dinner hosted by billionaire family
World.content:
Shadow Defence Minister James Paterson has hosed down suggestions of a Coalition deal with One Nation after the next election.

Earlier this morning, Shadow Housing Minister Andrew Bragg left the door open to a potential coalition with the right-wing party after the next election.

Angus Taylor has previously ruled out doing a deal with the right-wing party to form government, including on the ABC's 7.30 program.

Asked about Bragg's comments, the shadow defence minister tells ABC Radio National Breakfast they don't reflect his understanding of the Liberal senator's views.

"We have one coalition partner already, which is the National Party, our traditional coalition partner, and we are not in the market for any other coalition partners. If we seek from the Australian people as a mandate to govern in that traditional coalition," Paterson says.

World.title: Hotel 'crisis' looms for new Sydney airport just months ahead of opening
World.content:
The lack of hotels near the soon-to-be-opened Western Sydney Airport (WSI) has been flagged as a major issue that could potentially impact the initial economic benefits of the new airport.

Due to open to passenger flights on October 25, operational trials at Australia's only 24/7 airport have been taking place, with cargo services set to officially start today.

Adam Leto, chief executive of Western Sydney Leadership Dialogue, said the area badly needed more hotels.

"We have got thousands of visitors landing on our doorstep starting from the end of this year that are going to be looking to stay, play and spend time in Western Sydney," he said.

"And we want to be able to keep them here, not have them move across the city for accommodation."

Mr Leto says more hotels are needed in the area to accommodate the numbers of projected passengers. (Supplied)

He said there were some new hotels in the pipeline near WSI, as well as in Parramatta, some 40 kilometres away.

Currently, there are only a handful of hotels within a 20km radius of the airport.

"There is no denying we have a hotel crisis at the moment. The state government has recognised there is a shortfall of beds in Western Sydney."

A spokesperson for the planned 200-room Courtyard by Marriott hotel, set to be built near the airport, said "there is not an opening timeline to share at this stage".

Do you know more? If you have any information about the story, contact Danuta Kozaki.

Established hotels set to benefit

Lauren Raffen is the owner and licensee of one of the hotels closest to the airport, the Wallacia Hotel.

While her hotel is set to benefit from the influx of travellers, she is concerned Western Sydney will not be able to accommodate the projected numbers.

"There's not too much around for the travellers coming in," she said.

"I don't know how we're going to keep them out here because there is not enough [hotels]."

Ms Raffen is also concerned about the lack of facilities locally for travellers. (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

She said there was great anticipation ahead of passenger flights in and out of WSI

"There is a lot of excitement here in Wallacia, reservations too because of the aircraft noise," she said.

"But a lot of the locals are excited, and business owners are too because it's going to bring in a lot of people."

The historic hotel is 14km west of the new airport and has 29 rooms with ensuites.

According to the Wallacia Progress Association's website, the 1930s hotel was requisitioned by the army during World War II.

"During the Second World War the hotel was used as the Army headquarters for radiophysics," it said.

The Wallacia Hotel is 14 kilometres west of the new airport. (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

With little public transport in the area, Ms Raffen said the hotel had plans to help passengers who have made reservations.

" We are putting a courtesy bus in place to make it convenient for travellers to and from the airport. "

She said the hotel, including its bistro and bar, already had many visitors from all over Sydney and the state on the weekends. There had also already been requests ahead of the airport's opening, especially from regional NSW.

"A lot of people from the state's Central West have said they will drive down and either stay the night before travelling if they have an early flight, or people planning to come in late at night have asked about staying here."

Mr Leto said other hotels in nearby Liverpool, Penrith and Rooty Hill were also expected to benefit.

Construction costs and red tape

Adding to the lag in new hotels, Mr Leto said, has been the cost of construction across Sydney.

"The market conditions, particularly when it comes to costs, whether you are talking residential or new hotels, the cost of construction across the city, particularly Western Sydney is challenging at the moment."

The cost of construction has been blamed as one of the reasons behind the lag in new hotel builds. (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

He added that red tape and the unknown were also factors.

"The market is also a little hesitant and not quite sure what the demand is going to look like," he said.

"But as soon as the planes start touching down and we start to see the numbers rolling in, I am expecting that will spur a bit more confidence."

A spokesperson for WSI said it expected private sector investment to increase.

"We fully expect that the private sector will respond to this demand as it develops," they said.

"WSI has already been the catalyst for billions of dollars in broader infrastructure in the Western Sydney Aerotropolis, supporting road networks, and beyond."

A spokesperson for the airport says "the private sector will respond to this demand". (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

Look to the future

The spokesperson for WSI said business was expected to grow.

New airport's neighbours feel overlooked Luddenham is a five-minute drive from Western Sydney International Airport, but some residents say they are missing out on the benefits it should be bringing them.m.

"Western Sydney International is built to meet demand for decades to come and will drive growth for the NSW visitor economy well into the future," they said.

"The airport is currently built to service 10 million passengers annually and will grow to service more than 80 million by the 2060s."

Mr Leto said it would become a major economic centre for Western Sydney over the next decade.

"It is going to take some time, like the broader picture around the Aerotropolis. You know Rome wasn't built in one day."

World.title: Live: ASX set to open higher after tech stocks dumped on Wall Street
World.content:
After trading at a loss for most of the session, the S & P 500 enjoyed a buying spurt just before closing to eke out a marginal gain, but not nearly enough to push it into positive territory over the week.

The litany of recent worries — doubts about the durability of AI valuations in the tech sector, war and the attendant inflationary spike in oil prices — was joined by the Trump administration wheeling out another round of very broad and inflationary tariffs.

Still, the overall mood seemed to be cautious rather than fearful, although many would characterise it more as complacent.

S & P 500: +0.05% (-0.6% over the week)

+0.05% (-0.6% over the week) Dow: +0.5% (-0.4% over the week)

+0.5% (-0.4% over the week) Nasdaq: -0.6% (-1.6% over the week)

The tech retreat is still a dominant theme. Shares in chipmaker Intel fell 8% despite posting a strong quarterly result.

The so-called "Magnificent Seven" tech stocks, such as Amazon, Microsoft and Meta Platforms, collectively shed around 5% for the week. Amazon and Tesla fell around 10% and 18% respectively post results.

Across the Atlantic, European stocks recouped much of Thursday's sharp losses to be up 0.8% for the session and 0.7% higher for the week.

When ASX 200 futures trading closed on Saturday morning (AEST), the prospects for today were promising, pointing to a 0.6% gain today, which would recoup last week's 0.3% slide.

Global oil prices eased back below the $US100/barrel mark despite two weeks of missiles, drones and threats whizzing back and forth across the Gulf.

Brent crude futures: -3.9% to $US96.78/barrel

-3.9% to $US96.78/barrel West Texas Intermediate crude: 3.1% to $US89.31/barrel

The fall in prices came after news filtered out that China had initiated a push to resume stalled peace talks between the United States and Iran.

Oil prices may ease more today with the news overnight that the US and Iran had called a halt to their bombing campaigns, at least temporarily.

However, as Price Futures Group senior analyst Phil Flynn told Reuters, energy markets remain in a precarious state.

The global Brent crude benchmark gained around 10% over the week.

"Overall stocks remain pretty tight — and that situation could turn on a dime, so it's worth keeping a close watch as things develop," Mr Flynn said.

The easing in oil prices saw US Treasury bond yields dip from their 18-month high, but the fear of inflation and the Fed being forced to jack up rates meant investors remained cautious.

The Fed's rate-setting committee (the FOMC) meets this week, with markets still pricing in another "hold".

Most currencies were steady against the Greenback, although the Aussie dollar nudged higher to trade just under 70 US cents.

World.title: Inside Hobart council's 'snack saga' and why the police are involved
World.content:
The City of Hobart is like many other councils where tempers fray, harsh words are exchanged, and insults fly, but a stoush over taking snacks and drinks seems to have kicked it up a notch.

Deputy Lord Mayor Zelinda Sherlock has admitted to and apologised for taking provisions from a council lounge over several years.

The issue reared its head earlier this month after photos of Cr Sherlock entering the council chambers and leaving with bags of items were released by Cr Louise Elliot.

It has led to heated social media posts, a claim of blackmail, a referral to the police commissioner and calls for Cr Sherlock to resign — all of which is playing out on the public stage.

In a letter to all Hobart councillors, Acting Director of Local Government Luke Gregory implored them to respect their obligations as elected members, and to act in the best interest of their community.

"Should conduct and standards continue to deteriorate, I will need to carefully consider and balance all potential regulatory options that may be appropriate in those circumstances," he said.

Louise Elliot has tabled a motion calling for an investigation into the incident. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Cr Elliot has tabled a motion to be debated at Monday night's council meeting.

It will be held behind closed doors, so councillors will not be able to discuss the outcome publicly, but the motion calls for Mr Gregory's office to investigate the incidents and the council's handling of them.

Mr Gregory said the motion was unnecessary because his office was already aware of the matter.

"I wish to make clear that my office and its regulatory responsibilities are not to be utilised as a tool to further agendas by individual members against their political opponents," he said.

The motion also calls for support to write to Tasmania Police about Cr Sherlock's conduct, but Mr Gregory said the allegations had already been referred to police.

Meanwhile, Cr Sherlock has reported claims Cr Elliot blackmailed her to police, which they are reviewing.

What actually happened?

In January, a motion was put forward by four councillors calling for an independent investigation into allegations Cr Sherlock had taken ratepayer-funded food and drink from the Town Hall's elected members' lounge for personal use.

The motion failed, but the issue gained traction again earlier this month after Cr Elliot obtained documents and emails under Tasmania's right-to-information laws.

They contained images from CCTV footage showing Cr Sherlock and an unidentified companion entering and leaving the council building after hours, with a shopping bag supposedly filled with workplace refreshments, on two occasions in January 2024.

CCTV shows Zelinda Sherlock with a person, whose identity has been obscured, leaving with the snacks. (Supplied)

Emails revealed items had been removed from the lounge after no events had been held, including soft drinks, three bottles of wine, seven bottles of beer, nuts and chocolates, and that employees had been noticing unexplained dwindling stock since at least June 2023.

On LinkedIn, Cr Sherlock wrote she had been taking the snacks from Town Hall for her home office, until she was told by staff a couple of years ago they could not be consumed elsewhere.

She referred herself to Tasmania's Integrity Commission, which chose not to investigate, finding it did not constitute misconduct.

A divided council

There has been a fierce divide across the current Hobart council chamber at times between two unofficial factions.

The larger of the groups, which includes current Lord Mayor Anna Reynolds and Cr Sherlock, is considered more progressive and more left-leaning.

Anna Reynolds is stepping down next month, meaning Zelinda Sherlock is set to become acting mayor. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

A smaller, more conservative faction, which includes Cr Elliot, is often at odds with them.

Former mayor and local government association president Sue Smith said during her time on council, conflict was mostly managed internally.

"I always used to say, we don't have to like one another to know that out of respect for our community that's put us there, we have to work together," Ms Smith said.

"Now, everybody wants to bring their issues right to the forefront, and I think more often than not, before they've attempted to show some maturity and solve those problems."

Kerry Vincent has called on Hobart councillors to leave their egos at the door and serve their constituents. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Local Government Minister Kerry Vincent said the issue was "extremely disappointing".

"You need to leave your ego at the door sometimes, you need to focus on what needs to happen … you are there to represent everybody, not just your separate opinions," Mr Vincent said.

"I ask them to show a bit of respect for everybody, and to focus on what they need to be for the community and understand what their role is for their community."

He said a combination of differing opinions, amid the heat of an upcoming election, can create an "explosive situation that isn't appropriate."

Cr Sherlock, who recently became a member of the Tasmanian Greens, is due to become Hobart's acting lord mayor once Anna Reynolds resigns in August, before local government elections are held in October.

World.title: Refugee searching for rental home rejected more than 100 times
World.content:
Congolese refugee Jay Biayi applied for more than 100 rentals over almost six months but was rejected every time.

His family moved to South Australia from the Democratic Republic of the Congo after obtaining refugee visas.

"Housing … that's very challenging because we spent close to six months just to get accommodation," he said.

" I went to over 100 house inspections, and our applications were rejected. "

After spending months of searching for a home, his family finally settled in Adelaide's northern suburbs.

What do you want to tell us? Have Your Say Our best stories start with listening to yours. Tell us what Australia should know.

Mr Biayi's experience is not uncommon — national rental vacancy rates remain near historic lows, according to Domain's latest quarterly rent report.

Adelaide's vacancy rate sat at 0.4 per cent in June, while the data also showed median rent for a house rose by 1.6 per cent to "a record" $650 per week.

Migrants part of the workforce solution

Mr Biayi has a social work qualification, but is developing his language skills at TAFE before he enters the workforce.

"As someone who is not working in Australia, finding a house is really, really challenging," he said.

Mr Biayi said he hoped to find a job in social work, health or aged care — sectors which SA Multicultural Communities Council chief executive Helena Kyriazopoulos said were "desperate for workers".

Helena Kyriazopoulos says helping migrants access affordable housing is important. (Supplied: MCCSA)

"We shouldn't see people like Jay through the lens of a disadvantage, but through the lens of potential," she said.

"If we want people to contribute, we need to ensure they have a fair opportunity to establish themselves, and that starts with access to affordable housing."

SA Council of Social Service chief executive Catherine Earl said "migrants are certainly part of the solution" to address worker shortages, but said housing was a "real problem".

"It's really hard … landlords are able to pick and choose who they provide their property to," she said.

"If someone's got a restricted or very limited income, they may not be the most attractive person in terms of who's applying to move into that property, which is really unfortunate, especially for someone who's intending to enter the labour force."

Catherine Earl says migrants can help address workforce shortages. (ABC News: Marco Catalano)

Despite the long wait for a home, Mr Biayi and his family said they had been welcomed as newcomers in their new neighbourhood.

"The neighbours are all so happy and friendly, we really like it," he said.

He encouraged people to learn from different cultures and backgrounds.

"Australia is a multicultural community … so approach other people, so it will be more useful and interesting," he said.

Ms Kyriazopoulos said workers with diverse backgrounds were particularly important.

"They come in with an amazing wealth of cultural understanding and great experience they can actually share," she said.

"That's what we're asking for, in ensuring that we have the migrant population coming in, in servicing our industries."

World.title: Jacinta Allan leadership threat LIVE updates: Victorian Premier under pressure as state Labor chiefs hold crisis meeting
World.content:
Premier Jacinta Allan, who spent Sunday night at her home in Bendigo with senior advisers, has refused to resign despite mounting internal pressure.

Deputy Premier Ben Carroll has said he will not challenge Premier Jacinta Allan, but would run if the leadership became vacant. Ruby Alexander

World.title: Fire ‘at the gates’ of Bordeaux as Europe battles blazes
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeExtreme weather Fire ‘at the gates’ of Bordeaux as Europe battles blazes Manuel Ausloos and David Latona Updated July 27, 2026 — 7:05am ,first published 2:34am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Bordeaux/Madrid: Wildfires advanced towards the outskirts of the historic French city of Bordeaux at the heart of the country’s winelands as France and Spain battled blazes that have already forced the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of people. About 220,000 people have been evacuated in France, while in Spain more than 75,000 people have had to leave their homes and about 30,000 more were ordered to shelter in place, authorities said. Firefighters battle a forest fire on Sunday in Saint-Jean-d’Illac, about 30 kilometres from Bordeaux. AFP In France, fires have ravaged the Cap Ferret peninsula on the Atlantic coast, a popular tourist destination, and spread through areas surrounding Bordeaux, where firefighters were trying to prevent the flames from reaching the regional capital. Bordeaux Mayor Thomas Cazenave described the blaze as being “at the gates of the metropolitan area”, about 15 kilometres away from the entry points to the main city.



“We have a fire that is not under control and which is moving in the direction of the city area,” Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said late on Sunday (French time). “The overall situation is very unfavourable, we are in a situation that is unprecedented.” Related Article Updated

Bushfires Wildfires threaten Bordeaux as more than 200,000 people flee flames in France, Spain Cazenave said earlier on Sunday that there were no plans to evacuate Bordeaux, whose wider metropolitan area has a population of about 850,000. Nunez said authorities would continue to assess the situation calmly and realistically. As the blaze advanced, police went door-to-door overnight in the municipalities of Marcheprime and Cestas, evacuating residents one home at a time. French authorities released footage showing officers knocking on doors in the dark and urging people to leave. In Spain, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez visited fire-hit areas in Avila, one of three central provinces affected by major blazes alongside Madrid and Toledo, where more than 45,000 hectares (111,000 acres) have burnt.



A separate blaze in Spain’s eastern Castellon province has ravaged more than 4300 hectares, regional authorities said. “The fire is out of control, it’s very difficult to extinguish from a technical standpoint, especially because of the adverse weather conditions that will continue throughout the day,” the regional leader of Valencia, Juanfran Perez, told reporters near the site. Flames engulf trees at La Adrada, in Spain’s Avila province overnight on Saturday. Anadolu via Getty Images A firefighter battles a wildfire in San Martin de Valdeiglesias, west of Madrid, Spain, on Sunday. AP Photo/Manu Fernandez The wildfire has entered the Sierra de Espadan natural park, which contains large forests of pine trees and cork oaks.



The fires are the latest disasters linked to prolonged drought and successive heatwaves that scientists say have been intensified by climate change. Related Article Heatwave Europe’s summers are changing. The continent isn’t ready In both Bordeaux and Avila, July high temperatures have averaged 32 degrees, almost 6 degrees above the month’s normal high between 1961 and 1990, the Reuters Climate Monitor noted. Under the European Union’s civil protection mechanism, Greece and Italy have each sent two Canadair firefighting aircraft to Spain, while Portugal has deployed more than 100 military personnel along with equipment. Two more planes will arrive “as soon as possible” from Turkey, the Spanish interior ministry said on X.



Sanchez said that his government would declare a civil protection emergency on Tuesday for the central provinces plagued by the wildfires, unlocking additional recovery funding. More than 150,000 hectares have burned across Spain since January, he said, six times the area destroyed during the same period last year. Loading While wildfires have long been a feature of Spain’s summers, Sanchez said their growing scale and intensity, fuelled by increasingly extreme weather, required policies grounded in climate science.



In the highlands of Scotland, as many as 500 firefighters have been dealing with a large blaze within Cairngorms National Park since July 15. Residents of the village of Nethy Bridge, who were evacuated on Friday evening after a change in weather conditions, were allowed to return to their homes late on Saturday. A firefighter takes a break while battling a wildfire near Le Temple, outside Bordeaux. AP Photo/Emma Da Silva In Italy, several bushfires forced the closure of a southern section of the Rome ring road as well as a motorway leading into the capital, causing major traffic disruption. In Italy’s southern Puglia region, tourists were evacuated from seaside resorts due to a large wildfire in the Gargano area, the national fire department said. Some were taken away by sea by the coast guard, the ANSA news agency added.



Pope Leo, speaking from his summer residence of Castel Gandolfo outside Rome, offered spiritual support. “In light of the devastating wildfires that have affected various areas of France and Spain in recent days, I wish to express my solidarity and closeness, and I invite everyone to pray for those affected and for the rescue workers engaged in relief efforts,” he said. A burnt vehicle sits outside a charred house in Navas del Rey, west of Madrid. AP Photo/Manu Fernandez Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Berlin Pride van attack suspect shot dead in confrontation with police
World.content:
WorldEuropeCrime Berlin Pride van attack suspect shot dead in confrontation with police Geir Moulson , Kirsten Grieshaber and Stefanie Dazio July 27, 2026 — 6:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Berlin: The suspect in the deadly Berlin Pride attack that left one person dead and 29 injured was shot and killed by police during a confrontation in a suburb of the city, authorities said. Abdul Ballout, a German citizen with Lebanese roots, was killed following a search that lasted nearly 24 hours after the attack in downtown Berlin. Prosecutors said he had previously sought to join the militant Islamic State group. Police stand in a garden house colony in Berlin’s Spandau district, where authorities said the suspect in the deadly Berlin Pride van attack was shot dead in a confrontation on Sunday. Getty Images Ballout was suspected of driving a van into a crowd near Berlin’s Pride festival on Saturday night (German time) before apparently stabbing others with a machete in what authorities believe was an Islamic extremist terror attack. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the attack occurred a few hundred metres from a party near the Brandenburg Gate that was supposed to close out the city’s Pride festival.



An undated image of Abdul Ballout. Ballout, 21, was tracked down about 6pm Sunday (German time) at a garden in Spandau, a Berlin suburb, the city’s police department wrote on X. They said he apparently ran toward officers with a sharp instrument, and police fired at least one shot. He died at the scene. Ballout was born in Germany, the minister said. His mother was naturalised in 2002, three years before he was born. Ashley Jump, a 26-year-old UK resident, had travelled to Berlin for Saturday’s Pride parade but had left the celebrations before the attack. They returned Sunday to leave flowers at a memorial near the crime scene in support of the LGBTQ community. “They’ll never erase us, we’ll never be gone,” they said. “As long as humanity has existed, we’ve existed. And as long as humanity exists, we will exist. We will not be removed.”



Ballout travelled to Lebanon in 2025 with the goal of going to Syria to join the Islamic State group, Berlin prosecutors said Sunday. There, he made contact with several people who were presumed members of the militant group – or at least he believed them to be, prosecutors said. He was arrested in Lebanon last year and sentenced by a military court to three months’ imprisonment for offences including incitement to religious and sectarian conflict. The vehicle used to ram into a crowd at the Pride March is removed from Berlin’s Tiergarten park on Sunday. AP Photo/Ebrahim Noroozi He returned to Germany after completing his sentence, where he was arrested at the Berlin airport. In May, a juvenile court in Berlin convicted Ballout of preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state, as well as publishing Islamic State propaganda on his Instagram account and other charges, prosecutors said.



The court handed down a suspended sentence of 1 year and 10 months in youth custody, which Berlin prosecutors had appealed. Related Article Crime ‘Our freedom has been attacked’: Manhunt after van rams crowd at Berlin Pride parade The court said it took Ballout’s months of pre-trial detention in Germany and Lebanon into account. It also said it considered that Ballout had confessed to the crimes, appeared to distance himself from the militant group and no actual threat had ever materialised. He was released from detention pending the appeal. According to police, a white van drove into the Tiergarten park about 10pm on Saturday (Berlin time) and hit several people before crashing into a tree.



The closing party at the Pride festival, known as Christopher Street Day, was ongoing at the time next to the Brandenburg Gate, a short distance away. The party followed a parade with some 80 trucks that had made its way through downtown Berlin earlier in the day. The attack did not occur at the festival, along its route or at the closing party. Rather, the violence took place a few hundred meters away on a track in the Tiergarten park. The van drove into a crowd that was likely a mix of festivalgoers and other locals or visitors. Police said a woman was killed. On Sunday afternoon, hundreds of mourners gathered at a memorial at the iconic gate. They hugged each other and laid down flowers, candles, rainbow flags and homemade signs, including a cardboard one that said: “The only thing more powerful than hate is love.” Hundreds of thousands had come to Berlin to celebrate on Saturday, though it’s unclear how many were still at the festival by late evening. It’s one of Europe’s largest LGBTQ celebrations.



“We are simply stunned by what happened,” said Andre Lehmann, a top official with the main national LGBTQ association, LSVD+. “This suspected attack hits the heart of the queer community.” Mourners embrace at a makeshift memorial at Pariser Platz, in front of the Brandenburg Gate. Getty Images Chancellor Friedrich Merz urged the nation to remain united in the aftermath of the attack. “I would like to say this to Christopher Street Day participants here in Berlin but also across Germany: Don’t let yourselves, let us not let ourselves, be intimidated,” he said. “These acts have only one purpose: They aim to divide our society. They want to take away from us the most important thing we have: Namely our openness and our freedom.”



Dobrindt said he expected security measures at other major events in Germany, including Pride events elsewhere, to be reviewed and if necessary significantly boosted. Berlin has seen Islamic extremist attacks before. In December, 2016, a rejected asylum seeker from Tunisia ploughed a hijacked truck into a Christmas market, killing 13 people and injuring dozens. He was killed days later in a shootout in Italy. The van was crashed into a tree after the attack on the march. AP Photo/Markus Schreiber In February last year, a Spanish tourist was stabbed and seriously wounded at Berlin’s Holocaust Memorial, an attack that saw a Syrian man convicted in March and sentenced to 13 years. This week, Amsterdam will be hosting World Pride alongside its own annual Pride celebrations.



Mayor Femke Halsema said authorities and organisers were “closely monitoring the security situation” after the Berlin attack but aim to prevent any extra measures getting in the way of celebrating freedom and love. People gather near the Brandenburg Gate supporting the LGBTQ community after the Pride March attack. AP Photo/Markus Schreiber AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Mark Speakman labelled her a bully; now this anti-abortion activist is donating to the NSW Liberals
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsNSWNSW State Parliament Mark Speakman labelled her a bully; now this anti-abortion activist is donating to the NSW Liberals Michael McGowan July 27, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The NSW Liberals received a donation from an anti-abortion activist who was accused of “brazen bullying” and attempting the “Americanisation of NSW politics” by former party leader Mark Speakman. The $2000 donation from strident anti-abortion activist and campaigner Joanna Howe was made at one of a series of political fundraisers that the NSW Liberal Party has held with firebrand federal senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price since September. Anti-abortion activist Joanna Howe donated $2000 at a Liberal Party fundraiser with Jacinta Nampijinpa Price. She previously campaigned against the party’s former leader Mark Speakman. Aresna Villanueva A Rhodes scholar and a legal academic, Howe has drawn criticism from across the political spectrum for what South Australian Deputy Premier Kyam Maher has described as her “Trumpian” tactics. She has been accused of attempting to import a MAGA-style debate about abortion into Australia, and in 2024 was banned from parts of South Australia’s parliament after MPs in that state claimed she used “threatening and intimidating” tactics during an abortion debate. Howe has previously denied this, and described the ban as an “appalling” abuse of power.



Related Article Immigration ‘Deep hurt’: NSW Coalition apologises to Indian community after Price’s comments More recently, Howe has organised a series of large anti-abortion protests outside NSW parliament, including one attended by former deputy prime minister turned One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce last month. Her attendance at the fundraiser and the donation is expected to anger some senior Coalition figures given Howe, who has a large social media following, has been targeting NSW Nationals MPs in the lead-up to next year’s election, and had previously campaigned for Speakman to be sacked. As recently as this weekend, Howe held community forums targeting the seats of Bathurst and Cootamundra MPs Paul Toole and Steph Cooke because of their previous support for an abortion decriminalisation bill in 2019. Her campaigning activities in NSW drew the ire of Speakman during a debate over a Greens bill that gave greater access to the right to prescribe medical abortions for terminations up to nine weeks.



The bill, which was ultimately passed, was modelled on recommendations of a NSW Health review of abortion law that found so-called “abortion deserts” were undermining the functionality of the 2019 legislation. During debate over the bill in 2025, Speakman accused Howe of having “threatened” his leadership, accusing her of “brazen bullying” and declaring he would not “cave in” in the face of political threats. He read out an email from Howe in which she said that she would “suspend my planned campaign against Labor, in order to lead a public campaign aimed at encouraging a grassroots opposition to you as Liberal leader” if he supported the bill. At the time, Howe ran Facebook ads urging people to “join the Liberal Party to axe Speakman”. She rejected the idea that she had bullied Speakman, saying she had been critical of all sides of politics “without fear or favour”.



Related Article Opinion

Abortion How anti-abortion influencer’s MAGA-style campaign fell flat Alexandra Smith Senior writer “[A]ll I did was write to him to ask him to vote against [the] bill and to notify him, which, I thought, was quite a polite thing to do, that I intended to run a political campaign against him if he sided with the Greens on their radical abortion bill,” she said. Howe frequently posts on social media in support of Pauline Hanson’s One Nation. She insists that she is not aligned to any party, and supports MPs such as Liberal upper house MP Rachel Merton, who opposes abortion. At the Farrer byelection, she issued a how-to-vote card that encouraged her supporters to back Family First candidate Rebecca Scriven above successful One Nation candidate David Farley. Though her campaigning focuses on issues such as the sex-selective abortion ban now before the NSW parliament, she said her ultimate goal is to “bring the number of abortions to zero”. “But I recognise that we have to bring people on a journey, and that’s going to happen through incremental law reform,” she said.



Howe, who refers to Labor as “the party for abortion”, said that changes to introduce more restrictive abortion law would happen only “through parties on the right”. “My interest is for the Liberal Party to be a pro-life party, to be against late-term abortion,” she said. “And so, where I can support good politicians in that party who stand for the human rights of children, I will support those politicians.” Electoral disclosures show that Howe made the donation at one of three political fundraisers the Liberals held with Price after she made the inflammatory claim last year that the Albanese government was encouraging Indian migration to bolster its vote. She later walked back the comments, but was dumped from former leader Sussan Ley’s frontbench before being reappointed by Angus Taylor in February. One of the fundraisers, in September, came just days after she made the remarks and prompted an apology at the time from Speakman. The three fundraisers included one with Merton, which Howe attended, another with the Willoughby branch of the Liberals, and a third “in conversation” with Sky News host Rowan Dean organised by the party’s Roseville branch.



NSW Liberals are concerned that the party’s parlous financial state could undermine its already outside chances of reclaiming government and has forced hard decisions about seats to target at the 2027 state election. Other donors at the events have included the Pharmacy Guild of Australia, Insurance Australia Group and industry lobby group Coal Australia. World.title: Christmas in July: Wanganeen-Milera delivers another performance worthy of three votes
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 Christmas in July: Wanganeen-Milera delivers another performance worthy of three votes Peter Ryan Updated July 27, 2026 — 5:49am ,first published 7:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Key points The AFL has 112 listed players in their 30s. A decade ago it was only 65.

Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera has done it again in July.

‘F--- off’ should not be the phrase of choice between Suns teammates.

Carlton’s Lewis Young went back on his mark further than Michael Holding.

Nasiah the messiah should get the three votes Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera defeated the Kangaroos to keep the Saints’ wildcard chances alive. He charged into the game like a fire truck scattering traffic when he kicked three goals and created another goal for Darcy Wilson after chasing down Finn O’Sullivan in the third quarter. Not only did his sheer brilliance shift the contest, his presence lifted teammates and signalled a return to form after he lost his way against the close checking Cat in round 19.



He became the first player to reach 30 disposals, gain 750 metres and kick three goals in the first three quarters. Then he kicked the Saints’ first goal of the final quarter with a steal from Caleb Daniel that ended with a running banana. View post on X The performance was a reprise of his memorable two-vote winning effort against Melbourne on July 27 last season (it was July 26 on Sunday) and a reminder of the reason the Saints paid such a large percentage of their salary cap this season to keep him. Does he get changed in a phone box before games at this time of the year? Thankfully, the umpires have the statistics on hand when voting for the Brownlow. Surely 46 touches (even allowing for kick-ins), four goals, and five clearances will earn him BOG honours.



The 34-year-old who out-scored Essendon Jack Gunston’s seven-goal haul against Essendon helped the cause of veterans wanting to play on in 2027. He is 34, has kicked 100 goals in his past 30 matches, and kicked a matchwinning behind for the Hawks on Easter Monday against Geelong. He has now kicked five bags of five goals this season. According to @sirswampthing he became the third-oldest player to outscore the opposition with his 7.2 (44) topping the Bombers 5.9 (39) on Saturday. Hawthorn star Jack Gunston kicked his 600th goal during a brilliant third quarter. AFL Photos via Getty Images



His performance was a timely reminder of the increased presence and influence of older players in the competition in the same week he and 36-year-old Cat Patrick Dangerfield signed on for another season. Unusually, the trend has become the old-timer’s friend. It’s no longer unusual to have at least half a dozen players on a club list who are 30-something. In 2026, there were 112 listed players still getting dirty in their 30s. In 2016, there were only 65. In 2026, eight players of the top 20 highest rating players in the competition are 30-something. In 2016, the only player was then Suns’ champion Gary Ablett jr. Four of the top players in this year’s coaches’ votes are in their 30s right now. In 2016 there were zero.



The shift has not just occurred because the money is too good to pass up and sports science has improved player longevity. Games record holder and the oldest player in the game Scott Pendlebury makes a huge contribution to the Magpies AFL Photos Clubs now recognise how valuable it can be to have older players on their list as long as they fill a few preconditions. They need to lose the grumpy pills which are allocated to everyone in greater numbers after each year after they reach 30. That means accepting a different role which may mean playing out of the midfield, or less game time, or fewer games, or even playing VFL and accepting the importance and satisfaction of the often underappreciated teaching job.



The AFL’s oldest current players 38 Scott Pendlebury (Collingwood)

37 Dayne Zorko (Brisbane Lions)

36 Patrick Dangerfield (Geelong)*

36 Taylor Walker (Adelaide)

36 Dane Rampe (Sydney Swans)

36 Jeremy Howe (Collingwood)

35 Steele Sidebottom (Collingwood)

35 Rhys Stanley (Geelong)

35 Mason Cox (Fremantle)

34 Mark Blicavs (Geelong)

34 Jake Melksham (Melbourne)

34 Jack Gunston (Hawthorn)*

34 Max Gawn (Melbourne)*

34 Nick Haynes (Carlton)

34 Tom Liberatore (Western Bulldogs) Of the top 15 oldest players in the league, only Melbourne’s Max Gawn has played every match and remains at his peak every match. The rest have accepted something different. Even Gawn has pulled back a little to give Max Heath a taste when possible. Resisting the temptation to be grumpy means taking notice of players and people in the program, passing on wisdom and enjoying the achievements of those many years your junior. You can set some people straight or you can expand your own sense of what is possible and gain a new lease of life. Anyone who saw teammates celebrate the 600th career goal of the friendly curmudgeon that is Gunston by making him the centre of attention understood how great clubs are built on connections between generations. To play on, a player needs to maintain their weapons so they can be deployed in a role that suits the team’s needs – if not every match then often enough.



The skipper Patrick Dangerfield will play on in 2027 Getty Images Dangerfield’s power remains although it’s used to win or halve contests inside 50 rather than in the midfield where he would need to work too hard to stay in the game. Scott Pendlebury’s poise and ability to put teammates into space is a feature, Jeremy Howe’s leap and defensive know-how is strong, Dayne Zorko hasn’t lost his pace or capacity to kick darts. In an excellent piece of coaching, Gunston has had a role created for him inside 50 which suits his strengths. The disconnected forward leads hard and is an accurate set shot. It’s not easy but certainly his workload is less than others. Imagine what Ben King will learn from him next season? They are no longer their club’s best players – although they can be the best man on the ground in a quarter or half occasionally as Gunston was in the third quarter on Saturday – but the team is better for their presence.



Clubs have also decided a veteran who can play can add depth to their list and complement their team in a way a mediocre mid-20s player can’t. It’s why free agency has proved a bigger boon for strong teams than weaker ones (Good old Lachie Neale forever?). They can add quality players who increase competition for spots, add poise and experience and therefore valuable lessons to both AFL and VFL teams, and during the week when clubs undergo situational training their input is useful. It’s recognition of a point champion cricketer Greg Chappell made in his book Not Out - accepted wisdom among coaches without ego - that players learn better from their peers than coaches.



There is also an in-built resilience in veterans as they navigate a long season under scrutiny with all sorts of ups and downs that helps younger players find perspective when challenges inevitably arise. The extra man on the bench has also given an impetus to the clubs’ willingness to retain veterans as they can manage their time better and have more options when planning how they are going to cover roles. Going on might be good for Gunston and his peers, but this situation has not arisen because clubs have suddenly become generous. The times they are a-changin’ and the veterans’ importance will be on display in September when they challenge the relatively inexperienced premiership favourite Fremantle.



For the Suns, it’s a season not to forget ‘F--- off’ should not be the phrase of choice between Suns’ teammates given the unfortunate pattern of players taking the direction literally. That teenager Leo Lombard chose to direct that response to animated feedback from a frustrated veteran Christian Petracca is not ideal but it can be easily addressed. It’s not uncommon for interactions between teammates to get off track midway through games. Leo Lombard looks on after a spray from Christian Petracca. Fox Footy



The problem for the Suns is that it reinforces the sense among other clubs that Suns’ players argue on field more than other teams in 2026 (officials at two clubs had mentioned this Suns’ characteristic to this column in the past few months). It also symbolises a season that has spun out of control since their win over Port Adelaide in round 10 in Darwin, when they sat fourth on the ladder and Ben King indicated he wanted to stay at the club. No doubt they have unravelled, but a more in-depth look at their performances indicates more lies behind the drop-off than suggestions of discord, of which there have been plenty, all denied by the Suns. In those first 10 matches, they beat an underdone Geelong, followed by wins over battlers West Coast, Richmond, Essendon, Giants, St Kilda and Port Adelaide. Since Darwin they ran out of legs against North Melbourne then have lost to Brisbane, Geelong, Hawthorn, Fremantle, Collingwood, Adelaide, Western Bulldogs and now Carlton.



That’s like a racehorse being found wanting when stepping up to the wrong grade. Add other elements and a clear picture emerges than the shadow the Suns are casting right now. Injury has ruined Matt Rowell’s year, Mac Andrew’s development has been slow, the ruck rules have pushed Jarrod Witts off the cliff, Bailey Humphrey became distracted by trade talk, and Ben Ainsworth, Sam Flanders, Brayden Fiorini, Connor Budarick and David Swallow all exited after playing in the winning final and were replaced with more talented but less ready players such as Lombard. The other - more existential issue - is that problems of retention have not been solved with Rowell the next contract discussion to be had. And their team needs to deal with frustration better and bounce back from disappointment. That is something they can’t stick their head in the Surfers Paradise sand and hide from.



Smart play young man Carlton’s Lewis Young consoles his Suns’ opponent Ned Moyle AFL Photos Carlton’s Lewis Young went back on his mark further than Michael Holding on his run-up when he had a set shot late in the game against Gold Coast. He not only used the 30 seconds available for players taking a set shot but by taking the Ben Brown run up was able to drain another 14 seconds off the clock during his run-up before kicking. The time remaining went from 3.48 to 3.04 minutes left in the game. It will be interesting if someone tries the same [long] approach in finals. Later that night, Richmond’s Luke Trainor kicked the ball out on the full from outside the boundary line after receiving a free kick for out on the full. However, because he had not returned into play the ball was brought back to where he kicked it for a boundary throw-in. It was a strange rule anomaly that requires consideration post-season. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: When it comes to sex education, teachers and students need answers
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaEducation When it comes to sex education, teachers and students need answers Nicole Precel July 27, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

At a school in Melbourne’s inner north, Vanessa Hamilton asks 13 primary school teachers where their students are learning about sex. From a large table in the staff room, they call out answers: social media, television, YouTube, spicy novels, older siblings. For Hamilton, a former sexual health nurse turned sexuality educator, these answers are unsurprising. Talking the Talk sexuality educator Vanessa Hamilton says teachers feel ill-equipped to deliver relationship and sexuality education. Jason South “You’d hope they’d say parents or school, but not necessarily,” she says. “That’s not what I’m seeing.”



Having run the same professional development session at the same school previously, Hamilton says most teachers believe that once they have the right tools, delivering sex education lessons is less daunting than they had imagined and can be empowering. Despite the introduction of national guidelines in 2015 and national mandates in 2023, La Trobe University’s Third National Study of Australian Teachers of Relationships and Sexuality Education shows that two-thirds of teachers still don’t feel equipped to deliver classes on the subject, while students say they want more practical guidance. The survey, published on Monday, also found two-thirds of teachers (68.1 per cent) still have no formal training in providing sexual education to their students, while 60 per cent say they fear saying the wrong thing or facing negative reactions from parents. In recent years, the scope of topics has broadened from puberty, contraception, HIV and sexually transmitted infection prevention, and protective behaviours to also include discussions on consent, respectful relationships and digital literacy, including online safety, sexting and the influence of pornography. However, La Trobe researcher Lily Moor said young people were still reporting education often lacked the nuance or practical guidance they needed. With recent research showing condom use among sexually active Australian teenagers was at its lowest recorded level since 1992, Moor said ensuring teachers felt confident to tackle these issues was critical.



Related Article Education Safe sex decline: Teenage condom use hits 30-year low Lead researcher Professor Jennifer Power agreed, saying increasing misogynistic, homophobic and transphobic content online had heightened the scrutiny of lessons for students and parents, leaving some educators feeling uncertain about their role. “These broader moral and political dynamics shape teachers’ comfort and confidence in delivering RSE [relationship and sexuality education], as they navigate concerns sometimes raised by parents or others in the community,” Power said. Hamilton said in her experience, most parents were supportive, but one vocal parent could be enough to derail a program. “I’ve had one or two cancellations due to just one parent agitating, and leadership weren’t able to stand up to those parents,” she said. “Some of these people who object can be very threatening.”



La Trobe’s survey also found about one in four educators had no training on how to respond to disclosures of sexual violence or harassment from students, and felt least comfortable discussing topics of sexual pleasure, pornography and abortion. “If we’re putting all of this investment into keeping young people safe, we really need to make sure that schools are engaging in a way that is relevant for young people,” Moor said. Talking the Talk sexuality educator Vanessa Hamilton says teachers feel ill-equipped to deliver relationship and sexuality education. Jason South “Even if it’s not necessarily … these sort of explicit things about sex that young people are really yearning for, we still need to be making sure that we’re adequately engaging with young people about sexual safety, sexual health, sexual wellbeing, or else it does end up falling by the wayside.” Having spent decades in the sexual education sector, Hamilton said withholding age-appropriate information from students was “unethical” and potentially neglectful.



“The evidence is so crystal clear, and our rates of abuse and gender-based sexual violence are so high, and education absolutely can help prevent that,” she said. Related Article Investigation

Medical misogyny Penny was told her agonising pain was just ovulation. The next day, she was begging to die Among younger children, she said not providing information about topics such as menstruation until they were 12, which some parents chose to do, was “neglectful” because some children got their periods when they were as young as eight. In Victoria, the state Department of Education has allocated $129 million to the Respectful Relationships initiative and employs 42 dedicated staff to provide professional learning and support to educators delivering the program, a government spokesperson said. The age-appropriate teaching and learning resources had been developed by experts and were provided to teachers to freely use in class, and covered a range of topics, the spokesperson said.



“Teaching consent and pornography awareness matters more than ever, given the new risks posed by AI misuse,” the spokesperson said. Of the 482 primary and secondary school teachers surveyed across government, Catholic and independent schools, 93.4 per cent said that when they were given enough time and adequate resources for professional development in the topic, they felt more prepared to deliver it. The survey came with 13 recommendations, including making training compulsory and developing a national outcomes framework to ensure consistent, evidence-based delivery across schools. It also recommended frameworks and policies to ensure the programs were being implemented properly. The federal government said it had provided $83 million to support the delivery of evidence-based, age-appropriate, and expert-developed respectful relationships education.



The National Respectful Relationships Education Framework was published in March and provided guidance to help schools deliver consent and respectful relationships education. Federal education minister Jason Clare said it was rolling out in every state and territory, and included specialist knowledge, developing resources to support classroom delivery of respectful relationships education and professional development. But Sexual Health Victoria’s head of education services, Sam Read, said the approach to sexuality and relationships education was fragmented and lacked national governance. She said a whole-of-school or whole-of-community approach was vital. “Age and stage-appropriate conversations need to happen really early on. If they have the device in their hand, or the capacity to have their device, education needs to happen beforehand,” Read said.

World.title: From Spaceballs to Avengers – Comic-Con delivers a knockout punch
World.content:
CultureMoviesPop culture From Spaceballs to Avengers – Comic-Con delivers a knockout punch Michael Idato July 27, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

They came hoping to get a glimpse of the year’s big-ticket Marvel blockbuster, Avengers: Doomsday, but the more than 150,000 fans who came to this year’s San Diego Comic-Con left with a goodie bag of new trailers, A-list stars and already rare collectible toys. Robert Downey Jr, left, and Pedro Pascal attend a panel for Marvel Studios at Comic-Con. AP Photo/Richard Shotwell First, the big stuff. Marvel Studios stormed into the convention’s Hall H, giving fans their first taste of Avengers: Doomsday and a surprise appearance from the film’s A-list cast, assembling most of them on stage in front of thousands of screaming fans. In a presentation that was among the most complex at this year’s Comic-Con, Marvel set up a series of staggered reveals, featuring cast members from the various Marvel films, including Chris Evans, Rebecca Romijin, Paul Rudd and Anthony Mackie. And in a tease that implies the new film will upend the franchise’s ethical axis, star Robert Downey Jnr — who plays the film’s villain Dr Doom — said audiences would not “know what team to go for this time.” Pedro Pascal, from left, Chris Evans, Hayley Atwell, and Robert Downey Jr at Comic-Con. AP Photo/Richard Shotwell



In other Marvel news, it was revealed Ryan Gosling will join the MCU as the titular character in Ghost Rider, due to land in 2028. The character was previously played by Nicolas Cage in the 2007 film Ghost Rider and its 2011 sequel Ghost Rider: Spirit of Vengeance, and by Gabriel Luna in the TV series Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. Ryan Gosling attends a panel for Marvel Studios during Comic-Con International at the weekend. AP Photo/Richard Shotwell Fans also got a first look at HBO’s Lanterns, the new season trailer for The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power coupled with confirmation that actor Simon Pegg will voice the iconic Balrog, trailers for the new film Matchbox and the new TV series Blade Runner 2099, a surprise appearance by Johnny Depp to promote Ebenezer, and a convention-shaking debut for the long-awaited sequel Spaceballs: The New One. The last of those almost stole the show, with an audience of thousands packed into Hall H cheering and taking part in a shoutout of “May The Schwartz Be With You” – an iconic line from the film – which was filmed and sent to the legendary director of the original, Mel Brooks. Loading



So, what’s actually happening here? In real terms, Comic-Con is a four-day marketing machine, intended to join the dots between the multibillion-dollar movie and TV business, and then connect it to the fans. The take-out? The social media noise needed to successfully launch new movie and TV projects. In a sense, the proof is in the comic book pudding, so to speak. A month ago, films like Spaceballs: The New One and Ebenezer, and even a TV series like Lanterns or its HBO Max sitcom stablemate Stuart Fails To Save The Universe, were not quite on the radar. In the wake of Comic-Con, Spaceballs might be the most anticipated film of 2027 so far, and Ebenezer, while not quite the match of a Marvel-powered movie like Avengers: Doomsday, generated the kind of media noise in a single stunt that money can’t buy. “I geek out on geeks.” Australian actor Joel Edgerton among the stars at San Diego Comic-Con. AP Photo/Richard Shotwell Matchbox star John Cena told this masthead that San Diego’s “original” Comic-Con had an almost unique place at the intersection of marketing and audience engagement.



“The passion and the fandom, this is the epicentre. San Diego Comic-Con was the first, and by far has the most gravity,” Cena said. Companies like Apple, Mattel, Marvel, they come here, this is the place to break the news. You walk the floor, and it’s still very much fans first.” Matchbox, directed by Sam Hargrave, hopes to do what Barbie did for toy company Mattel, and deliver a story-rich hit film that turns the iconic tiny toy cars into a high-octane action-comedy motion picture. Billie Joe Armstrong of Green Day performs at San Diego Comic-Con to promote the film Nimrods. Todd Williamson/January Images, via Inaugural Entertainment Australian actor Joel Edgerton, who was at Comic-Con to promote his television series Dark Matter, knows the Comic-Con universe well. He first came to the annual fan-fest promoting Star Wars: Attack of the Clones – in which he played Luke Skywalker’s adopted father, Owen Lars – back in 2002. “I was very nervous [then], and now, someone asked me what I geek out about, and I geek out on geeks,” Edgerton told this masthead.



Related Article Pop culture Star, humbug! Johnny Depp charms as cranky Scrooge in Comic-Con stunt “I love the obsession, I love the hours spent sewing a costume and dressing up, I love that the imagination of a child, that usually gets kicked out of us by the time we’re grown-ups, is still alive in most of the people that are here.” To some extent, the marketing machinery is already at work. Disney dropped the first trailer for Avengers: Doomsday last week, and it cracked more than 500 million plays in its first 24 hours. That made it the second-biggest trailer launch of all time. And if you didn’t realise trailers now have their own launches, the trailer for Tom Cruise’s Digger just had its own LA premiere. The stars of the current Star Trek flagship series Strange New Worlds came to play – actors Anson Mount, Rebecca Romijn, Ethan Peck, plus producer Alex Kurtzman and others. Marking the 60th anniversary of the Paramount-owned franchise, they were joined by stars from other Star Trek projects, including the legendary George Takei, and actors Michael Dorn, Michelle Hurd and Jerry O’Connell. Rick Moranis, Daphne Zuniga and Keke Palmer at the panel for Spaceballs: The New One at San Diego Comic-Con. AP Photo/Richard Shotwell



Elsewhere, Green Day hosted a surprise concert at Petco Park in San Diego to promote the upcoming film Nimrods. Billie Joe Armstrong performed from the roof of an ice-cream truck, while Tré Cool and Mike Dirnt from the band, writer/director Lee Kirk, and stars Mason Thames and Jenna Fischer passed out merchandise to fans. Named after the band’s 1997 album, the film is a punk rock comedy produced by Live Nation Studios in collaboration with Green Day, inspired by the band’s early days, about a band of young musicians who embark on a wild cross-country adventure, falsely believing they have been booked to open for Green Day. San Diego Comic-Con was launched in 1970, with just 300 people attending. This year, around 200,000 people are expected, either ticketed in the convention itself or visiting the city to attend the various studios “activations”. It is estimated that the event sinks as much as $US150 million into the San Diego economy. San Diego Comic-Con runs until Monday, Australian time.
