World.title: Found lifeless in the water, Vicky is now a swimming medallist
World.content:
When athlete details are listed, Vicky Belando Nicholson's birthplace is listed as "unknown".

We don't know where her journey to Glasgow began, but we do know one of the earliest, terrifying moments when a young baby was pulled lifeless from the Mediterranean after falling off a refugee boat in 2008.

Her sister, Destiny, was aboard. Her birth mother, whose name we also do not know, had died.

Vicky and Destiny were taken to an orphanage in Malta, where they lived for a couple of years.

At the same time, two people just happened to be trying to adopt a child: Australian Ewan and Spanish wife Susana.

"We got a cold call from social services saying: 'We've got two girls here, two and three years old, who are in an orphanage in Malta. Would you be interested in adopting them?'" Ewan told the Sydney Morning Herald this month.

The family lived in Malta, then Spain, before moving to Australia in 2021.

Vicky – who has a condition called fibular hemimelia, meaning she is missing part of the smaller bone in the lower leg – had every reason in the world to never want to see water again.

Belando Nicholson was sixth at the turn and stormed home. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

On Sunday night in Glasgow, she won Commonwealth Games bronze in the women's 100m backstroke S9 with a frankly stunning swim, coming from sixth at the turn to win her first bit of major jewellery.

"It's a bit of a 360 moment," she said.

"When I first started swimming, I was always scared of the water and now to be a bronze medallist for the Commonwealth Games is just absolutely amazing and hopefully there's more to come.

"Coming into this event I wasn't ranked high enough, but I ended up coming third, so anything can happen. Just believe."

To make the moment all the more special, she was joined on her first podium in her first final at her first meet with the Australian team, by her 16-year-old bestie, silver medallist Gemma Sellick.

Besties bound by brilliance. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

"I'm so proud of her," Sellick said.

"I know we've both worked so hard for this and it makes the moment feel even better knowing I can share it with Vicky and very grateful that we got to share our first together."

The moment was almost too perfect to wish for.

"This was not even a thought I had, I was not expecting this at all," Belando Nicholson said.

"To do it with my best friend is actually insane."

For a young woman who has had so much focus on her remarkable history, this feels like the beginning of a spectacular future.

World.title: Luke Bateman earned $400K a year and gambled away every cent
World.content:
During his darkest chapter, things would go missing from Luke Bateman's apartment.

"My partner would come home from work and be like, 'Where's this?'" the former NRL player-turned-fantasy writer tells Australian Story.

"I would've taken it to Cash Converters and sold it for cash so I could go and gamble."

Luke Bateman says in the elite sporting environment gambling was "like breathing". (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

It was 2019, and Bateman was at the height of a debilitating gambling addiction so severe he couldn't afford to feed himself. He was a professional NRL player with the Canberra Raiders at the time, earning $400,000 a year.

"I was so broke … I couldn't pay for anything. I couldn't buy groceries," Bateman says.

"My gambling slowly progressed [until] it consumed my life. Every single thing I did revolved around that gambling app on my phone."

Luke Bateman pictured in a 2016 game against Melbourne Storm, a year after making his NRL debut. (Getty Images: Brett Hemmings)

Bateman says he felt in control of his habit until his gambling saw him lose tens of thousands of dollars in just a few weeks.

" I had $70,000 or $80,000 in my bank account, and in the space of a month, I had nothing. "

Hitting rock bottom with his addiction and mental health, and then finding his way back again, has compelled Bateman to speak out about the federal government's gambling changes, which aim to limit gambling advertising.

He says they would not have helped him through his hardest moments.

Luke Bateman removed himself from temptation when he went bush. (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

"I was in so much debt … I was earning $400,000 a year, and I couldn't afford a lollipop," Bateman admits.

"I don't think they [the proposed laws] will move the needle at all when it comes to gambling harm, " he says. "I'd love to call it the bare minimum, but I don't think they got even there."

The legislation, which would cap the number of gambling ads broadcast per hour and ban advertising during live matches, was introduced into parliament earlier this month and is being scrutinised in a Senate inquiry.

Luke Bateman speaks at a panel in parliament house about the role sport, alcohol and gambling play in gender-based violence. (Supplied: Michael Conlin, FARE)

Bateman says the proposed changes do not "even come close" to reflecting community concerns on gambling, with researchers finding that the majority of Australians believe gambling is too easily accessible.

"I would love to see all gambling advertising phased out, and for all incentives that gambling companies can offer a customer [to continue betting] to be banned," Bateman says.

Australia has the highest per capita gambling losses in the world, according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.

Bateman's passion for the issue could be enough to see him run for parliament one day. He tells Australian Story that a run at politics is "definitely a possibility".

"I don't think parliamentarians are doing anywhere near enough in terms of protecting … young people from the harms that gambling companies and gambling itself causes."

Loading...

'Rugby league like a religion'

Bateman grew up in the small town of Miles, about 400 kilometres west of Brisbane. He showed exceptional athletic ability from a young age, playing his first game of rugby league when he was four.

"He was probably one of the better players in under-7s at four years old," his stepfather Don Hills says.

"I remember his PE teacher saying to me, 'We'll be reading about this kid in later life. He's destined for big things,'" mum Leanne Bateman recalls.

Luke Bateman (bottom right) with his older brother Sam, twin sister Sarah, mother Leanne and stepfather Don. (Supplied: Leanne Bateman)

By the time he was 12, Bateman had represented Queensland in rugby league, touch football and swimming.

It was around the same time that Bateman was scouted by NRL clubs at the state rugby league carnival.

Luke Bateman was recruited by the Canberra Raiders when he was 12. (Supplied: Leanne Bateman)

"We were approached by a couple of different scouts for different NRL teams. One was the Canberra Raiders," Leanne says.

When the Raiders signed 12-year-old Bateman, it was a big deal, not only for his family, but the whole community.

"Growing up in the country, rugby league is like a religion out there," brother Sam Bateman says.

"It would've been like extremely exciting for him, but also probably a lot of pressure for him as well."

Luke Bateman pictured with Don, Sarah, Leanne and Sam after his first Canberra Raiders game in 2015. (Supplied: Luke Bateman)

Watch Luke Bateman's Australian Story "Turning the Page" Monday 8:00pm (AEST) on ABC TV and ABC iview.

$80K gone: Luke's 'shameful' gambling habit

Despite having an early aptitude for all things sport-related, Bateman says he was a "soft and gentle kid" who found solace in fantasy books.

"I think what really drew me to those specific books was the sense of wonder … my world on the farm is so small, but my world in books is so big."

But Bateman kept his love of reading hidden.

"It was not something that men did. I never saw any of my male role models, my male heroes, reading books."

Luke Bateman had a love for reading from a young age. (Supplied: Leanne Bateman)

So Bateman leant into sport instead.

"Growing up, I saw one dream as possible, and that was the NRL dream.

"I think all the other parts of myself really took a back seat to the athlete and the sporting part of me, because they weren't things that received praise," he says.

Luke Bateman says his book collection charts every phase of his life. (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

The beginning of his NRL career was an exciting time for Bateman, now 31.

"I was really just happy to be a part of the team," he says.

But a feeling of doubt slowly crept in, and Bateman's 2015 NRL debut at the age of 20 brought up some unexpected feelings.

"I'd worked my entire life to get to this moment … then I played the game, and I remember thinking, 'Huh, that was really underwhelming.'

"I thought that was a thing that would complete me. And then I came off the field, and I thought, 'Oh, I'm still exactly the same.'"

Luke Bateman runs the ball in a match between the Raiders and Dragons in Canberra in 2017. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

Bateman was enjoying the benefits of being a cashed-up, young sports star. But his gambling addiction, and the mental health impacts that went alongside it, were getting worse.

After losing nearly $80,000 in one month, Bateman rang his mother and asked her to take control of his bank accounts.

"Luke's gambling got really bad. He had no money. He would literally be borrowing off family and friends. He would regularly ask me to take control of his money and take it back again," she says.

"They were very dark, hard times."

Now back home in Brisbane, Luke Bateman takes time out for himself at the gym. (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

Bateman's mental health deteriorated, and he contemplated suicide.

"I was just so filled with shame, and I couldn't share it," Bateman says. "I was just in so much pain. I saw no way out."

If you or anyone you know needs help: National Gambling Helpline on 1800 858 858

Lifeline on 13 11 14

Kids Helpline on 1800 551 800

MensLine Australia on 1300 789 978

Suicide Call Back Service on 1300 659 467

Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636

Headspace on 1800 650 890

Leanne noticed the deterioration, too.

"I rang the police in Canberra on two different occasions to go and do welfare checks on him. I rang the Canberra Raiders [welfare officer] on a couple of occasions."

Leanne says Luke "did not appreciate" the checks and was in denial about needing help.

Bateman acknowledges that he hid the worst of his addiction and mental health problems from the Raiders and did not seek support, believing that disclosing them could see him removed from the team.

The Canberra Raiders would not comment on this story.

Luke Bateman says he was the "best liar in the world" when he was hiding the extent of his gambling. (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

Bateman goes bush to pay $130K debt

One Monday in 2020, Bateman woke up in Newcastle after a three-day bender with no idea what happened or how he got there.

"Something just broke within me and I [thought] I have two options: I either end my life, or I get help," he remembers.

Instead of driving back to Canberra, Bateman headed north to Brisbane, straight to Leanne and Don's house.

"I collapsed into her arms, and I said, 'I need help.'"

After shaking off a three-day bender, Luke Bateman drove 8 hours home to his parents in Brisbane. (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

After years of resisting and insisting he could cope with his addiction on his own, Bateman agreed to go to rehab. It was around this time that he returned to one of his first loves, books.

"I started reading because I was doing a lot of therapy and I was starting to try and change my life," Bateman says.

After coming out of rehab, Leanne and Don sat Bateman down and gave him an ultimatum: they would absorb his debts, and he would go and work for Don in his logging business, which operated in remote locations in Queensland, to repay them.

Bateman estimates his parents took on about $130,000 of his debt, which he recently paid off.

"It was a turning point that he was then out of Canberra, out of the culture [of gambling and drug-taking]," Leanne says.

Luke Bateman and Don chat by the fire. (Australian Story: Shalailah Medhora)

Living outside of the city came with unexpected benefits: it would take several years before Bateman had access to the internet from his campsite.

"All my gambling was done on my phone. So in the beginning, even if I wanted to gamble, I couldn't. [It] was fantastic for my recovery," he says.

Luke Bateman at the family property at Injune. (Supplied: Luke Bateman)

#BookTok success and controversy

Bateman bought a campervan and buried himself in work. To pass the time, he'd listen to audiobooks in his tractor. It was here that his next big career move was made.

He recorded a TikTok video for a part of the platform dedicated to lovers of reading, called #BookTok, from the tractor.

Luke Bateman filmed all his early TikTok videos from this tractor. (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

"I made my first BookTok video because I literally just wanted some friends to talk about books with," he says.

He uploaded the video at 8pm, hoping to wake up to a few comments from like-minded people. Instead, his video went viral.

"I woke up the next morning, and it had a million views," Bateman says.

Loading...

The #BookTok videos caught the eye of publisher Anthea Bariamis.

"After seeing some of his content for several weeks, I thought it might be worth reaching out to see if he had written or was writing a book," she says.

In the meeting, Bateman and Bariamis ended up speaking for hours about their shared love of fantasy.

"He sent me a sample of his writing, and I could absolutely see the potential … it certainly wasn't something he had come up with on a whim," Bariamis says.

Bateman was working on his tractor when he found out he would be offered a book deal.

"I just bawled my eyes out because I was so happy. It was the culmination of decades of something that I kept really secret and felt a lot of shame around."

A hat in Luke Bateman's room displays the phrase "romance reader". (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

Bateman posted the news on #BookTok, eager to share the win with the community.

But the reaction was not what he expected.

"When I first announced my book deal, it received a heap of criticism and backlash," Bateman says. "People filled my comment section with really hateful, spiteful, vile comments."

People had wrongly assumed Bateman was using a ghostwriter for his work and had been offered a deal without a fully sketched-out proposal. They also pointed out how difficult it can be for writers of colour to get book deals, a criticism Bateman acknowledges as fair.

After working all day, Luke Bateman would retreat to the caravan to write his debut novel. (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

Bateman now has a three-book deal, with the first novel due in 2027.

He says his "north star" is to help young men and boys through the power of storytelling, and he wants to use his platform to advocate for change, including reducing gambling harm.

"I understand that I have the position, the power, and the voice that can create change, that can change people's lives, and I don't want to squander that."

Luke Bateman is motivated to make real change, even saying politics could be possible" in his future. (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

Watch Luke Bateman's Australian Story "Turning the Page" Monday 8pm (AEST) on ABC TV and ABC iview.

World.title: Diamonds disappointed Glasgow games only live on Seven's streaming service
World.content:
The Diamonds are one of the most successful and beloved teams in Australian sport, but some fans back home trying to tune in to their Commonwealth Games campaign have been left disappointed.

The reigning netball gold medallists kicked off with dominant wins by a combined 80 goals on Saturday and Sunday, but neither match was carried live on any of Seven Network's linear television channels.

The 99-38 victory over Tonga and 66-47 win over England were only shown live on streaming service 7Plus, while Seven carried the swimming heats.

For Sunday's prime-time match against rivals and 2018 champions the Roses, Seven aired 2021 Ryan Reynolds film Free Guy on Mate, and crime drama Vera on TWO.

The Diamonds' Glasgow games have been carried live on 7Plus, but not on Seven's linear TV channels. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Seven's main channel broadcast made clear the Diamonds were live on Plus.

After the swimming finished and the Diamonds had won, the Australia-England game was aired on delay on Seven's main channel.

ABC Sport broke the news to a few of the Diamonds stars after their game.

"That's obviously disappointing, obviously we want to be on TV and have every fan able to watch. I wasn't aware of that," goalkeeper Courtney Bruce said.

"I don't know, hopefully we'll be able to be on the live games [at some point]. It is disappointing, we obviously want netball to be highlighted and want the rest of the sports here at the Commonwealth Games and for Australia to be highlighted too."

Games debutant Jamie-Lee Price said she hopes fans keep making their voices heard.

Sunday's game was between the last two Commonwealth gold medallists. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"I think maybe if we put lots of pressure on maybe we can get there," she said.

"I didn't realise that. We want to be on TV, we want eyes on our sport and if we can get that that's amazing. So, yes please."

The silver lining of the situation is the reminder of the support this team has in Australia and in Glasgow, where the Australians in the Hydro were challenging the English fans for sheer volume and passion.

"We definitely feel the support from home, obviously we're nothing without the supporters back in Australia," Bruce said.

The Diamonds' next match is against Malawi in two days' time. (Getty Images: Rob Casey/SNS Group)

"We definitely feel it today and there's quite a few out there. That was really nice to have them out there today."

A Channel Seven spokesperson responded to requests from the ABC, saying:

"The Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games features multiple events taking place simultaneously, which is why Seven is delivering wall-to-wall coverage across Seven and 7plus Sport — including 15 live channels on 7plus Sport — ensuring Australians can watch every event live and free."

World.title: Piastri blasts '****ing stupid' backmarker, Norris wins Hungarian GP
World.content:
Oscar Piastri was forced to retire from the Formula 1 Hungarian Grand Prix, but not before he blasted a "stupid" backmarker and slammed his team for a poor strategy at the Hungaroring.

Lando Norris claimed his first victory of the season, ahead of Max Verstappen in second and world championship leader Kimi Antonelli in third.

Piastri was left desperately frustrated after a brilliant start saw him overtake his teammate on the opening lap to take the lead from third on the grid.

"It was definitely the highlight of my race," Piastri said of the start.

"And it went pretty downhill from there.

"A lot of things to unpack."

The Australian leaped into the lead but never was able to pull away, complaining of rear tyre wear as Norris was all over the back of his teammate in a clearly faster car.

"The pace on the hard tyres was nowhere," Piastri bemoaned.

At the half-way point, when he was brought into the pits for his second stop in response to Lewis Hamilton doing so.

McLaren, wary of the under-cut, had been pestered by Norris to allow him to pit first and had even told him to box on lap 32, saying he was "miles" faster than Piastri, but the team said the reigning world champion was unable to come in as Piastri had first choice on the pit stop.

Oscar Piastri leads Lando Norris. (Getty Images" Andy Hone/LAT Images)

Piastri did come in, but was then caught behind back markers and, as he tried to complete his outlaps was hit by Carlos Sainz as he battled with the Aston Martin.

"Is he ****ing stupid or what? Get out of the ****ing way, you idiot! Oh my god," Piastri said as Sainz first held him up, then clipped his front wheel.

Piastri's mood did not improve soon after when Norris, having stayed out longer on his second set of tyres, was able to pit and come out ahead of Piastri.

"Oh mate, just don't ****ing talk to me now," he said when told that the Sainz collision had cost them the virtual race lead.

"Nice of you guys to factor that one in by the way, thanks," he added, in reference to the traffic he had to go through.

Already fuming, Piastri was then dealt an even more bitter blow, his gearbox failing on lap 56 forcing him to retire.

After the race though, Piastri said he was simply frustrated by the sequence of events.

"Obviously being taken out by a back marker is never really one of the things you think that can go wrong, but I was proven wrong," Piastri told media after the race.

"I was hoping they wouldn't pit Lando in that moment, to at least give me the chance to stay in the lead," he added.

"But I think that's not very reasonable, so I was more just very upset in the moment about what had happened.

"The timing of my pit stop was fine, we wanted to beat Lewis [Hamilton] and that's what we needed to do."

Lando Norris overtook Oscar Piastri in the opening lap. (Getty Images: Alastair Staley/LAT Images)

McLaren team principle Andrea Stella said he thought both drivers excelled during the race.

"I think today it was actually great racing," he told Sky Sports.

"It was great to see Lando and Oscar fighting at the start for good position, something that was fair.

"Oscar had his own chance to take the lead and see what pace he might have had.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"And how the race unfolded meant that with Oscar we then covered Hamilton and then there was some situation with the backmarkers.

"Lando was very quick once he had the lead and he take advantage of this pace and the fact that there was some delay for Oscar.

"That's racing. We are McLaren racing. It was great racing."

It was also a tough weekend for Ferrari and Lewis Hamilton, who was penalised five seconds for speeding in the pit lane, relegating him to fifth, with his teammate Charles Leclerc in fourth.

Meanwhile, Malaysia's Sepang circuit will host a Formula 1 race for the first time since 2017 as replacement host of the Bahrain Grand Prix.

Liberty Media said in a statement the race will take place on October 4, and would officially be called the 'Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia'.

World.title: Live: McEvoy creates history as Aussie gold rush continues in Glasgow
World.content:
(Getty)

Iona Anderson emerged as Australia's biggest backstroke star of these Games when Kaylee McKeown withdrew due to glandular fever.

In the 200m, she swam the third best time of her life, but finished well outside the medals.

In the 100m tonight, she touched first and it could not have been a better place for her first individual gold medal at a senior meet.

Yes, even better than doing it on home soil in regional Victoria, as was the initial plan.

"Personally, for me, I think Glasgow's better than Victoria. Sorry," she says.

Basically, her entire family is from Scotland, Grangemouth on her mum's side and Dumfries and Galloway on her dad's. She's only been back four times in her life, so this is a pretty remarkable moment for the 20-year-old.

"I love the Scottish. I've got quite a few friends here and obviously my family. So it was great to come back here and do it," she said.

She was even named after the small island of Iona off the west coast of Scotland.

Gee, let's hope she doesn't pull a Matthew Richardson on us.

World.title: Fozball and finals on the brink as Cronulla maul Manly
World.content:
Manly's hopes of a fairytale NRL finals berth are on life support after an insipid 48-12 loss to Cronulla, who appear genuine premiership contenders.

The Sea Eagles suffered their worst defeat of the Kieran Foran era as Sharks halves Nicho Hynes and Braydon Trindall lit up Brookvale Oval.

The 10th-placed Sea Eagles (9-10) have a losing record for the first time since round six and must win at least four of their last five regular-season games to play finals.

They are four competition points out of the top eight and face top-eight sides Newcastle, the Dolphins and Warriors on the run home.

It's been quite the fall from grace for the Sea Eagles, who rose from the doldrums and won eight of 10 games immediately after Foran replaced Anthony Seibold.

Manly have since lost five of six, and for the first time since club legend Foran became coach in March, they were never in the contest on Sunday.

The Sea Eagles' playmakers gave away four seven-tackle sets with poor kicks.

Reuben Garrick sprayed the kick-off out on the full after the Sharks' fourth try and put the visitors in place for Sione Katoa to score their fifth only minutes before the half.

Tom Trbojevic's replacement Lehi Hopoate had an afternoon to forget at fullback, notably spilling a regulation Hynes kick directly ahead of the Sharks' third try.

The fourth-placed Sharks have won eight from their last nine games and look ready to take the leap from good to great in Craig Fitzgibbon's fifth season as coach.

So long a lightning rod for criticism, halfback Hynes is playing as well as he has since winning the Dally M Medal in 2022.

He embarrassed the Manly middle barging over for the Sharks' fourth try and sent a bullet-like pass for Ronaldo Mulitalo's second try just after the break.

Hynes dummied through rookie five-eighth Joey Walsh, who had a difficult day, and then passed inside for Sifa Talakai to score in the second half.

He also kicked a career-best 26th consecutive goal and finished the afternoon with three line breaks.

Trindall's suspect ball to Teig Wilton gave Cronulla their opening try, before the five-eighth floated a lovely cut-out pass for Mulitalo's first.

He kicked past Hopoate for KL Iro to cross with 15 minutes to play.

Just before halftime, the Sea Eagles lost second-rower Ben Trbojevic to his second game-ending head knock in as many appearances.

Earlier, the makings were all there for another devastating Gold Coast loss, but coach Josh Hannay has credited the Titans' ongoing evolution for their slashing 38-18 win over St George Illawarra.

With the Dragons celebrating co-captain Clint Gutherson's 250th NRL game on Sunday afternoon, the permanent signing of coach Dean Young and Old Boys' Day to boot, the visitors had to overcome an early deficit to secure consecutive wins for the first time in the Hannay era.

Gold Coast's 20-point win allowed them to leapfrog three other clubs, and out of the competition's bottom four for the first time since their round-eight bye, and all but confirmed the Dragons' maiden wooden spoon.

"When you're coming into an environment like this, it felt like we were walking into a trap with them having so much to play for, so I just loved how we went about it," Hannay said.

"We have had some tight losses and haven't had a lot of reward at different times. There have been a few instances where we have had a level game at halftime and we'd flinch in the second half. I feel like this group, little by little, are growing.

"We're fully aware of where we're at, the journey we're on and that there's going to be some hard lessons. They have had to learn a lot on the run these guys and they're growing exponentially."

AAP

World.title: Lion's 'stupid action' sparks war of words as Nasiah magic inspires Saints
World.content:
Brisbane defender Ty Gallop faces an anxious wait on the match review officer after a contentious incident in the second quarter of the Lions' heavy win over Port Adelaide at the Gabba.

The emerging Gallop had rolled Mitch Georgiades in a heavy tackle, but while the Power key forward's head did not hit the turf, it was what happened next that raised eyebrows.

As the Lions swept the ball downfield, Gallop appeared to lift Georgiades by the jumper before slamming him back into the turf head first.

While Georgiades played out the game uninjured, he was returning from an earlier concussion against St Kilda in round 18 after being knocked out in a heavy mid-air collision.

The incident spurred a defensive reaction from both coaches after the match, with Port's Josh Carr saying Gallop's actions were the mark of a team that played its football on the edge.

"It wasn't a great look, but I'm on the other side of it," he said.

"They're a team that plays tough and pushes the limits. We got the free kick, so we got rewarded. There's not much more to say."

Carr said Georgiades was unaffected by the incident after the game.

But the coach's words spurred a response from his counterpart Chris Fagan, who said he hadn't seen the incident.

Asked if he agreed with Carr's assessment that his team played on the edge, Fagan said: "That's his opinion. He's allowed to have it.

"You don't be one of the better teams of the competition if you don't play a hard physical brand.

"That's what we do. I don't think we do it unfairly. I think we brought good pressure today."

Brisbane Lions great Alastair Lynch was also unimpressed by Gallop's actions, citing Georgiades's history with concussions as well.

"That's just a stupid action. We don't want to see that," he said on Fox Footy's coverage.

"Mitch [Georgiades] has had some problems with concussion and we don't want to see actions like that."

Fagan said he had yet to view a replay of the incident.

"It's interesting that Josh has had a chance to watch it; I haven't. He's not as busy as what I am," he said.

Fagan said he was hopeful defender Darcy Gardiner was available next week should Gallop be suspended.

"It's not really up to me; it's up to what the match review mob [and] what they decide," he said.

In Sunday's second match, St Kilda ran out 13.15 (93) to 8.14 (62) winners over North Melbourne as Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera finished with 46 disposals and four goals.

Tech.title: Champagne and Bullets belongs on the Mount Rushmore of bad movies
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

There’s something about a movie like The Room, Troll 2, or Fateful Findings that I find irresistible. These sorts of “so bad they’re good” films are marvelous curiosities where ambition far outstrips resources, ability, and self-awareness to become something much greater than the sum of their parts. Champagne and Bullets (also released as GetEven and Road to Revenge) is a film on par with those classics of outsider cinema.

The movie is almost entirely the work of one man, John De Hart. Hart wrote, directed, and stars as Rick Bode in the film. He even performs a musical number early in the proceedings — The bizarre “Shimmy Slide.” During the performance, Hart, who was reportedly pumped full of painkillers after throwing out his back, is stiff and looks around the room as if he’s only performing under threat of violence. And somehow, this lifeless performance of a cringy country rocker isn’t the most awkward scene in the movie.

The relationships and interactions between characters in Champagne and Bullets are just as inexplicable and unnatural as those in The Room. Bode and his partner Huck Finney are cops who lose their badges five minutes into the movie. This precipitates the alarmingly quick mental decline of Finney, who is also going through a divorce after discovering his wife has been sleeping around. He fires a handgun through his bills, drinks bleach to get out of prison, and seemingly starts a cult.

Oh, and speaking of cults, a good portion of the plot revolves around the reemergence of Bode’s old girlfriend Cindy, who is fleeing a satanic coven that “sacrificed a human baby.”

While ostensibly an action film, the fight scenes are few and far between, and staged with all the believability of a theme park stunt show. Hart seemed far more interested in cramming in as much gratuitous nudity as possible. There are three uncomfortably long sex scenes with costar Pamela Bryant, who plays Cindy, all set to songs sung by Hart. In total, they take up 12 minutes of runtime in a movie that is only 90 minutes long. One scene that takes place in a jacuzzi apparently even led Hart’s girlfriend at the time to break up with him. (Warning: One scene not involving Hart and Bryant does depict a sexual assault.)

If you’re a fan of bad movies, cult classics, or the podcast How Did This Get Made, you owe it to yourself to go watch Champagne and Bullets. It’s available on Hoopla, Amazon Prime, and Tubi.

Tech.title: Apple is banking on privacy to set its smart glasses apart
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

According to Mark Gurman, Apple is planning to reveal its first smart glasses at WWDC next June, with an expectation that they’ll launch by the end of 2027. Part of the hold-up may be around the company’s efforts to get its privacy features and messaging in order. Smart glasses in general, and Meta’s in particular, have ignited controversy over their ability to stealthily capture photos and videos. As Gurman points out:

The company has spent more than a decade making privacy one of its defining product messages. Simply entering the same category as Meta risks undermining that reputation, regardless of how Apple’s approach differs.

Apple is likely to rely on on-device processing and skip out on more controversial features like facial recognition or an always-on-recording similar to Meta’s “super sensing.” Gurman also believes Apple will avoid using customer recordings to train AI models.

Other hardware and software privacy features are also reportedly in the works. It’s also possible that Apple could eventually release a version of its smart glasses without a camera, or with a camera that is exclusively for sensing and won’t be able to capture video or photos at all, similar to what is rumored for Apple’s AI-enabled AirPods.

Tech.title: The US is charging an American citizen for wiping his phone at the border
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

The government is prosecuting US citizen Sam Tunick for allegedly providing authorities with a “duress password” that wiped his phone when they tried to seize it at Atlanta’s Hartsfield-Jackson airport on January 24th, 2025. Federal agents detained Tunick at the airport, allegedly questioning him about child exploitation images. However, a motion filed by Tunick’s lawyers argues this was simply “a pretext for a fishing expedition into Mr Tunick’s connections” to the Stop Cop City movement in Atlanta.

The government is turning to a little-known and rarely-used statute that makes it illegal to destroy or damage property to stop authorities from seizing it. They allege that Tunick used a feature of the privacy-focused GrapheneOS to wipe his phone by giving authorities a duress password, instead of the actual passcode to unlock the phone. The defense has argued that the detention and seizure were unlawful, and therefore all evidence should be tossed.

According to Tunick’s attorneys, agents refused him access to a lawyer, did not provide a warrant, or inform him of his legal rights. They also allege that access to his phone was sought under false pretenses. The government has countered that they were not required to produce a warrant because Tunick had not yet been granted permission to enter the US.

Marlon Kautz, a member of the Atlanta Solidarity Fund, told the Guardian earlier this week that, “we all have a right to secure our private data against unconstitutional searches. And we should — especially in a time of rising authoritarianism.” Under the Trump administration, entering the US has become a much more fraught process, even for citizens who can face hours-long detention and scrutiny of social media accounts. Most agree the only way to protect your data is to delete it.

Tech.title: Carrie is just trying to make a friend in the new trailer
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Mike Flanagan’s latest Stephen King adaptation, Carrie (this will be his fourth), is slated to make its debut on Amazon Prime on October 7th. The new trailer dropped at Comic-Con 2026 and doesn’t contain many surprises. If you’re familiar with Carrie at all, it hits all the expected notes. Though it’s clearly been updated for the modern era.

According to Deadline, Flanagan’s take on the classic King novel will tackle very modern teen challenges like active shooter drills and bullying on social media. The director apparently invited high schoolers into the writers’ room, using their real-life traumas to inform the script:

“They shared shocking one-off situations or constant treatment and microaggressions and things that are not necessarily present themselves as targeted harassment. [We will dive into] the cruelty in today’s world and how the internet has encouraged cruelty, rewards and celebrates and amplifies it. This is awful for adults to deal with, and for teenagers even more so.”

Brian De Palma’s iconic 1976 adaptation of Carrie is iconic and features an unimpeachable performance from Sissy Spacek. But it’s undeniable that Summer H. Howell, who was 21 at the time of shooting, is much more believable as a high school student than Spacek, who was 26 at the time.

Subscribing to Xbox Game Pass Ultimate on a recurring basis has been tough to justify recently, even after Microsoft reduced the monthly cost from $29.99 to $22.99. But you can get a better deal on a three-month subscription (valued at $69) by grabbing a digital code at Eneba that costs $39.01 at the time of publication.

Game Pass Ultimate grants you access to the full Game Pass library on Xbox (compared to a more limited slice with Premium), including first-party titles and online multiplayer access. The subscription also gives PC gamers access to Microsoft’s catalog of Game Pass games through the Xbox app, though the selection differs a bit between console and desktop.

You don’t need me to tell you why deals like these are nice. The costs of subscriptions generally only go in one direction over time, and it is becoming more rare to find worthwhile discounts that give you a break. If you want to jump into Halo: Campaign Evolved when it launches July 28th on Xbox and PC, all you need is this subscription instead of buying the $49.99 re-remake.

Tech.title: The vertical video takeover is here
Tech.content:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on all things vertical video, follow David Pierce. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

For a while, every social and media platform had its own identity. YouTube was for clips of TV shows and movies, and the home of so many members of a burgeoning creator community. Instagram was mostly pictures. Netflix was trying to be the on-demand HBO. Facebook was about friends. Twitter was about news. Snapchat was a messaging app.

All these apps did have one important thing in common, though: They were growing up alongside the smartphone. Billions of new people were coming online for the first time, and they began to make content that made sense for the tall, skinny new devices in their hands. Selfies were a vertical art form, both because the photos filled the screen better and because it was just easier to hold the phone and take the photo that way. Some resisted the idea of vertical video for years — they’d argue that our eyes are meant to scan horizontally rather than vertically, and that vertical video looked bad on widescreen laptops. But ultimately phones won, and we hold our phones upright, so our phone experiences turned upright. That includes entertainment.

As has been true so many times, Snap figured this out before anyone. It launched Stories in late 2013 as a slightly more relaxed way to see what your friends are up to. CEO Evan Spiegel called it a “totally new way to share your day with friends — or everyone.” It took off in a massive way, and by the middle of 2014 was the most popular feature on Snapchat. That’s the kind of virality that Mark Zuckerberg tends to notice, and by August of 2016, the feature had been copied more or less exactly into Instagram. Kevin Systrom, then the CEO of Instagram, said of Spiegel and Snapchat that “they deserve all the credit” for Stories. The implication? That this was no longer a proprietary feature of a single social network; it was just in the air. Stories were for everyone. They started showing up on LinkedIn, Tinder, Medium, and so many other places.

Stories weren’t always video, but as cameras and upload speeds improved, video became the dominant medium in many ephemeral spaces. And video stories had two semi-magical properties: They were perfectly suited to endless, mindless scrolling, and they made it really easy to integrate ads. Only a few months after turning on Stories in Instagram, by which point half the platform’s users were already using Stories, Facebook began flooding ads into the product. The semi-randomness of Stories made ads actually seem less intrusive — you’d see a photo of a dog, a video of a hike, an ad for jeans, your friend’s makeup routine, brunch pics, an ad for blush. Video ads felt more premium, took up the whole screen, and were thus far more lucrative for the social platforms.

With apologies to the short, brilliant life of Vine, the six-second video platform that helped invent so much about the video-first social network, it wasn’t until TikTok took off that things really turned again. The platform launched in the US in 2018, but had been popular for a few years in China as Douyin and elsewhere as Musical.ly. TikTok combined the vertical-first format of Stories with the permanence of YouTube, but it also made video easier than ever. It had filters like Instagram and Snapchat, but also supplied a steady stream of video ideas through the platform’s many trends, offered access to music and sound effects, and made it easy to stitch or duet a video.

By defaulting to the purely algorithmic For You page, TikTok also freed creators from caring about curating their profile or worrying about posting too much — you could just pump out videos and trust the algorithm to deliver them. And so that’s what people did. Pretty quickly, TikTok became one of the fastest growing apps on the planet, and its daily usage numbers became the envy of the industry. Instagram may have had more users, but TikTok users spent far more time TikToking.

When TikTok became a phenomenon, just about everyone jumped on the vertical video bandwagon. Reels launched in 2020 and became a core feature of both Instagram and Facebook; YouTube created Shorts a year later. By the end of 2021, Twitter had both launched and killed a similar feature called Fleets. By this point, this kind of full-screen, vertical-scrolling video was part of the lingua franca of the smartphone. At the same time, in a search for ever more engagement, these platforms were learning another lesson from TikTok: to stop relying on your friends to post interesting content, and instead to show you whatever the algorithm thinks you might like. Social networks were gone, replaced by social media — entertainment with a comments section.

How it’s going

Short-form, vertical video has effectively won the internet. Business is booming, and viewers show no sign of tuning out. Meta said in 2024 that Instagram users were spending more than half their time in Reels, and said in 2025 the feature was turning into a $50 billion annual business across Meta’s apps. About 63 percent of young adults and teens are on TikTok, per Pew Research Center, and one in five teens reported being on the app “almost constantly.” YouTube reported 200 billion daily views of Shorts at the end of 2025, and said that Shorts earned more money per watch hour than standard YouTube videos.

The last three or four years have been about relentless standardization in social media. The pace with which these products copy each other, and regress back toward parity, has been absolutely astonishing. First, Shorts and Reels both aped TikTok’s design, its duetting and stitching, and its close relationship with sounds and music. Then they bought into TikTok’s idea of prioritizing content over connection — followers are dead, long live the algorithm. TikTok pushed hard into shopping, then suddenly Reels and Shorts became a lot more shoppable. YouTube began to grow on TVs, and suddenly TikTok and Instagram started investing in its own TV apps. Videos got longer and longer across platforms, to allow more ads. All the apps got really into livestreaming for a while. And micro dramas. They’ve relentlessly copied each other on big things like letting users control their algorithm, and small things like Clear Mode.

There are two reasons for the ongoing onslaught of short-form vertical video: time spent and advertising. The endlessly scrolling video feed turns out to be one of the most engrossing forms of entertainment ever devised (to the point that it has become a regulatory problem for the social platforms), and in a relentless competition for eyeballs and attention, it has become everyone’s best idea. In 2024, when Meta switched its default video player to a vertical-first layout across all platforms, the race was officially won.

Meanwhile, as those platforms have captured more of our time and attention, short-form video has become a dominant force of advertising on the internet, which means advertisers are already comfortable making ads designed to go between videos in the feed. And as so many companies turn to AI to do their ad targeting, all they really need is the creative to get started. “So long as clients give us different assets — a six-second ad, a 15-second ad, a long-format, a vertical ad — AI is essentially powering everything else,” YouTube’s Brian Albert told me last year. “From the audiences you’re reaching, to the contextual placements, to the ad that’s actually showing.” The combination of AI and vertical video has become a self-fulfilling prophecy: The more it wins, the easier it becomes for everyone else to get on board, and so it just keeps winning.

What happens next

Vertical video haters, I have bad news: It’s only going to get worse. TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram are if anything going to become more short-form and vertical, since those short videos are easier to make and easier to load into endlessly scrolling feeds. Video services used to require you to pick something and press play, but now all they need is for you to open the app and they can start showing you ads. They’re not going to want to go back. Here’s how dominant video is: Facebook is testing a new version of the app that loads a full-screen video feed when you open the app. If that happens, there will be no Facebook — only Reels. After all this time, they’ve trained users to want and expect this kind of fast-paced, instant-gratification entertainment, to the point where even a full-length movie can feel like a chore.

Meanwhile, after years of raising prices, streaming services around the world are hoping they can turn to advertising to keep growing. For a while, they could coast on the back of linear TV, borrowing those ads to run on digital platforms. But a TikTok ad won’t make any sense on Netflix, so Netflix decided the best thing to do is build something that looks more like TikTok. A recent HubSpot report found that short-form video was by a wide margin both the most-used and most successful form of marketing content in 2025, and that it was the format in which marketers planned to invest the most this year.

All that said, there are glimmers of a bigger shift beginning to happen. Fed up with the algorithm, some users are starting to demand the return of friends and family in social media. But more broadly, more and more young people are deciding to put down their phones, resist the invasion of AI into their lives, and look for different kinds of entertainment. Movie theaters are having a big year; one of the year’s most exciting new phones is a flip phone. As long as we live in this era of social media and entertainment, vertical video is going to win. It would take a cultural revolution to stop it — and there might just be one brewing.

By the way

The best way to understand TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat in particular right now is as a combination of two things: a streaming service and an inbox. Studies have found that the most popular thing to do is watch videos, and the second most popular thing is to send videos to someone else. Actually posting? Way down the list. (YouTube, by the way, is desperately trying to make DMs happen .)

If you’ve made it this far and you’re thinking, no way, you’re way overstating it? I’m so sorry to say this, but you might just be old. At this point, YouTube and Facebook cross generations and demographics, but Pew and others have found that TikTok, Snapchat, and Instagram are effectively ubiquitous among young people in particular.

It’s important to remember that views are lies . Everyone on the internet has an incentive to make their platform seem big and vibrant and popular, and they will invent whatever new metrics they need to do so.
